# Preface

## About this book

A pada is a short song sung in kirtana; at its close the poet usually names himself (the signature, *bhanita*). Sri
Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (1486–1533) was surrounded by poets: Vasu, Madhava and Govinda Ghosha sang before Him in Navadvipa
and Puri, and Narahari Sarkar, Murari Gupta, Ramananda Vasu and others made songs about His lilas while He was still
present. These padas are the earliest witnesses to the Lord in Bengali, and in them one hears the living voice of His
companions: the rapture of the Navadvipa kirtanas, the grief of Nadia after the sannyasa, the longing for Nilachala.

The padas lie scattered through later anthologies. We have gathered those which research (above all Bimanbihari
Majumdar, *Sri-Chaitanya-chariter upadan*, ch. 2) assigns to Mahaprabhu's contemporaries, established their text from
several editions and translated them into Russian and English — 754 padas in all. The book has three parts.

- **Part I. Padas of the Contemporaries** (chapters 1–16) — the core of the collection: padas signed by the Lord's
  contemporaries, from the *Padakalpataru*, the *Bhakti-ratnakara*, the *Gaura-pada-tarangini* and other collections;
  first the padas Majumdar dates to the Lord's lifetime, then by poets and themes.
- **Part II. Appendix: Padas Signed "Narahari" from the Gaura-pada-tarangini** (chapters 17–26). Two poets sang
  under this name: Narahari Sarkar of Srikhanda, the Lord's companion, and Narahari Chakravarti (18th c.), author of the
  *Bhakti-ratnakara*. Whose each pada is, is stated in its heading; how we distinguish the two poets is explained in the
  introductory note to chapter 17.
- **Part III. Nagari Padas** (chapters 27–34) — songs in which the women of Nadia speak of Gaura in amorous feeling
  (*nagari-bhava*). They are translated in full and faithfully to their authors, but the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition —
  Vrindavana Dasa, Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati — does not accept the worship of Gaura in this
  mood: Gaura is Krishna Himself in the mood and lustre of Radha, come to taste Her love as a devotee, not to enjoy. This
  is set out in the introductory note to chapter 27, and every sharp passage has a short note. Concluding notes to the
  section stand at the end of chapters 33 and 34.

## Sources

The text of the padas is established from editions in the public domain; where a pada is found in several
collections, the base text follows the oldest or most correct one, and the variants are given in the notes and in the
Russian full edition.

- **PK** — *Padakalpataru* of Gokulananda Sena (Vaishnavadasa), 18th c.; ed. Satishchandra Ray, Bangiya Sahitya
  Parishat, 1915–1931, vols. 1–5 (the pada number is the running number of this edition; a "pallava" is its section).
  Ray records manuscript readings; their sigla are in the list of abbreviations.
- **BR** — *Bhakti-ratnakara* of Narahari Chakravarti (18th c.); eds. 1888, 1912/1913, 1960 (Gaudiya Mission), 2006.
  Its chapters are "waves" (*taranga*).
- **GPT1, GPT2** — *Gaura-pada-tarangini*, compiled by Jagadbandhu Bhadra: 1st ed. 1903, 2nd ed. 1934.
- **PS** — *Padamrita-samudra* of Radhamohana Thakura (18th c.); ed. 1878.
- **KGC** — *Kshanada-gita-chintamani* of Vishvanatha Chakravarti (17th–18th c.); ed. 1925.
- **GCC** — *Gaura-charita-chintamani* of Narahari Chakravarti; ed. Haridasa Dasa, 1947. Its chapters are "kiranas"
  (rays).
- **GCd** — *Gita-chandrodaya* of Narahari Chakravarti; ed. 1948.

For dating and attribution we have consulted Majumdar, but his arguments are given only briefly, in our own words; the
editors' prefaces and notes are not translated.

## Principles of the translation

**Faithfulness to the author.** Each pada is translated as it stands — line for line, without rhyme, keeping the
song's images and tone; nothing is added and nothing softened. Where an author speaks otherwise than the Gaudiya
Vaishnava tradition teaches, the translation stays exact and a note explains how the passage is to be understood. The
measure of interpretation is Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati.

**Theology.** The Lord is not subject to maya (His "maya" is yogamaya, His internal energy); He is not born but
appears; the Deity is the Lord Himself, not an image; the prema of Radha and the gopis and the Lord's bhava are not
worldly passion. Pronouns referring to the Lord are capitalised (Me, My, Mine; "I" is unchanged), also in His own
speech and in speech in the mood of Radha.

**Attribution and authority.** The heading of each pada gives its source, its lila and, where needed, its attribution.
We grade the reliability of the attribution on a scale A–D:

- **A** — a contemporary of the Lord with a reliable signature (confirmed by several witnesses or by Majumdar);
- **B** — a recognised later author of established authorship (above all the padas of Narahari Chakravarti from his
  BR, GCC and GCd: a later poetic elaboration of the lila accepted by the tradition), or a contemporary with a probable
  but not certain attribution;
- **C** — author not established or attribution disputed (the pada is known only from GPT, the signatures differ
  between sources, it is unclear which of the two Naraharis is meant);
- **D** — authenticity doubtful (a forgery, an anachronism, another's couplet bearing the signature).

The heading marks "**probably Sarkar**", "**probably Chakravarti**", "**not established**" concern the padas signed
"Narahari" and say to which of the two poets we incline.

**Numbering.** The padas in each chapter are numbered; a couplet (in a tripadi, a stanza) is marked "pada.couplet":
**1.1**, **1.2**, … **2.1**. The refrain (*dhruva*) is marked "(Refrain)" and counts as a separate unit; the kirtana
singers' insertions in some padas of Lochana Dasa are given in brackets. Notes are numbered within each chapter; a
reference "ch. 22, no. 7" means pada 7 of chapter 22, "n. 36 of chapter 22" — note 36 of that chapter. Labels like
VG-…, NG-…, NS-…, LD-… are the numbers of our working catalogue of padas (from the initials of the poet or section);
they are kept in the notes so that a pada can be found in the project materials.

**Transliteration.** Bengali words are given in IAST, with the inherent vowel written in full; ব is rendered *v*
(but *b* in the clusters ম্ব, ব্দ, ব্ধ, ব্জ), ঁ is *m̐*, ং is *ṃ*, ড় is *ṛ*, য় is *y*.

## How to read the full version

The book appears in two forms. The **standard** version gives the translation with notes. In the **full** version
each couplet is preceded by:

1. the Bengali original (medieval spelling; Vrajabuli as in the source);
2. a transliteration in IAST;
3. a word-for-word translation;
4. the translation.

The readings of the witnesses are recorded in the notes; their full apparatus appears in the Russian full edition.

## Abbreviations

- **CC** — *Chaitanya-charitamrita* of Krishnadasa Kaviraja (Adi, Madhya, Antya — its parts; the number is the chapter).
- **CB** — *Chaitanya-bhagavata* of Vrindavana Dasa (Adi, Madhya, Antya).
- **Murari** — *Sri-Krishna-Chaitanya-charitamrita* (*Kadacha*) of Murari Gupta (prakrama.sarga.verse).
- **Lochana** — *Chaitanya-mangala* of Lochana Dasa (Sutra-, Adi-, Madhya-, Antya-khanda; references follow the parts
  of our translation).
- **GGD** — *Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika* of Kavi Karnapura.
- *Bhag.* — *Srimad-Bhagavatam* (canto.chapter.verse).
- **BRS** — *Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu* of Rupa Gosvami.
- **PK, BR, GPT1, GPT2, PS, KGC, GCC, GCd** — see "Sources".
- **PVP** — *Prachina vaishnava padavali*, vol. 1, collected by Chandranatha Bandyopadhyaya, 1922 (a late anthology,
  not an independent witness).
- **M.**, **Majumdar** — Bimanbihari Majumdar, *Sri-Chaitanya-chariter upadan*; **M-1961** — a reference to its pages
  and pada numbers (ed. 1961).
- **ka, kha, gha, cha** (ক, খ, ঘ, চ) — manuscripts of PK in S. Ray's apparatus; **P-R-Sa** (প-র-সা) — the manuscript
  of the Bangiya Sahitya Parishat.
- **VG-, NG-, NS-, LD-** etc. — numbers of the working catalogue of padas.
- **IA** — Internet Archive (identifier of a scan).
- **sect.** — a section of GPT (e.g. sect. 3.2); **no.** — the number of a pada in a GPT section or in PK; **pallava**,
  **wave**, **kirana** — sections of PK, BR, GCC.
- **ch.**, **no.**, **n.** — chapter, pada, note of this book.

# Part I. Padas of the Contemporaries

---

# Chapter 1. Padas Dated to the Lord's Lifetime (after Majumdar)

*Padas by Sri Chaitanya's companions which Bimanbihari Majumdar (*Sri-Chaitanya-chariter upadan*, ch. 2) assigns to the
Lord's lifetime, arranged in the order of events: from Nimai's journey to East Bengal, through the Navadvipa kirtanas of
1509 and the sannyasa, to the first years of separation (the padas of the Puri period follow in the next chapter). The text follows the *Padakalpataru* (PK), the *Bhakti-ratnakara* (BR) and
the *Gaura-pada-tarangini* (GPT); the Bengali original, variants and word-for-word translation are in the full version of the book.*

## 1. Govinda Ghosha — "gorā gelā pūrvadeśa…" (PK 1597)
*Lila: Vishvambhara in East Bengal; in Navadvipa His dear ones pine for Him. According to Majumdar it was composed while
the Lord was away, before Gaya: if so, it is the earliest surviving pada about Gaura. Raga pahida.*[^01-1]

**1.1.** Gora has gone to the Eastern land, and His own people, in anguish,
lament in so many ways.
Devi Lakshmipriya weeps — to hear it the heart breaks;
broad day is darkness to her.[^01-2]

**1.2.** *(Refrain)* Hari, Hari! Separation from Gauranga cannot be borne!
Once more we shall see Gora's face, and the sorrow will go —
if only life holds out till then.

**1.3.** Hearing Shachi's piteous weeping, every living being weeps;
Malini consoles her.[^01-3]
The townswomen of Nadia weep without cease;
neither clothes nor ornaments please them.

**1.4.** When, going to the bank of the Suradhuni, shall we see Gauranga on the way —
after how many days will that auspicious day come?
We shall hear the words of His moonlike face, and the burning soul will be cooled…
Govinda Ghosha's body is wasting away.

[^01-1]: Govinda Ghosha was the eldest of the three Ghosha brothers (Govinda, Madhava, Vasudeva), kirtana singers of the
Lord (CC Adi 10, Madhya 13). The journey to East Bengal: CB Adi 14, CC Adi 16, Murari 1.11.5–16, Lochana
(lochana/en/20.md, vv. 61–103). Majumdar's argument: the pada has no hint of Nimai's divinity or of kirtana — the poet
knows Him only as a youth he has seen on the bank of the Ganga; such simplicity is natural only in verses made before the
change at Gaya. In PK the pada stands as a gaura-chandrika (prelude) to the section on "distant separation" (Krishna's
departure for Mathura).
[^01-2]: Lakshmipriya was the Lord's first wife. According to CB (Adi 14) and Murari (1.11.17–20), while the Lord was in East
Bengal she left this world, bitten by the "serpent of separation"; the pada finds her still alive, pining for her husband.
[^01-3]: Malini, the wife of Srivasa Pandita, was a close friend of Shachi.

## 2. Vasu Ghosha — "śaṅkha dundubhi-nāda…" (BR, p. 893; PK 1536)
*Lila: the abhisheka-bathing of the Lord in Srivasa's house (the mahaprakasha), 1509. According to Majumdar, the song of
an eyewitness; raga bhupali (PK), suhai (BR).*[^01-4]

**2.1.** Conchs and the roll of kettledrums sound melodiously:
the companions perform the abhisheka of Gorachand.

**2.2.** Fragrant sandal on the stone, incense, lamps alight;
the women of the town bring platters of arghya.[^01-5]

**2.3.** All the people of Nadia look on and rejoice;
again and again they cry "Jaya, jaya!" and sing songs.

**2.4.** All gaze upon the face of Gorachand;
Vasu Ghosha sings the sweetness of Gora's abhisheka.

[^01-4]: Vasudeva (Vasu) Ghosha was the youngest of the Ghosha brothers and the most prolific of Gaura's singers. The great
bathing of the Lord in Srivasa's house: CB Madhya 9; Murari 2.12; Lochana (*Chaitanya-mangala*, Madhya-khanda, part 9, vv. 93–113); Karnapura,
*Chaitanya-chandrodaya*, act 1. In the *Bhakti-ratnakara* (wave 12) Narahari Chakravarti cites precisely this pada as an
eyewitness's testimony, though he had Murari, CB and CC to hand — and on this Majumdar rests its early date. In PK it
stands as a gaura-chandrika to the snana-yatra (the bathing of Jagannatha at the full moon of Jyeshtha).
[^01-5]: Arghya is a respectful offering of water (with flowers, rice and durva grass). Majumdar notes that the pada keeps a
detail the biographies pass over — the part women took in the rite.

## 3. Vasu Ghosha — "taila haridrā āra kuṅkuma kastūrī…" (PK 1537)
*Lila: the same abhisheka — the anointing, bathing and dressing of the Lord. Raga varadi.*[^01-6]

**3.1.** Oil, turmeric, kunkuma and musk
the women, one after another, apply to Gora's body.

**3.2.** Bringing scented water, they fill the pitchers
and mix fragrant sandal and other things into it.

**3.3.** Crying "Jaya, jaya!" they pour the water over Gora's body;
wiping the holy body, someone dresses Him in garments.

**3.4.** Behold, in the bathing pavilion — Gora, king of dancers!
With joy at heart Vasudeva Ghosha sings.

[^01-6]: In PK (and in GPT1) this pada follows directly on the preceding one; Majumdar assigns it to the same abhisheka of
1509 (PK 1536, 1537, 1571 — the "historical" padas of Vasu Ghosha). "King of dancers" (nata-raya) is a frequent name
for Gaura, the leader of the dancers in kirtana, among the kirtana poets.

## 4. Govinda, Madhava and Vasu Ghosha — "vasilā gaurāṅgacandra ratna-siṃhāsane…" (PK 1538)
*Lila: after the abhisheka the Lord on the throne: the feast, Shachi's arati, the worship of the devotees. Signed by all
three Ghosha brothers.*[^01-7]

**4.1.** Gaurangachandra sat upon the jewelled throne;
Srivasa Pandita anoints His body with sandal.

**4.2.** Gadadhara placed a garland of malati on His neck;
by the radiance of His beauty all ten directions were lit.

**4.3.** Many offerings, every kind of sweet dish
He ate, sitting together with Nityananda.

**4.4.** Having chewed tambula, He sat on the throne again;
Shachi-devi came together with Malini.

**4.5.** Lighting the five-wicked lamp, she performed arati,
waved [the flame] round Him and placed paddy and durva on His head.[^01-8]

**4.6.** At that moment all shower Him with flowers;
Advaita Acharya offers tulasi and sandal.

**4.7.** Gods and men come together to see it;
Nityananda, sitting at His right, watches with delight.

**4.8.** This is the matchless lila of Gora's abhisheka:
Govinda, Madhava and Vasu floated away in prema.

[^01-7]: Majumdar cites this pada together with the preceding ones as a description of the same abhisheka in Srivasa's
house; from the signature "Govinda, Madhava, Vasu" (as in Vasu Ramananda) he infers that Govinda was the eldest. The
Lord sitting on Vishnu's throne in Srivasa's house, accepting offerings and receiving the devotees' worship: CB Madhya 9;
CC Adi 17.
[^01-8]: Paddy (dhanya) and durva grass placed on the head are a Bengali mother's blessing.

## 5. Ramachandra — "pahu mora gaurāṅga rāya…" (BR, p. 919; PK 2186)
*Lila: the Lord in Navadvipa in the mood of Radha, with Gadadhara and Narahari beside Him. According to Majumdar, the
song of an eyewitness (Narahari Chakravarti cites it as testimony). Raga shri (PK), suhai (BR).*[^01-9]

**5.1.** *(Refrain)* My Lord is Gauranga Raya,
whose glories Shiva, Shuka and Brahma sing!

**5.2.** He for whom Kamala ever pines,[^01-10]
that very Lord raises His arms, weeps and cries out, "Hari!"

**5.3.** The body at whose sight Kamadeva became bodiless[^01-11]
is now ever grey with the dust of kirtana.

**5.4.** Now and again He starts up, crying, "Radha, Radha!" —
Gadadhara and Narahari stand gazing at His face.

**5.5.** His body thrills with the deep love of former days.
Says Ramachandra: who would not understand this play?

[^01-9]: Who this Ramachandra was is unclear: Majumdar rejects Ramachandra Puri, Ramachandra the brahmana and Ramachandra
Khan, and suggests Ramachandra Kaviraja of Nityananda's branch (not Narottama's friend, whom Narahari Chakravarti would
not have passed off as an eyewitness). In BR (wave 12) the pada stands among testimonies to the Navadvipa pastimes,
directly after Govinda Ghosha's pada on the Lord's dancing with Narahari. Narahari Sarakara Thakura (of Shrikhanda) was a
singer of Gaura's moods; Majumdar confirms his presence with the Lord in Navadvipa from the padas of other
contemporaries. Cf. CC Adi 17 (Radha's mood in Navadvipa).
[^01-10]: Kamala is Lakshmi, the consort of Narayana. Here she is only mentioned as longing for the Lord; cf. *Bhag.* 10.16.36
(Lakshmi longs for the dust of Krishna's feet).
[^01-11]: The Lord's beauty put Kama (Kamadeva, the god of love) to shame, and he was as if bereft of his body (Ananga, "the
Bodiless", is his name). The "love of former days" (v. 5.5) is Radha's love for Krishna, which the Lord tastes in the
form of Gaura. BR reads: "He gazes at the faces of Narahari and Gadadhara."

## 6. Murari Gupta — "gadādhara-aṅge pahu aṅga helāiyā…" (BR, p. 922; PK 2121)
*Lila: the Lord in Radha's mood, leaning on Gadadhara, listens to the song of Vrindavana. According to Majumdar, composed in
1509 under the immediate impression of Nimai's moods. Raga patamanjari (PK), kamoda (BR).*[^01-12]

**6.1.** Leaning His body against Gadadhara,
the Lord is lost in the song of Vrindavana's glories.

**6.2.** Now He laughs, now He weeps, unaware of the outer world;
in Radha's mood His heart is restless — Gokula comes to His mind.

**6.3.** The grace of His form surpasses countless Kamadevas;
millions of moons weep to see His face.

**6.4.** The three worlds melt in the rasa of these two.[^01-13]
I know not for what fault Murari Gupta is left without it.

[^01-12]: Murari Gupta, the Lord's companion from childhood, wrote the Sanskrit biography (the "Kadacha"); apart from it only
a few Bengali padas are his. Narahari Chakravarti cites this one in BR (wave 12) among eyewitness testimonies.
Majumdar's argument: the pada was written in 1509, when Nimai's moods were still new; the signature of the poet, lamenting
that he himself is "deprived" of this rasa, is an eyewitness's humility. Cf. CC Adi 17.
[^01-13]: "These two" are Gaura and Gadadhara. According to the *Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika* (vv. 147–153) Gadadhara Pandita is a
manifestation of Radha in Gaura's lila; the Lord, Himself in Radha's mood, remembers Gokula beside him.

## 7. Paramananda (Gupta) — "gorā-tanu dhūlāya loṭāya…" (PK 2120)
*Lila: in Navadvipa the Lord, dressed as Natavara (Krishna the dancer), calls for Radha and asks for the flute; the
companions caution the singers. According to Majumdar, an eyewitness's testimony from 1509. Raga kalyani.*[^01-14]

**7.1.** *(Refrain)* Gora's body rolls in the dust.
Embracing Gadadhara, He calls, "Radha, Radha!" —
and asks for the yellow garment and the flute.

**7.2.** Dressed as Natavara, His hair bound up in front
and a peacock feather shining in it,
standing thrice-bent, He cries again and again, "Hari!" —
and Gora looks about for the kadamba branch.

**7.3.** Hearing of Vrindavana's glories, His mind maddened with rasa, [He asks,]
"Where have the sakhis gone, alas?"
Not grasping His mood, all the dear companions
sing His glories, calling Him "Gauranga".

**7.4.** And someone says, "Take care! Do not sing songs of rasa:
if [prema] surges up, the earth will not hold it!"
In the joy of his heart says Paramananda:
"Who then will keep life in the body?"

[^01-14]: The signature is "Paramananda". S. Ray ascribed the padas bearing it to Kavi Karnapura (Paramananda Sena); Majumdar
separates six Vrajabuli padas by a certain Paramananda of Vrindavana and gives the rest, this and the next among them, to
Paramananda Gupta, in whose house Nityananda stayed (CB, Antya-khanda) — Karnapura was not yet born in 1509. His argument for
the date: only a close companion could know the detail "do not sing songs of rasa", and the Lord did not wear the
Natavara dress in Puri — hence Navadvipa. The attribution to Paramananda Gupta is Majumdar's conjecture. Cf. Murari
2.15.3 (the Lord asks for His flute).

## 8. Paramananda (Gupta) — "śacīra nandana gorācānda…" (PK 2528)
*Lila: in Navadvipa the Lord in the mood of new love (anuraga); the same mood overcomes His companions. According to
Majumdar, an eyewitness's pada.*[^01-15]

**8.1.** Shachi's son, Gorachand,
is the enchanting snare of all the worlds.

**8.2.** In the mood of new love He is lost to Himself:
incessantly tears flow from His lotus eyes.

**8.3.** His body is full of thrills, His speech falters;
now He steadies His heart, now He is utterly unsettled.

**8.4.** Likewise the companions with Him are overcome [by this mood].
Says Paramananda: these are waves of prema.

[^01-15]: Only in PK, as a gaura-chandrika to the section "anuraga". Majumdar regards this pada too as an eyewitness's: in it
the Lord's mood overcomes His companions as well. (In the catalogue the first line of this pada had been given wrongly,
from a line of a different, neighbouring song.)

## 9. Vasu Ghosha — "cām̐cara cikura cūṛā cāru bhāle…" (BR, pp. 934–935)
*Lila: Nimai in the dress of Natavara (Krishna the dancer), 1509. According to Majumdar, something seen with his own eyes.
Raga kamoda.*[^01-16]

**9.1.** His curling hair is bound in a topknot above the lovely brow
and wound with a garland of malati;

**9.2.** in it is set a peacock feather
and a flowering sprig with its leaves.

**9.3.** His body outshines assayed gold,
about His waist is a bright-coloured cloth;

**9.4.** a sandal tilaka shines on His brow,
a garland of forest flowers hangs to His knees.

**9.5.** Gorachand in the dress of Natavara —
what a snare for the women!

**9.6.** Seeing this, Vasudeva weeps:
my heart can find no rest.

[^01-16]: This and the next two padas of Vasu Ghosha are known only from the *Bhakti-ratnakara* (wave 12): Narahari
Chakravarti introduces them as songs composed at the very places in Navadvipa that are shown to Srinivasa Acharya on
his circuit of Navadvipa ("here, under this kadamba, Gora, dressed as Natavara and standing thrice-bent, played the
flute"). Majumdar takes them as describing what was seen with one's own eyes in 1509. "A snare for the women" (9.5) is a
poetic image of the Lord's irresistible beauty (Krishna the Natavara captivates the gopis); Vrindavana Dasa stresses that
in this incarnation the Lord never so much as glanced at another man's wife, and the Gaudiya tradition does not accept
the worship of Gaura in the spirit of "Gaura-nagari".

## 10. Vasu Ghosha — "soṅari puruva-līlā tribhaṅga hailā…" (BR, p. 935)
*Lila: Gora, remembering His former lila, plays the flute on the bank of the Ganga. Raga dhanashi.*[^01-17]

**10.1.** Remembering His former lila, He stood thrice-bent,
and Gora raised the enchanting flute to His lips.

**10.2.** Gorachand blew into the flute's opening
and, moving His fingers, played a most lovely song.

**10.3.** All the townspeople are enchanted to hear it;
on the bank of the Suradhuni the trees and creepers thrill.

**10.4.** What can Vasudeva Ghosha say of it?
With the song of His flute Gora enchanted the world.

[^01-17]: Cf. Murari 2.15.3 (the Lord asks for His flute); CC Adi 17 (the Lord in Krishna's mood in Navadvipa). The pada is
also in GPT2.

## 11. Vasu Ghosha — "pūrvalīlā gorācām̐dera manete paṛila…" (BR, p. 935)
*Lila: the goshtha-lila in Navadvipa — the Lord in the mood of a cowherd boy calls the cows; with Him are Nityananda,
Ramai, Sundarananda, Gauridasa. Raga tori.*[^01-18]

**11.1.** His former lila came to Gorachand's mind,
and He began to call aloud: "Shangali! Dhavali!"

**11.2.** Sounding horn, venu and murali in triumph,
shouting "hai, hai!" He keeps twirling the cowherd's stick.

**11.3.** Ramai, Sundara, and Nityananda with them,
Gauridasa and all the others were filled with bliss.

**11.4.** With joy at heart Vasudeva Ghosha says:
Gorachand has revealed the goshtha-lila.

[^01-18]: Shangali and Dhavali are names of Krishna's cows ("the dark one", "the white one"); venu and murali are kinds of flute.
Sundara is Sundarananda; Gauridasa Pandita (of Ambika-Kalna) — companions of Nityananda, cowherd boys of Vraja according
to the *Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika* (Gauridasa is Subala). "Ramai" is probably Abhirama (Ramadasa), the cowherd Shridama
according to GGD; the identification is not certain. Majumdar's argument: this pada explains why Nityananda's companions
lived in the mood of cowherds (as CB describes) — they had seen the Lord's goshtha-lila.

## 12. Vamshivadana — "śacīra nandana gorā o cām̐da-vayāne…" (PK 2564)
*Lila: the same goshtha-lila: Nityananda sounds the horn, Gauridasa and Abhirama come running. According to Majumdar, more
detailed than Vasu's and bearing "the stamp of an eyewitness"; 1509. Raga bhatiyari.*[^01-19]

**12.1.** Gora, the son of Shachi, with that moonlike mouth
calls again and again: "Dhavali! Shangali!"

**12.2.** Understanding where His mood is leading, Nityananda Raya
sounds a call with His mouth, imitating a horn.

**12.3.** Hearing the horn-call from Nitaichand's mouth,
the devotees fall senseless with prema.

**12.4.** Up ran the pandita whose name is Gauridasa,
and Abhirama runs, crying, "Brother, brother!"

**12.5.** Seeing Gauranga's form, all are seized by prema:
on His head a topknot with a peacock feather, the dress of Natavara,

**12.6.** anklets ringing on His feet, sandal on all His limbs.
Says Vamshivadana: "Come, let us go to Govardhana!"

[^01-19]: Vamshivadana (Vamshi) was a companion of the Lord, and after the sannyasa the guardian of Vishnupriya and Shachi in
Navadvipa. In PK the pada is a gaura-chandrika to the section "going out to the pastures" (goshtha-gamana). Majumdar
notes that the pada explains why GGD calls Gauridasa Subala and Abhirama Shridama. He dates it to 1509 (the OCR of his
book has "1507", probably a misprint).

## 13. Vasu Ghosha — "gaurāṅgacām̐dera mane ki bhāva uṭhila…" (PK 1368; BR, pp. 935–936)
*Lila: the Lord in Krishna's mood remembers the dana-lila and "collects a toll" on the roads of Nadia. According to
Majumdar, seen with his own eyes, 1509. Raga suhai (PK), kamoda (BR).*[^01-20]

**13.1.** What a mood arose in Gaurangachand's heart!
In the midst of Nadia Gora set up a toll.

**13.2.** A toll of what rasa does Gora, the jewel of brahmanas, demand?
Barring the way with a cane, He holds back the young women.

**13.3.** "Pay the toll, pay the toll!" Gora calls,
and the women of the town were in a fix.

**13.4.** "In the Krishna-avatara I collected the toll" —
that mood came back to His mind, sings Vasu Ghosha.

[^01-20]: The dana-lila is Krishna's pastime of stopping the gopis, together with His cowherd friends, on their way to
Govardhana and demanding a "toll" for their milk and butter; it is a lila of pure prema, not of worldly passion. Here
the Lord, seized by Krishna's mood, re-enacts it: Majumdar sees in the pada the explanation of Gadadhara Dasa's mood
("who will buy Gora?"). The reading "taruṇī" ("young women", BR, PK) Majumdar holds correct, "taraṇī" ("boat", GPT) not.
Vrindavana Dasa stresses that in this incarnation the Lord never so much as glanced at another man's wife; the Gaudiya
tradition (Vrindavana Dasa, Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Bhaktisiddhanta) does not accept the worship of Gaura in the spirit
of "Gaura-nagari".

## 14. Shivananda Sena — "holi khelata gaurakiśora…" (BR, pp. 944–945)
*Lila: Holi in Navadvipa: the Lord in Krishna's mood with Gadadhara; Narahari sings of Vraja, Mukunda, Murari and Vasu
dance. According to Majumdar, apparently 1509. Raga kamoda; Vrajabuli.*[^01-21]

**14.1.** The youthful Gaura plays Holi;
in His embrace is Gadadhara, the beloved full of rasa.[^01-22]

**14.2.** Drops of sweat on His face, His body thrilling,
under the weight of the mood tears stream from His eyes.

**14.3.** They sing of the rasa of Vraja together with Narahari;
Mukunda, Murari and Vasu dance with delight.

**14.4.** Again and again He swoons in the Pandita's arms;
seeing it, the companions are lost in joy.

**14.5.** The Lord laid out a bower-temple,
falls to the ground and says: "Where is My flute?

**14.6.** Where is Govardhana, where the Yamuna's bank?
Where are the malati, yuthi and champaka flowers?"

**14.7.** Says Shivananda, hearing the Lord's words full of rasa:
where the Lord and Gadadhara are, there is a mine of rasa.

[^01-21]: Shivananda Sena of Kumarahatta was the father of Kavi Karnapura and later led the Gaudiya devotees to Puri every
year (CC Madhya 1, Antya 12). The pada is known from BR (wave 12) and GPT; it is not in PK. Its historical value,
according to Majumdar, is the list of the companions of the Navadvipa kirtanas; it is also confirmed by Vasu Ghosha's
pada on Holi with Gadadhara (BR, pp. 942–943). Holi (dola) is the spring festival of colours at the full moon of
Phalguna, the day of the Lord's appearance.
[^01-22]: "The beloved" (rasavati nari) is Gadadhara in Radha's mood (GGD 147: Gadadhara Pandita is Radha), and the Lord is
in Krishna's mood. This is the spiritual lila of Radha and Krishna remembered by the Lord and His companion, not a
worldly feeling.

## 15. Govinda Ghosha — "prāṇera mukunda he ki āji śunilum̐ ācambita…" (PK 1606)
*Lila: the first news that the Lord will leave Navadvipa; Gadadhara runs to Mukunda. According to Majumdar, late January
1510, a few days before the sannyasa. Raga pahida.*[^01-23]

**15.1.** *(Refrain)* "O Mukunda, dear as life! What have I suddenly heard today!
To say it, life departs; it will not leave my lips:
Sri Gauranga will leave Navadvipa!

**15.2.** We knew nothing. In the morning I came to Gora —
He sits with bowed head;
tears stream from His eyes and run in rivulets down His chest,
the moon of His face has grown pale.

**15.3.** Seeing this, my heart was at once in turmoil,
but there was no chance to ask.
After a moment He came to Himself; then I asked —
and, hearing me, He gave this answer.

**15.4.** And I, overwhelmed, saying nothing to Him,
ran to you.
So I have told you; do what you can —
I have no hope of living."

**15.5.** Hearing this, Mukunda weeps, his heart finds no rest,
as he looks into Gadadhara's face.
Says this Govinda Ghosha: may this not happen!
Or else I shall die.

[^01-23]: In PK the pada is headed "spoken by Pandita Gosvami", i.e. by Gadadhara Pandita: in the pada he tells Mukunda Datta
of the Lord's words, and Mukunda weeps looking into his face; the signature is Govinda Ghosha's. Majumdar takes the
heading as a tradition going back to Gadadhara himself and dates the pada to the end of January 1510. In PK it opens the
section "separation to come". Cf. CB Madhya 26, Murari 2.18.17–23: the devotees learn of the Lord's decision to take
sannyasa.

## 16. Govinda Ghosha — "hede re nadīyāvāsī kāra mukha cāo…" (PK 1622)
*Lila: the day the Lord leaves Navadvipa for sannyasa. According to Majumdar, written on that very day (1510). Raga
suhai.*[^01-24]

**16.1.** O people of Nadia! Whose face are you looking to?
Stretch out your arms — bring Gorachand back!

**16.2.** Who else will take you all into His arms?
Who, seeing the afflicted, will offer them prema unasked?

**16.3.** What a spear in the heart, alas, what a spear in the heart!
The darling of our life is leaving Navadvipa.

**16.4.** No more shall we go to Gauranga,
no more shall we delight in kirtana.

**16.5.** The devotees weep, their hearts breaking;
only stony Govinda Ghosha does not die.

[^01-24]: In PK the pada stands in the section "words of the devotees of Navadvipa in separation from Gaura". The Lord's
leaving home at night at the end of Magha 1510 and crossing the Ganga towards Katwa: CB Madhya 28, CC Adi 17, Murari
3.1.6–7.

## 17. Vamshi(vadana) — "āra nā heriva prasara kapāle…" (PK 1855)
*Lila: Navadvipa's grief after the sannyasa; the weeping of Shachi and Vishnupriya. According to Majumdar, soon after the
sannyasa (1510). Raga gandhara.*[^01-25]

**17.1.** No more shall I see on the broad brow
the adornment of curls and tilaka,
no more see on the golden lotus [of His face]
the dance of the wagtail eyes.

**17.2.** No more will He dance in Srivasa's house
with His chataka-bird devotees,
no more will He dance in His own house
for us to gaze at Him.

**17.3.** Will the two brothers, Nimai and Nitai,
ever dance together again?
I keep crying, "Nimai!" —
but Nimai is nowhere.

**17.4.** Pitiless Keshava Bharati came
and brought down a thunderbolt on our heads.
How, not seeing beautiful Gauranga,
shall I stay on in Nadia?

**17.5.** Who is there now to bring back
my Gaura Raya?
Hearing the weeping of mother-in-law and daughter-in-law,
Vamshi rolls in the dust.[^01-26]

[^01-25]: The signature is "Vamshi". The PK index ascribes the pada to Vamshidasa; Majumdar distinguishes Vamshidasa (a disciple
of Srinivasa Acharya, 17th century) from Vamshivadana and assigns this pada to Vamshivadana, who looked after Shachi and
Vishnupriya — hence the poet's grief at hearing "the weeping of mother-in-law and daughter-in-law". One manuscript
(according to GPT) has a signature of Vasu Ghosha, so the attribution is not beyond doubt. Keshava Bharati was the
sannyasi who gave the Lord sannyasa at Katwa; "pitiless" is the reproach of those who love, not a condemnation (cf. CB
Madhya 28).
[^01-26]: The mother-in-law and daughter-in-law are Shachi and Vishnupriya, the Lord's second wife.

## 18. Ramananda (Vasu) — "pāpī māghe pahum̐ kayala sannyāsa…" (PK 1711; GPT1, p. 390)
*Lila: longing for the Lord in the spring of 1510, soon after the sannyasa. According to Majumdar, written a few days
after the sannyasa. Raga suhai; Vrajabuli.*[^01-27]

**18.1.** In the accursed month of Magha my Lord took sannyasa —
and then my hope of life departed too.

**18.2.** Day by day my body wastes, my eyes stream;
how many days without Gora shall I keep my life?

**18.3.** Now it is spring, and all are happy —
yet this wretched, hard life will not leave me.

**18.4.** All the love my Lord showed me! —
I remember it, and my life hangs by a thread at my throat.[^01-28]

**18.5.** Says Ramananda: He is the lord of my life.
When shall I see Him again beside Gadadhara?

[^01-27]: The signature is "Ramananda". Majumdar (who knew the pada only from GPT) argues that this is not Ramananda Raya (who
did not know the Lord before the sannyasa and could not pine for Him beside Gadadhara) but Vasu Ramananda of Kulinagrama,
a descendant of Maladhara Vasu, Gunaraja Khan (CC Madhya 15). His argument for the date: "now it is spring" — the pada was made in
Phalguna–Chaitra, some weeks after the sannyasa taken at the end of Magha (January–February 1510). The reading "māghe"
("in Magha") is given by PK and GPT1; Majumdar (in the OCR of his book) has "māthe". In PK the pada is a gaura-chandrika to
the section "separation in spring".
[^01-28]: The reading "kaṇṭhahim̐ ḍora" follows the PK scan; in GPT the line is corrupt. The sense: life "has risen to the
throat" (is about to leave the body).

## 19. Shivananda Sena — "dayāmaya gaurahari naidyā-līlā sāṅga kari…" (GPT1, p. 382)
*Lila: from Shantipura the Lord leaves for Puri and tells the devotees of Gauda to come to Him once a year. According to
Majumdar, written right after the Lord's departure (1510). Raga mangala.*[^01-29]

**19.1.** Merciful Gaurahari, having ended the Nadia-lila —
alas, alas, what ill fate! —
my Lord has gone to Nilachala, leaving this servant alone:
my worldly bonds were not cut.

**19.2.** What You have commanded I shall surely carry out,
but how shall I live alone?
My sons and all my family will be like poison to me:
how shall I pass my days without You?

**19.3.** You told me to come to Nilachala
with the pilgrims of Gauda at the year's end, for darshana.
How shall I endure, how pass a whole year,
when a moment seems a hundred yugas?

**19.4.** Be merciful, Lord, grant me leave
to see Your feet every day.
If You do not command it, O Lord Vishvambhara,
Shivananda will take his own life.

[^01-29]: The pada is known only from GPT (signature "Shivananda"). Majumdar's argument: the words "my sons and all my family will be
like poison to me" and "how shall I live through the year until the next journey with the Gaudiyas" make sense only
directly after the Lord's departure from Shantipura for Puri; later, when the journeys had become a custom, they would
not have been written. The Lord's instruction to the devotees of Gauda to come to Puri every year: CC Madhya 3, CB Antya
1. "Will take his own life" is a hyperbole of separation, common in Bengali padas; cf. the devotees' threats to give up
their lives in separation from the Lord in CC (Madhya 3).

## 20. Narahari (Sarakara) — "sonā śatavāna jini gaurāṅga āmāra…" (PK 1729)
*Lila: the first chaturmasya after the sannyasa — the devotees do not know where the Lord is. According to Majumdar,
written during the first chaturmasya (1510). Raga suhai.*[^01-30]

**20.1.** My Gauranga outshines gold refined a hundred times —
what is a chamara whisk beside that thick mass of His hair?

**20.2.** Why did He shave His head, to what land has He gone?
In whose house is He spending this chaturmasya?

**20.3.** I remember and remember, and my heart breaks:
where has Gora Raya gone, dear as life itself?

**20.4.** The devotees weep and heave sighs;
Narahari Dasa cannot keep his patience.

[^01-30]: The signature is "Narahari Dasa". Narahari Sarakara Thakura of Shrikhanda was a companion of the Lord and a singer of
His moods; Majumdar assigns to him the padas in plain Bengali known from PK (not only from GPT). In PK the pada is a
gaura-chandrika to the section "separation in the rainy season"; Majumdar dates it to the first chaturmasya after the
sannyasa (1510), when the Lord was travelling in the South. According to CC (Madhya 9) He spent that chaturmasya at
Shrirangam, in the house of Venkata Bhatta.

## 21. Shivananda Sena — "jaya jaya paṇḍita gosāñi…" (PK 2355)
*Lila: Gadadhara Pandita gives up his vow to live in the Kshetra and his service of Gopinatha to follow the Lord to Gauda
(1514). According to Majumdar, composed at that very time. Raga patamanjari.*[^01-31]

**21.1.** Glory, glory to Pandita Gosani!
By the power of his mercy I sing Chaitanya's glories.

**21.2.** So does he love Gaurangachandra
that He is famed by the name "Lord of Gadadhara's life".

**21.3.** Who can understand the love of one whose life is given to Gaura,
who for His sake gave up life in the Kshetra and the service of Krishna?[^01-32]

**21.4.** Gadai's Gauranga, Gauranga's Gadadhara:
like Sri Rama and Janaki — one body.

**21.5.** As Radha and the Moon of Vrindavana are one soul,
so Gaura and Gadadhara are waves of one prema.

**21.6.** Says Shivananda: in love for Her the Lord,
dark of body, became golden and begs for prema.[^01-33]

[^01-31]: Gadadhara Pandita (Gadai) took in Puri the vow of kshetra-sannyasa (never to leave the Kshetra) and served the
Deity of Tota-Gopinatha. When in 1514 the Lord set out for Gauda (on His way to Vrindavana), Gadadhara followed Him,
abandoning both vow and service, and only at Cuttack did the Lord persuade him to go back — CC Madhya 16. Majumdar's
argument: later, knowing from CC that the Lord sent Gadadhara back, no one would have written "for His sake he gave up
life in the Kshetra" — the pada is contemporary with the event (1514/15).
[^01-32]: "The service of Krishna" is the service of the Deity Gopinatha in Puri.
[^01-33]: "In love for Her" — for Radha: Krishna (Shyama, the dark one) took on Radha's golden form to taste Her love.
Majumdar sees in the last verse an echo of Svarupa Damodara's teaching (CC Adi 1.5–6, 4). Gadadhara is Radha (GGD 147).

## 22. Vasu Ghosha — "ājukāra svapana-kathā śuna lo mālinī sai…" (BR, pp. 982–983)
*Lila: Shachi tells Malini her dream: Nimai, unable to stay in Nilachala, came home. According to Majumdar, an
eyewitness's pada from the years of separation (about 1514/15). Raga kamoda.*[^01-34]

**22.1.** Listen, friend Malini, to the dream I had today:
Nimai came home.
Standing in the courtyard, gazing and gazing at the house,
He called me: "Mother!"

**22.2.** I was lying in the house — and, beside myself, came out,
hearing Nimai's voice.
Nimai put the dust of His mother's feet on His head,
and weeps and weeps: "Mother!"

**22.3.** "Captive to your love, I wandered about —
I could not stay in Nilachala.
To see you I have come to Nadia" —
so He says, weeping.

**22.4.** "Come to me, my child!" — I lifted Him to my breast —
and at that moment sleep left me.
Not seeing Him again, how my heart aches!
The night passed in tears.

**22.5.** Weeping and weeping, Shachi fell fainting to the ground;
Malini wails aloud.
What can I say — alas, alas! — this pain cannot be borne:
why does Vasu not die?

[^01-34]: The pada is known from BR (wave 12): Narahari Chakravarti cites it in the account of Shachi's house, to which
Nityananda comes. Majumdar values this and the next pada as testimonies which the later biographers left out, as if they
"diminished" the sannyasa. Cf. CC Antya 3: the Lord says that He comes unseen to eat what Shachi cooks. *Addendum (chapter
05):* the same pada is found in PK — no. 2270 (vol. 3, PDF p. 293, printed p. 282; 21st pallava, raga vibhasa; MS
P-R-Sa no. 2374) and in GPT1 (p. 386, no. 11, raga pahida) — signed by Vasudeva Ghosha and with a different
last stanza: "Since then my soul weeps, my heart finds no rest: what shall I do, tell me, what way is there? Says Vasudeva
Ghosha: Gauranga is yours — otherwise would you always see Him?" Stanzas 22.1–22.4 in PK have minor variants (see
bn/01.md). PK 2268 "viraha-vikala māya…", which the stage-1 catalogue took for this pada (VG-138), is a pada of Premadasa.

## 23. Vasu Ghosha — "āola nadīyāra loka gaurāṅga dekhite…" (GPT1, p. 413)
*Lila: the sannyasi Chaitanya comes to Nadia (1514/15); the people of Navadvipa and Mother Shachi see Him. Raga shri.*[^01-35]

**23.1.** The people of Nadia came to see Gauranga:
their hearts so overwhelmed with joy they cannot walk.

**23.2.** Seeing Gorachand's face after so long,
their hungry chakora-eyes are intoxicated.

**23.3.** The devotees are lost in joy, gazing at Him;
the mother runs up and embraces Gorachand.

**23.4.** As if life had returned to a dying body:
Gauranga is in Nadia, sings Vasu Ghosha.

[^01-35]: The pada is in GPT (GPT1, p. 413, no. 31) and in PK — no. 1991 (vol. 3, PDF p. 190, section "The joy of all Vraja: first Navadvipa", raga shri, reading "dhāola" — "came running" for "āola" — "came"; established in chapter 4); it is not in BR. Majumdar sees in it a testimony to the coming of the sannyasi Lord
to the neighbourhood of Navadvipa on His way to Gauda (1514/15), told by Murari (4.14.3–11) and Lochana (Shesha-khanda);
CC (Madhya 1) and CB (Antya 3) speak of His stay at Kuliya, opposite Navadvipa. The chakora is a bird that, in poetic
tradition, feeds on moonlight.

## 24. Krishnadasa — "ṭhākura paṇḍitera vāṛī gorā nāce phiri phiri…" (PK 2358)
*Lila: the Lord and Nityananda at Ambika with Gauridasa Pandita; Gauridasa begs Them to stay, and the Lord tells him to
serve Their Deities. According to Majumdar, a contemporary testimony that the worship of the Lord's Deity began in His
lifetime. Raga bhatiyari.*[^01-36]

**24.1.** In Thakura Pandita's house Gora dances, whirling round;
Nityananda cries, "Hari, Hari!"
Weeping, Gauridasa falls at the Lord's feet and says:
"Never leave my house!

**24.2.** Grant my request — stay in Ambika:
this is my plea at Your feet.
If You go away, I shall surely die:
looking at whom shall I live then?

**24.3.** If You two brothers stay here with me,
then everyone will be delivered.
Again I pray: do not leave me, Gaurahari —
then I shall know that You are the saviour of the fallen."

**24.4.** The Lord says: "Gauridasa, give up such a wish:
serve My Deity and you will see —
I am present in it, know this for certain;
keep this true word of Mine."

**24.5.** Hearing this, Gauridasa heaved a long sigh
and again weeps aloud.
Again the two brothers console him,
yet his heart finds no rest.

**24.6.** Says lowly Krishnadasa, whose hope is Chaitanya's feet:
the two brothers stayed there.
Both were taken captive by Thakura Pandita's love —
hence They are sung as "loving to Their devotees".[^01-37]

[^01-36]: Krishnadasa was the younger brother of Gauridasa Pandita, of Nityananda's branch (according to Majumdar). Gauridasa
Pandita (here "Thakura Pandita") was a companion of Nityananda, Subala according to GGD; at Ambika-Kalna he served the
Deities of Gaura-Nitai. Cf. Murari 4.14.12–14. Majumdar's argument: the pada is a contemporary's testimony that the
worship of the Lord's Deity began in His lifetime. The next pada of PK (2359) continues the story.
[^01-37]: "The two brothers stayed there" — the Lord and Nityananda remained at Ambika in Their Deity forms, in which, by
Their own word, They Themselves are present: the Deity is not an image but the Lord Himself, manifest through the
devotee's love.

## 25. Chandrashekhara — "kṣaṇeka rahiyā caliyā uṭhiyā paṇḍita jagadānanda…" (PK 1854)
*Lila: Jagadananda Pandita comes from Nilachala to Navadvipa, to Shachi and Vishnupriya. According to Majumdar, written
"before one's eyes", in the Lord's lifetime.*[^01-38]

**25.1.** After pausing a while, Pandita Jagadananda
rose and went on.
Entering the town, he sees that in every house
all the people are joyless.

**25.2.** The shops are not open, no one eats,
no face has a smile.
The women of the town weep with stifled sobs,
sitting apart, alone.

**25.3.** Having seen the town, he went
and entered the Lord's house.
As if half dead, senseless,
Ai lies on the ground.[^01-39]

**25.4.** And the Lord's wife, forsaken,
having lost the Lord,
lies in faded clothes,
tears flowing from her closed eyes.

**25.5.** All the servants and maids are silent;
seeing the traveller,
they ask him: "Tell us now,
where have you come from?"

**25.6.** The Pandita says: "I have come
from Nilachala.
Beautiful Gauranga sent me
to see you all."

**25.7.** Hearing these words, with tearful eyes
they went and told Shachi,
and another set off at once
running to Srivasa's house.

**25.8.** Hearing it, Srivasa, Malini in delight,
and all the people of Navadvipa,
who had been as if dead, came running at once —
and, coming, came back to life.

**25.9.** Malini came and gently raised
Shachi and Vishnupriya
and told them: "The Pandita has come;
Gaurahari has sent him."

**25.10.** Hearing it, Mother Shachi looked up with a start
and saw the Pandita.
She says to him: "My Nimai —
how far off is He now?"

**25.11.** Seeing the utmost of love, the greatness of a mother's tenderness,
the Pandita says, weeping:
"That jewel Gora, I know, age after age
is subdued by your love."

**25.12.** Having told everyone
of Gauranga's ways and doings,
the Pandita stayed on in the town of Nadia,
giving joy to all.

**25.13.** Chandrashekhara, no better than a beast,
is fond of the poison of sense-objects:
to Gauranga's life, the supreme nectar,
his heart does not take.

[^01-38]: The signature is "Chandrashekhara"; by tradition (S. Ray) this is Chandrashekhara Acharya, the Lord's maternal
uncle; the attribution is traditional but not proven. In PK the pada continues the preceding one (PK 1853, signed
"Madhavi Dasa"), in which Jagadananda walks from Puri wondering whether he will find Shachi. Jagadananda's journeys to
Shachi at the Lord's bidding: CC Antya 12. Majumdar's argument: the restraint in mentioning the Lord's wife (her name is
not given — only "the Lord's wife") is a mark of a contemporary; Vrindavana Dasa does the same.
[^01-39]: Ai ("mother") — so Mother Shachi was called in Navadvipa.

## 26. Narahari (Sarakara) — "rase tanu ḍhara ḍhara gaurakiśora vara…" (PK 2259)
*Theme: the truth of Gaura — Shyama became Gaura to play with Radha; the poet fears to reveal the secret. According to
Majumdar, written before Svarupa Damodara's kadacha, i.e. in the Lord's lifetime. Raga pahida (GPT).*[^01-40]

**26.1.** The most excellent youthful Gaura, His body brimming with rasa —
His name is Sri Krishna Chaitanya.
To speak these hidden things pains the heart:
none but the devotees know them.

**26.2.** In the Dvapara-yuga Shyama, in Kali the name Chaitanya:
so Garga's words are written in the *Bhagavata*.[^01-41]
I have reasoned in my heart: Shyama has become Gauranga,
and the body of Radha and Krishna bears witness to it.[^01-42]

**26.3.** Within, the dark body; without, the golden:
wondrous is Chaitanya's lila!
To play with Rai and to share the rasa of the bowers,
out of love He became golden.

**26.4.** This is not to be told: tell it, and who knows what may happen;
leave it untold, and the heart burns.
Reasoning in his heart and holding Gauranga in his heart,
Narahari laments.

[^01-40]: The signature is "Narahari"; Majumdar assigns the pada to Narahari Sarakara. In PK it stands in the section on the
sannyasa, in GPT among the opening padas (mangalacharana). Majumdar's argument: this truth (Krishna became Gaura for
Radha's sake) was later set forth openly by Svarupa Damodara in his kadacha and after him by Krishnadasa Kaviraja (CC Adi
1.5–6, 4); the poet's fear of revealing the secret would be unintelligible after that — so the pada was written in the
Lord's lifetime.
[^01-41]: *Bhag.* 10.8.13: Garga, naming Krishna, says that in other yugas He took white, red and yellow colours, and now has
become dark (krishna). The Gaudiya tradition sees in the "yellow" (pita) a reference to Gaura.
[^01-42]: The reading "sāthī" (PK, GPT) means "companion"; the sense may require "sākhī" (witness). Within He is Shyama
(Krishna), without He is clad in Radha's golden radiance (cf. CC Adi 4).

---

# Chapter 2. Padas of the Puri Period

*Padas by contemporaries on the Lord's life in Puri after the sannyasa, in the order of events: the arrival in Nilachala
and Sarvabhauma's house, the darshan of Jagannatha, sankirtana on the seashore, Radha's mood in the company of Svarupa
Damodara and Ramananda Raya, the states of separation (dasha), the Gambhira, and the divine madness of prema
(divya-unmada). Majumdar (*Sri-Chaitanya-chariter upadan*, ch. 2) regards the Puri padas of Narahari Sarakara, Vasu Ghosha
and Vasu Ramananda as the testimony of those who came to the Lord every year with the pilgrims from Gauda. The text
follows the *Padakalpataru* (PK) and the *Gaura-pada-tarangini* (GPT1 — 1st ed., 1903; GPT2 — 2nd ed., 1934); the Bengali
original, variants and word-for-word translation are in the full version of the book.*

## 1. Madhavi Dasa — "kalaha kariyā chhalā…" (PK 2239)
*Lila: the arrival in Puri (1510). Making a quarrel His pretext, the Lord goes on ahead to Jagannatha; Nityananda and the
devotees follow His footprints; at the Lion Gate Nitai questions the people of Nilachala; the Lord enters the house of the
Bhattacharya (Sarvabhauma). Raga varadi (PK), suhai (GPT).*[^02-1]

**1.1.** Making a quarrel His pretext, the Lord went on ahead
to see the Lord of Nilachala.
All the devotees, their hearts full of grief,
run after Him, following His footprints.[^02-2]

**1.2.** *(Refrain)* Nitai, in the fire of separation, is as if in a daze.
From Atharanala, weeping and weeping on the road,
goes Nitai, the moon of avadhutas.[^02-3]

**1.3.** Coming to the Lion Gate, with pain in His heart,
Nityananda Raya stopped.
Crying "Hare Krishna, Hari!" He asks the people of Nilachala:
"Have you seen a sannyasi?

**1.4.** His golden form surpasses the gold of the Jambu river,
a red cloth shines on His body;
brimming with prema, He sheds tears from both eyes
and runs, crying 'Hari, Hari!'"[^02-4]

**1.5.** Leaving the dress of a nagara, the Lord wanders from land to land —
now He wears the garb of a sannyasi.
Madhavi Dasa says: the wondrous Gora Raya
has entered the house of the Bhattacharya.[^02-5]

[^02-1]: The signature in PK is "mādhavī dāsa" (Madhavi Dasa). Who this poet was is not established: Majumdar does not name
him among the contemporaries; some identify the poet with Madhavi Devi of Puri, the sister of Shikhi Mahiti, whom the
Lord counted among Radha's closest maidservants (CC Antya 2), but there is no proof — the attribution is doubtful. GPT1
and GPT2 give the same pada with different readings in almost every line and with another ending — the signature of
Govinda Dasa ("Govinda Dasa says: I saw His entry into Sarvabhauma's house"). In PK the pada opens the 21st pallava
("The sannyasa of Sri Gauranga, etc."). The events: CC Madhya 5–6; CB Antya 2; Murari 3.10–3.11; Lochana, Shesha-khanda.
[^02-2]: The "quarrel": according to CC (Madhya 5) and CB (Antya 2), Nityananda broke the Lord's sannyasa staff, and the
Lord, as if angered, went on ahead alone. The poet calls the quarrel a "pretext": the Lord Himself wished to come first
to Jagannatha (and to Sarvabhauma).
[^02-3]: Atharanala is the bridge of eighteen arches at the entrance to Puri; here, according to CC (Madhya 5), the Lord
learned that His staff had been broken and went on ahead alone. An avadhuta is a wanderer above outward rules; so
Nityananda is called.
[^02-4]: Jambunada is the gold of the river Jambu, the finest gold (Puranas). The red cloth is the saffron garb of a
sannyasi. According to CC (Madhya 6), on seeing Jagannatha the Lord fell senseless in the temple, and Sarvabhauma had
Him carried to his house; when Nityananda and the companions came to the Lion Gate, people told them of the sannyasi
who had been taken to the Bhattacharya's.
[^02-5]: The first line of this couplet ("Leaving the dress of a nagara…") is absent from the "P-R-Sa" manuscript.
"Nagarali" is the manner and dress of a nagara (an elegant young townsman): a hint at the Lord's Navadvipa form as it
is sung by the poets of nagari-bhava. Vrindavana Dasa stresses that in this incarnation the Lord did not so much as
glance at another man's wife; the Gaudiya tradition (Vrindavana Dasa, Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Bhaktisiddhanta) does not
accept the worship of Gaura in the spirit of "Gaura-nagari".

## 2. Madhavi — "nityānanda saṅgati mukunda gadādhare…" (PK 2240)
*Lila: the sequel to the previous pada — the companions find the Lord in Sarvabhauma's house; the people of Nilachala
gaze at Him. Raga — the same (varadi).*[^02-6]

**2.1.** Together with Nityananda, Mukunda and Gadadhara
beheld Gaurachandra in Sarvabhauma's house.

**2.2.** His lustre is like molten gold, His cloth is red;
His two reddish eyes brim with tears of prema.

**2.3.** His arms reach to His knees, adorned with sandal;
His nose is high, His brow graced with the urdhva-tilaka.

**2.4.** Gopinatha, Vaninatha, Sarvabhauma, Kashi —
all the people of Nilachala gaze at Gora's form.[^02-7]

**2.5.** Nitai sits on the right, Gadadhara on the left:
all the followers of Gorachand have gathered.

**2.6.** Whoever sees Gora's face floats in prema;
Madhavi alone is left out — through the fault of Madhavi's own deeds.[^02-8]

[^02-6]: The signature is "mādhavi" (MS "ka": "mādhavī"; "P-R-Sa": "mādhava"); on the poet see note 1. In GPT (GPT1, p. 402) the
pada follows the pada on Sarvabhauma seeing the Lord's forms. Cf. CC Madhya 6: Nityananda, Mukunda, Gadadhara (and
Jagadananda) come to Sarvabhauma's house, where the Lord lies senseless.
[^02-7]: Gopinatha Acharya, Sarvabhauma's brother-in-law (his sister's husband), had known the Lord in Navadvipa; Vaninatha
Raya was the brother of Ramananda Raya; Kashi is evidently Kashi Mishra, in whose house the Lord later lived. According
to CC (Madhya 10), the Lord met Vaninatha and Kashi Mishra after His return from the South; the poet gathers them into a
single scene.
[^02-8]: A formula of humility usual in a bhanita: the poet laments being deprived of what was given to others.

## 3. Narahari (Sarakara) — "dekhi gorā nīlāchala-nātha…" (PK 799)
*Lila: the darshan of Jagannatha — the Lord, in a gopi's mood, reproaches Krishna. In PK it is the gaura-chandrika to
the section "reproaches to Krishna" (akshepanuraga). According to Majumdar, an eyewitness description unequalled in
literature. Raga suhai.*[^02-9]

**3.1.** Seeing the Lord of Nilachala,
Gora, together with His own associates,

**3.2.** was overwhelmed by a gopi's mood,
and, reproaching, the Lord says:

**3.3.** "Without You I cannot live,
yet You will not even turn round to look at Me!

**3.4.** You wove a snare of love —
You put the moon of the sky into My hands;

**3.5.** and now to see You is only tidings and hearsay," —
so says Gora, overwhelmed by the mood.[^02-10]

**3.6.** His reddish eyes are brimming with tears,
His face, so full of sweetness, has grown wan.

**3.7.** Wondrous is Gauranga's play —
Narahari Dasa has told a little of it.

[^02-9]: The signature is "Narahari Dasa"; Majumdar ascribes the pada to Narahari Sarakara of Shrikhanda and places it among
the Puri padas written in the Lord's lifetime. GPT (GPT1, p. 299, no. 23) has the same pada with minor variants. In
Radha's mood the Lord sees Krishna Himself in Jagannatha — cf. CC Madhya 13 (at the Ratha-yatra: "You are the same, I am
the same…") and Antya 14 (darshan at the Garuda-stambha). The gopi's reproaches are a manifestation of the highest prema,
not of worldly resentment.
[^02-10]: The reading "sandeśa" (PK, GPT) means "tidings", "news"; a similar line of Chandidasa reads "sandeha" ("doubtful").
The sense is the same: the meeting that was once so close has become unattainable.

## 4. Vasu Ramananda — "nāchaye chaitanya chintāmaṇi…" (PK 2082)
*Lila: the Lord dances in the sankirtana. According to Majumdar, Puri: the Lord is called here by His sannyasa name —
"Chaitanya". Raga pathamanjari.*[^02-11]

**4.1.** *(Refrain)* Chaitanya dances — the chintamani gem;
streams of tears flow down His chest like strings of pearls.

**4.2.** In prema, His voice choked, He rolls on the ground;
suddenly, with a thundering cry, He rises to His full height.

**4.3.** Again and again He whirls, arms raised,
and makes the fallen say "Hari, Hari!"[^02-12]

**4.4.** He sings the name of Hari, ceaselessly repeating it —
no one can fathom these rare signs.

**4.5.** His boundless glory and virtues the whole world sings;
Vasu Ramananda begs Him for the treasure of prema.

[^02-11]: Vasu Ramananda was from Kulinagrama, a descendant of Maladhara Vasu (Gunaraja Khan); according to CC (Madhya 15),
the Lord charged the people of Kulinagrama — Satyaraja Khan and Ramananda Vasu — to bring silk ropes every year for the
Ratha-yatra. Majumdar regards him as a contemporary and an eyewitness. In GPT2 the pada is given twice (the section
"dance and kirtana", nos. 17 and 74); in the second instance the first couplet is marked as the refrain. Cf. CC Madhya 11,
13 (the Lord's kirtanas in Puri).
[^02-12]: The chintamani is the wish-fulfilling gem. "Makes the fallen say the name": the Lord gives the holy name to all
without distinction.

## 5. Narahari (Sarakara) — "tribhuvana-manohara śachīra nandana mora…" (PK 2241)
*Lila: from the sannyasa to Nilachala — the Lord leaves His former appearance and gives away the holy name and prema;
sankirtana on the seashore with Svarupa, Rupa, Ramananda, Govinda and Paramananda Puri. According to Majumdar, a pada by
an eyewitness of the Puri period. Raga bhatiyari.*[^02-13]

**5.1.** The enchanter of the three worlds, Shachi's son, my Lord,
who lived in the town of Nadia,
gave up all His wealth and took sannyasa —
and He is in Nilachala, near Jagannatha.

**5.2.** Those curling locks at the sight of which Rati's husband himself loses his wits —
such locks He has had shaved;
golden armlets and bracelets, necklaces of gems and pearls —
all that enchanting dress He has abandoned.[^02-14]

**5.3.** Compassionate to all living beings, giving everyone the name of Hari,
He delivers the greatest sinners;
the prema rare even for the gods, which Lakshmi and others long for,
He gives away to the fallen.

**5.4.** With all the devotees, in the great joy of sankirtana,
He roams along the seashore;
Svarupa, Rupa, Ramananda, Govinda, Paramananda —
all the companions have gathered.[^02-15]

**5.5.** Narahari Dasa says: my Gaurahari
became so out of love for Radha.
By such a flood of prema the whole world is blessed —
why then am I alone left out?[^02-16]

[^02-13]: The signature is "Narahari Dasa". Majumdar names the pada twice: as PK 2241 (kirtana on the seashore) and, by a
misprint, as "PK 1241" (the line about armlets and necklaces — his argument that the Lord's "dress" in the Navadvipa padas
is no invention). GPT1 (p. 403, no. 4) has the same pada with minor variants. In PK it stands in the 21st pallava ("The
sannyasa of Sri Gauranga, etc."), immediately after Madhavi's two padas.
[^02-14]: Rati's husband is Kamadeva, the god of love. The shaven locks: the sannyasa at Katwa (CC Adi 17; CB Madhya 28;
Lochana, Madhya-khanda).
[^02-15]: Svarupa Damodara and Ramananda Raya were the Lord's inseparable companions in the last years (CC Madhya 2; Antya 14–20);
Rupa Gosvami came to Puri (CC Antya 1); Govinda was the Lord's servant; Paramananda Puri, a disciple of
Madhavendra Puri, lived with the Lord in Puri (CC Madhya 10). "Rupa" is absent from MSS "ka", "kha", "cha" ("Svarupa"
without "Rupa"); "P-R-Sa" reads "Svarupa and others".
[^02-16]: "Became so out of love for Radha": cf. CC Adi 1.6 and 4 — Krishna took on Radha's lustre and mood in order to
taste Her love. A bhanita with the words "why then am I alone left out" is Narahari's habitual formula of humility (cf.
PK 2259 in chapter 1).

## 6. Narahari (Sarakara) — "rāmānanda svarūpera sane…" (PK 820)
*Lila: the Lord with Svarupa and Ramananda, in the mood of Radha who has heard Krishna's flute. In PK it is the
gaura-chandrika to the section "reproaches to the flute" (akshepanuraga). According to Majumdar, Puri, an eyewitness.
Raga suhini (PK), suhai (GPT).*[^02-17]

**6.1.** Sitting with Ramananda and Svarupa,
Gora is lost in thought.

**6.2.** With a start He cries: "Friend, friend!" —
and at times, falling silent, He rails at the flute.

**6.3.** And again He says to Svarupa:
"The flute destroys My family and My honour.

**6.4.** Its sound has entered My ears and stayed there —
it has deafened Me."[^02-18]

**6.5.** Narahari smiles within himself,
seeing this play of Gauranga.

[^02-17]: The signature is "Narahari"; Majumdar ascribes the pada to Narahari Sarakara and to the Puri period. In GPT1 (p. 299,
no. 24) it follows directly on "Seeing the Lord of Nilachala" (PK 799). In the last years Svarupa Damodara and Ramananda
Raya sustained the Lord with songs and verses answering to His mood (CC Madhya 2; Antya 14–17); on Krishna's flute heard by the
Lord in Radha's mood, see CC Antya 15–17.
[^02-18]: Radha's words: the sound of Krishna's flute draws the gopis out of their homes, making them forget their duty to
family and their good name. This is the language of pure prema, not of worldly passion.

## 7. Narahari (Sarakara) — "āre mora gaurakiśora. puruva prema-rase bhora…" (PK 840)
*Lila: holding the hands of Svarupa Damodara and Ramananda Raya, the Lord laments: "No one understands My heart." In PK
it is the gaura-chandrika to the section "reproaches to a friend" (akshepanuraga). According to Majumdar, Puri, an
eyewitness. Raga suhai.*[^02-19]

**7.1.** Ah, my young Gaura —
lost in the rasa of a former love!

**7.2.** Holding the hands of Svarupa Damodara and Ramaraya,
He cries: "Alas, alas!"

**7.3.** He speaks softly, His voice breaking,
and again and again heaves long sighs.

**7.4.** "No one understands My heart," —
says the Lord, beside Himself.

**7.5.** "Why did I let this love grow?
I am still alive — yet My heart is already lost."[^02-20]

**7.6.** Tears pour unceasingly from both eyes;
Narahari's face is sorrowful.

[^02-19]: The signature is "Narahari"; Majumdar (whose text misprints "PK 804") cites the third line ("Svarupa Damodara,
Ramaraya…") as proof that the pada describes Puri. GPT1 (p. 299, no. 26) has it with minor variants. A pada by
Chaitanyadasa, PK 1985, opens with the same line — but there it is the joy of meeting: "I have found the young Lord of
Vraja." Cf. CC Antya 14–20 (at night the Lord reveals His mood to Svarupa and Ramananda) and Antya 20 (Shikshashtaka 8:
Radha's words).
[^02-20]: Words in Radha's mood: love for Krishna in separation burns so fiercely that the heart seems already lost. The
line conveys the force of vipralambha, not worldly despair.

## 8. Narahari (Sarakara?) — "prema kari kulavatī sane…" (GPT1, pp. 309–310)
*Lila: the Lord, in the mood of Radha as khandita (wounded by Her beloved's faithlessness), complains to Svarupa of Kanu,
who did not come to the tryst. Only in GPT (section "khandita, mana"). Raga suhai.*[^02-21]

**8.1.** Having loved a wife of a noble house —
how much deceit there is in Kanu's heart!

**8.2.** With the sound of His flute He gave the sign —
and I came out of My house.[^02-22]

**8.3.** He said: "We shall meet again," —
so I came to the bower-grove.

**8.4.** In so many ways I adorned Myself,
and in hope I spent the night in the bower.

**8.5.** But Kanu, deceiving Me,
spent the night — in whose house?

**8.6.** Having said this to Svarupa, Gora
weeps in wounded love, beside Himself.

**8.7.** Narahari, seeing this, weeps:
how is he to steady his heart?

[^02-21]: The signature is "Narahari". The pada is in neither PK nor BR — only in GPT1 and GPT2 (identically); so by
Majumdar's criterion (1959) its authenticity is not proven: padas known only from GPT he regards as unreliable.
B. B. Majumdar in a later work (1961) accepts it as a pada of Narahari Sarakara, known from the collection of Advaitadasa
Pandita Babaji. The language is simple, without Vrajabuli, and there is no sambhoga — this fits the marks of Narahari's
genuine padas named by Majumdar. The khandita is one of the eight heroines of rasa-shastra; in Radha's mood the Lord
speaks to Svarupa as Radha to Lalita (cf. CC Antya 14–19).
[^02-22]: "I came" — in the original "mui āila" (a 3rd-person form with "I", so in both editions of GPT). The speech is
Radha's; the poet conveys what the Lord says in Her mood. Radha's jealousy and wounded pride (mana) are a manifestation
of the highest prema, not of a worldly feeling.

## 9. Narahari (Sarakara) — "gaura sundara mora…" (PK 853)
*Lila: the Lord, sitting in solitude, in Radha's mood reproaches Kamadeva. In PK it is the gaura-chandrika to the section
"reproaches to Kandarpa" (akshepanuraga). Raga tudi (PK), pahadi (GPT1).*[^02-23]

**9.1.** *(Refrain)* My beautiful Gaura!
Why, sitting alone in solitude, does He shed tears?

**9.2.** His heart is shaken by love for Hari;
He speaks softly, His voice breaking:
"How much harm Manasija does —
can the soul bear so much?

**9.3.** The body of a weak woman he has tormented,
entering the very depth of the heart."
Saying such words from the former lila,
He lowers His moonlike face.[^02-24]

**9.4.** Incoherently, as if in a trance, Gora says something —
no one knows the secret of His heart;
He is ever absorbed in His former deeds, —
sings Narahari Dasa.

[^02-23]: The signature is "Narahari Dasa"; Majumdar mentions the pada among Narahari Sarakara's gaura-chandrikas in the
akshepanuraga sections of PK; B. B. Majumdar (1961) also gives it as Sarakara's. GPT1 (p. 292, no. 51) has it with
variants. No place is named; the mood of separation from Krishna that the pada describes is, according to CC, the mood of
the last years in Puri (Antya 14–20).
[^02-24]: Manasija ("born of the mind") is Kamadeva. The scriptures call the gopis' love "kama" in name only: "the prema of
the gopis became known as 'kama'" (*Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu* 1.2.285; CC Madhya 8) — there is not a trace of
self-seeking desire in it. "Words from the former lila": Radha's speeches in separation from Krishna.

## 10. Narahari (Sarakara) — "ki lāgi dhulāya dhūsara soṇāra varaṇa gaura-deha…" (PK 1902)
*Lila: the mood of separation — the Lord's body has grown wan (malinangata, one of the ten states of separation). In PK
it is in the section "The ten states" (dasha-dasha). Raga malashi-vala (PK), suhai (GPT1).*[^02-25]

**10.1.** Why has Gaura's golden body
turned grey with dust?
His seat and adornments He has given up entirely:
I know not for whose love.

**10.2.** *(Refrain)* Hari, Hari! Gaurangachand has grown wan!
Moaning "uhu, uhu", crying aloud,
He beats His breast with His hand and weeps.

**10.3.** His whole body is drenched with sweat,
He heaves long sighs.
Such is the way of Rai's love, —
says Narahari Dasa.[^02-26]

[^02-25]: The signature is "Narahari Dasa"; Majumdar quotes the line "Moaning 'uhu, uhu'…" among Narahari Sarakara's padas on
the mood of separation (viraha). GPT1 (p. 311, no. 11) has it with variants. The ten states (dasha) of separation
according to rasa-shastra (*Ujjvala-nilamani*): anxious brooding, sleeplessness, agitation, emaciation, wanness of the
body (malinangata), incoherent speech (pralapa), sickness, the madness of prema (unmada), swoon (moha), and the last, extreme state. In PK the pada
is headed: "Now — wanness of the body. Sri Mahaprabhu, overcome by this mood".
[^02-26]: "The way of Rai's love": the Lord experiences Radha's separation from Krishna (CC Antya 14–20); this is no worldly
pining but the highest stage of prema — mahabhava.

## 11. Narahari (Sarakara) — "soṇāra varaṇa gaurāṅgasundara pāṇḍura bhai gela deha…" (PK 1908)
*Lila: the mood of separation — "sickness" (vyadhi-dasha): pallor, trembling, sweat, tears, incoherent speech. Raga
kamoda.*[^02-27]

**11.1.** Golden, beautiful Gauranga —
His body has turned pale;
as if from cold, He trembles again and again,
remembering a former love.

**11.2.** He says nothing, only heaves long sighs —
like a painted doll;
from both His eyes tears stream
like the currents of the Mandakini.[^02-28]

**11.3.** His whole body is drenched with sweat —
who knows from what fever;
now He sings, now He sobs,
He murmurs something incoherent.

**11.4.** Narahari says: my Gaurahari
gazes about like a beggar;
He cries "Hari, Hari", raising both His arms —
who will fathom His heart?

[^02-27]: The signature is "Narahari"; B. B. Majumdar (1961) gives the pada as Narahari Sarakara's. GPT1 (pp. 317–318, no. 17)
has it with minor variants. In PK it is in the section "The ten states", under the heading "The state of sickness
(vyadhi). Sri Gaurachandra, accordingly".
[^02-28]: The Mandakini is the heavenly Ganga. "A painted doll": stillness (stambha), one of the sattvika-bhavas.

## 12. Vasu Ramananda — "āre mora gaurakiśora. sahachara-kandhe pahum̐…" (PK 1924; GPT1, p. 318)
*Lila: the mood of separation — "the ninth state": leaning on His companions' shoulders, the Lord falls senseless and,
naming Mathura, calls: "O Natha!" According to Majumdar, Puri. Raga pahida (GPT1).*[^02-29]

**12.1.** *(Refrain)* Ah, my young Gaura!
Resting His arms on His companions' shoulders,
the Lord, in the ninth state, has lost Himself.[^02-30]

**12.2.** Fallen on the ground, He cannot utter a word;
no one dares to touch Him.
Golden Gaurahari says: "Alas, alas for Me!" —
His body has become thin as a thread.

**12.3.** With a fixed gaze, naming Mathura,
the Lord weeps: "O Natha!"
Vasu Ramananda says: why is Gauranga so —
I have not understood for what reason.[^02-31]

[^02-29]: The signature is "Vasu Ramananda". In PK the pada stands in the section "The ten states" (no. 1924), but the
available scan of PK vol. 3 lacks printed pp. 147–150, and only the last couplet survives (on p. 151); the full text is
given from GPT1 (no. 20, p. 318), where the pada follows the previous one (PK 1908). Majumdar (who misprints it "PK
1920") assigns the pada to Puri: the body "like a thread" and the weeping with the name of Mathura describe the mood of
the last years, not of Navadvipa.
[^02-30]: The ninth of the ten states of separation is moha, swoon (see note 25).
[^02-31]: Radha, in separation from Krishna who has gone to Mathura, calls Him "Natha" — "Lord" (cf. CC Antya 19–20;
Madhavendra Puri's verse "Ayi dina-dayardra natha…", which the Lord loved to repeat — CC Madhya 4, Antya 8).

## 13. Narahari (Sarakara) — "gambhīrā bhitare gorā rāya…" (PK 1643)
*Lila: the Gambhira — a sleepless night: the Lord laments, weeps, trembles, rubs His face against the walls and cries:
"Where is the Lord of My life?" In PK — "lamentation in the state of mere sleeplessness" (kevala-jagarana-dasha).
According to Majumdar, the quintessence of the Antya-lila of the *Chaitanya-charitamrita*. Raga — the same as that of
the preceding pada (PK).*[^02-32]

**13.1.** In the Gambhira Gora Raya
passes the night without sleep.

**13.2.** Again and again He laments,
now He weeps, now He trembles.

**13.3.** Now He rubs His face and head against the wall —
no one is beside the Lord.[^02-33]

**13.4.** Now He weeps, raising both His arms:
"Where is the Lord of My life?"

**13.5.** Narahari says: my Gora
is lost in the love of Rai.

[^02-32]: The signature is "Narahari"; Majumdar places the pada among Narahari Sarakara's Puri padas. Neither the archive.org
OCR nor the new recognition of PK contains the text — it has been read from the scan (vol. 3, printed p. 30); GPT1
(p. 314, no. 5) and GPT2 have it with variants. The Gambhira is the small inner room in Kashi Mishra's house where the
Lord spent His last years (CC Antya 6, 14–20).
[^02-33]: According to CC (Antya 19), one night the Lord, in the agony of separation, rubbed His face against the walls of
the Gambhira until it was covered with wounds; after that Svarupa asked Shankara Pandita to sleep at the Lord's feet.
Here is the same state: "no one is beside Him".

## 14. Narahari (Sarakara) — "gaurāṅga-chāndera bhāva kahane nā yāya…" (PK 832)
*Lila: in solitude the Lord tells His companions: "I will throw Myself into the sea." In PK it is the gaura-chandrika to
the section "reproaches to oneself" (akshepanuraga). According to Majumdar, Puri: the pada foreshadows the Lord's fall
into the sea. Raga tudi.*[^02-34]

**14.1.** Gaurangachand's mood cannot be put into words:
sitting in solitude, the Lord moans: "Alas, alas!"

**14.2.** His dear companions question Him —
He says: "I will throw Myself into the sea!"[^02-35]

**14.3.** "By My own will I began this cruel love:
disgrace has fallen on both families — and still life goes on."[^02-36]

**14.4.** Having said this, Gorachand sighs deeply;
understanding His heart, Narahari Dasa speaks.

[^02-34]: The signature is "Narahari Dasa"; Majumdar ascribes the pada to Narahari Sarakara and to Puri. GPT1 (p. 299, no. 25)
has it with variants. In PK the pada stands as the gaura-chandrika to the words of Radha reproaching Herself for Her love
of Krishna.
[^02-35]: Instead of "into the sea", MS "ka" of PK, GPT1 and GPT2 read "into the waters of the Yamuna", MSS "cha" and
"P-R-Sa" — "into the Yamuna". In Radha's mood the sea is the Yamuna to the Lord: according to CC (Antya 18), one night the
Lord, taking the sea for the Yamuna, threw Himself into it, and a fisherman drew Him out with his net. The PK reading
("into the sea") points to Puri; the reading "into the Yamuna" conveys Radha's words.
[^02-36]: "Both families" (du kule) — the father's family and the husband's; the words of Radha as parakiya. Her readiness to
give up everything for Krishna is the highest expression of prema, not worldly despair.

## 15. Vasu Ghosha — "siṃhadvāra teji gorā samudra āṛe dhāya…" (PK 1662)
*Lila: the divine madness of prema (divya-unmada): the Lord runs from the Lion Gate towards the sea, asking everyone:
"Where is Krishna?", and falls senseless. In PK — the section "Divya-unmada. Here — Sri Mahaprabhu". According to
Majumdar, an eyewitness's testimony whose vividness is matched only by Raghunatha Dasa. Raga suhai.*[^02-37]

**15.1.** Leaving the Lion Gate, Gora runs towards the sea,
asking everyone: "Where is Krishna? Where is Krishna?"

**15.2.** All around, the devotees sing the glories of Hari,
and in their midst a golden mountain rolls in the dust.

**15.3.** He falls headlong, He rolls on the ground;
tall Gora falls senseless.[^02-38]

**15.4.** He lies on His back, foam comes from His mouth;
Vasudeva Ghosha's heart is breaking.

[^02-37]: The signature is "Vasudeva Ghosha". Majumdar counts the pada among Vasu Ghosha's historical padas (the run to the
sea in Puri). GPT1 (p. 314, no. 6) and GPT2 have it with minor variants. The Lion Gate (Simha-dvara) is the main, eastern
gate of Jagannatha's temple. Cf. CC Antya 14 (seeing the sand hill Chataka-parvata, the Lord took it for Govardhana and
ran towards it) and Antya 17–18; Raghunatha Dasa's *Gauranga-stava-kalpataru*. In PK (no. 1663) and GPT (no. 7) there
follows a pada on how the Lord, coming to Himself, sees Svarupa and Ramaraya before Him: in PK it is unsigned, in the
"P-R-Sa" MS it bears the signature of Govinda Dasa, in GPT that of Vasu Ghosha; it is not included in this chapter.
[^02-38]: Falling, trembling, foam at the mouth, unconsciousness are sattvika-bhavas and manifestations of mahabhava,
described in CC as well (Antya 14, 17); this is not illness but the working of the highest prema.

---

# Chapter 3. Padas of Radha's Mood: Navadvipa, Sannyasa, Puri

*Narahari Sarakara's Navadvipa padas in which the Lord experiences Radha's mood (in the *Padakalpataru* they stand as
gaura-chandrikas to the sections on purvaraga, vasakasajja, vipralabdha and khandita) and which Majumdar
(*Sri-Chaitanya-chariter upadan*, ch. 2) regards as descriptions of real moods seen by an eyewitness; padas by Ananta and
Gauridasa on Gaura and Nitai, on the sannyasa and on Nityananda's "market"; then Puri and Navadvipa in the years of
separation: Sarvabhauma, the waiting for the Lord and a dream of His return, Radha's mood in the company of Svarupa, the
divine madness of prema. The text follows the *Padakalpataru* (PK), the *Bhakti-ratnakara* (BR), the
*Kshanada-gita-chintamani* (KGC) and the *Gaura-pada-tarangini* (GPT1 — 1st ed., 1903; GPT2 — 2nd ed., 1934); the
Bengali original, variants and word-for-word translation are in the full version of the book.*

## 1. Narahari (Sarakara) — "gaurāṅga ṭhekila pāke…" (PK 2122; BR, p. 924)
*Lila: Navadvipa — the Lord in Krishna's mood: the Ganga seems to Him the Yamuna, a flowering garden — Vrindavana; He asks
for yellow cloth and a flute and embraces Gadadhara. According to Majumdar — an eyewitness's pada (1509). Raga mallar
(PK, KGC, GPT), ashavari (BR).*[^03-1]

**1.1.** *(Refrain)* Gauranga is caught in a whirlpool:
absorbed in bhava, He calls, "Radha, Radha!"[^03-2]

**1.2.** Seeing the Suradhuni, the Lord takes it for the Yamuna;
seeing a flowering garden, He remembers Vrindavana.

**1.3.** In the mood of His former lila He stands bent in three places
and asks for yellow cloth and a flute.[^03-3]

**1.4.** Taking His beloved Gadadhara into His embrace,
the Lord says in a faltering voice, "Where were you? Where were you?"

**1.5.** Understanding His mood, the Pandita stays at His left.
Narahari Dasa does not fathom this play.[^03-4]

[^03-1]: The signature is "Narahari Dasa". Narahari Chakravarti quotes the pada in BR (wave 12, p. 924) with the note "a song
of Sri Narahari Sarakara Thakura" — the only pada signed "Narahari" in BR that he expressly ascribes to Sarakara, and Majumdar
puts it first among Narahari's Navadvipa padas. It is also found in KGC (27th kshanada, as a gaura-chandrika) and in GPT1
(p. 280, no. 9); in PK it stands in the section "The form of Sri Gauranga, etc." In BR it is preceded by the words: "By this
road Gora goes to the bank of the Suradhuni… He calls, 'Radha, Radha!'" Cf. CC Antya 18: in Puri the sea seems to the
Lord to be the Yamuna.
[^03-2]: Pak — a whirlpool, a noose: the Lord is as if drawn into the whirlpool of bhava. Suradhuni ("the river of the gods") is
the Ganga.
[^03-3]: The threefold-bending pose (tribhanga), yellow cloth (pitambara) and flute are Krishna's form; the "former lila" is His
Vrindavana lila. Here the Lord is in Krishna's mood, while Gadadhara Pandita, according to the *Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika*
(vv. 147–153), is a manifestation of Radha in Gaura's lila.
