*Nagari-bhava (by its place in the section; the speaker is probably Vishnupriya — then this is a lament of separation, not nagari-bhava). Lament after the sannyasa. "Gaura has gone without saying He was going — He has cast me, unfortunate, adrift on a shoreless sea":
cruel Fate did not let the tree grow, it broke the sprout; to whom has it given Gauranga? Who will bear the burden of youth — in the
fire of separation there is nothing left but to burn. The speaker is not named: in GPT the pada stands among Vishnupriya's laments.
Raga karuna.*[^28-38]

**15.1.** *(Refrain)* Gaura has gone without saying, "I am going" —
He has cast me, an unfortunate woman, adrift on a shoreless sea.

**15.2.** Alas, cruel Fate, pitiless, heartless!
You did not let the tree grow — you broke the sprout.[^28-39]

**15.3.** Alas, cruel Fate, what enmity you have wrought!
To whom have you given my Gauranga, my very life?

**15.4.** Who now will bear the burden of my youth?
Burning in the fire of separation, I shall be reduced to ashes.

**15.5.** Says Vasu Ghosha: to whom else shall I tell my grief?
Without Gorachand I will keep my life no longer.

[^28-38]: Signature: "Vasu Ghosha." GPT1 — p. 388, no. 18 (raga karuna; scan PDF p. 647), in the section of the laments of Shachi and
Vishnupriya (5.4), before Vasu's PK 1636 and PK 1669 (chapter 27, nos. 24, 25); GPT2 — sect. 5.4, no. 18. Not in PK, KGC or GCd;
attribution to Vasu by GPT only (C). In the catalogue its first line stood in row VG-076 together with PK 1636 (they are different
padas; see chapter 27, note 63); now it has a separate row, VG-187. The speaker is not named: by its place in GPT it may be
Vishnupriya (the words about the "burden of youth" and the "broken sprout" suit a young wife); by the catalogue (Majumdar's mark of
nagari-bhava in this series) a townswoman; therefore the pada is placed here, next to the nagaris' laments from PK. The speaker is probably Vishnupriya — then this is a lament of
separation, not nagari-bhava; the pada is left in the section by its place (coordinator's decision after the review of 27–30). On nagari-bhava
see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-39]: "Did not let the tree grow, broke the sprout" — an image of love (or of married life) cut off at its very beginning. Fate (vidhi)
is the arbiter of destiny, the Creator, not the Lord (cf. chapter 27, note 53). The Lord's going into sannyasa is His will and lila
(CB, CC), not the cruelty of fate: only the grief of those left behind speaks so.

## 16. Nayanananda — "premera sāgara nayana-kamala…" (PK 2170)
*Nagari-bhava. "What an auspicious moment — I have met the beloved of my life!" The townswoman saw Gora in enchanting attire: lotus
eyes, a moon-face, red garments, hands and feet redder than the lotus; He stands bent in three places; absorbed in bhava — Gora
within and without. In PK it stands in the pallava "Gauranga's form — the words of the nagaris." Raga bhatiyari.*[^28-40]

**16.1.** An ocean of love; lotus eyes, the pupils dancing wagtails:
what an auspicious moment, all omens favourable — I have met the beloved of my life![^28-41]

**16.2.** *(Refrain)* I saw Gora's form in enchanting attire:
whoever has experienced it alone knows it, others find no trace of it.

**16.3.** The abode of beauty — that moon-face, the fine red cloth;
red hands and feet surpass the red lotus; He stands bent in three places.[^28-42]

**16.4.** Absorbed in bhava, with the longing of the bhavini — Gora within and without.
This Nayanananda, bound by bhava, is ever lost in bhava.[^28-43]

[^28-40]: Signature: "Nayanananda." PK: vol. 3, PDF pp. 257–258 (printed pp. 246–247), 4th shakha, 19th pallava, section "atha
śrīgaurāṅgasya rūpa-varṇanaṃ nāgarīgaṇādyuktiḥ" (Gauranga's form: the words of the nagaris and others), no. 3 (mark "॥৩॥২১৭০॥"),
between Vasu's padas PK 2169 and 2171 (chapter 27, nos. 9, 10); raga bhatiyari; MS P-R-Sa no. 2277. GPT1 — p. 165, no. 27 (raga
bhatiyari); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 25 (catalogue: NN-009 and NN-026 — one pada; the first line of NN-026 in the catalogue is wrong —
"kāmera pāṭe ratira vilāsa" is taken from the neighbouring PK 2168 of Govinda Dasa). Nayanananda (Nayana Mishra), nephew of Gadadhara
Pandita, is a contemporary according to Majumdar; the pada is in PK with his signature (A). On nagari-bhava see the introductory note
to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-41]: "The beloved of my life" (prāṇa-piyārā) — the townswoman's words; "I have met" (bheṭalum̐) — she saw Him in the street or in
kirtana. MSS "ka," "kha," "cha": "lotus face" (vayāna) instead of "lotus eyes"; "ka"–"cha": "eyes" (locana) instead of "dancing"
(so also GPT1).
[^28-42]: "Bent in three places" (tiribhaṅga, tribhanga) is the pose of Krishna with the flute: Gaura, remembering the lilas of Vraja,
takes Krishna's form (cf. Vasu's pada "soṅari puruva-līlā tribhaṅga hailā" from BR — chapter 1, no. 10). The townswoman sees in Him
Krishna's beauty.
[^28-43]: "With the longing of the bhavini" (bhāvinī-lālase): bhavini, "the loving one," usually refers to Radha; it may mean that Gaura
is immersed in Radha's bhava (CC Adi 4), or it may be the longing of the heroine herself, who sees Gora "within and without." MSS
"ka"–"cha": "within, without" (antara vāhira).

## 17. Nayanananda — "sai cala dekhi giyā…" (PK 2177)
*Nagari-bhava. "Friend, let us go and see how wondrously charming Gora dances!" His form is adorned with love, yellow garments,
sandal, a forest garland round which bees swarm; absorbed in bhava He thrills all over, tears flow from His reddened eyes; the
townswoman longs to run and touch Him; the noble wives of Nadia have lost family and shame, but before people they dare not even
sigh. The poet advises: go to the bank of the Suradhuni — there you will see Gora. Raga shri.*[^28-44]

**17.1.** *(Refrain)* Friend, let us go and see
how wondrously charming Gora dances!

**17.2.** Golden, all made of love — so is His form adorned;
yellow garments, the red cord swaying.[^28-45]

**17.3.** Sandal on every limb, a fresh forest garland on His neck;
how many flower-arrows fly — in swarms of bees![^28-46]

**17.4.** Absorbed in bhava, His thrill knows no end;
from eyes reddened with anuraga tears flow.

**17.5.** My soul is tossed this way and that, I cannot hold my heart:
I so long to run up and touch Him.[^28-47]

**17.6.** The noble wives of Nadia have lost both family and shame —
but before everyone they dare not even sigh.

**17.7.** Says Nayanananda: there is a way —
go to the bank of the Suradhuni: there you will see Gora Raya.

[^28-44]: Signature: "Nayanananda." PK: vol. 3, PDF p. 260 (printed p. 249), 19th pallava, no. 10 (mark "॥১০॥২১৭৭॥"); raga "tathā rāga"
(= shri, as for PK 2174); MS P-R-Sa no. 2285. GPT1 — p. 165, no. 28 (raga shri); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 28 (catalogue: NN-010).
Signature in PK — A. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-45]: "Golden" (pīta, lit. "yellow"): Gaura's golden form; so also GPT1. The red cord (ḍora) is the dancer's waist-string.
[^28-46]: Bees flying to the garland are Kamadeva's "flower-arrows" (phulaśara): an image of beauty piercing hearts.
[^28-47]: The longing "to run up and touch" is a nagari motif; translated as in the original. Gaura Himself is here in kirtana, in the
ecstasy of prema (thrill, tears, 17.4); the townswomen are only onlookers (cf. Nayanananda's PK 2179 — chapter 10, no. 16).

## 18. Nayanananda (signature in GPT only) — "dekha jīva aparūpa gaurāṅgacāndera mukha…" (PK 291; GPT1 p. 166, no. 31)
*Nagari-bhava (only in the GPT recension). Gaura's form. "Look, O souls — the wondrous face of Gaurangachand: how many streams flow from His eyes!"
Hearing of His virtues, stone turns to water, the parrot weeps in its cage, and a noble wife who loves Hari's name weeps over Him in
solitude. According to GPT, Gaura has conquered the world by the rasa of love, even yavanas and chandalas were delivered — only the
poet's doubt has not gone. Raga malar.*[^28-48]

**18.1.** Look, O souls — the wondrous face of Gaurangachand:
how many streams flow from His eyes!
Kunda and karavira strung row upon row —
a charming garland swings on His neck.[^28-49]

**18.2.** Hearing of Gauranga's virtues, stone turns to water,
the parrot weeps in its cage;
the noble wife of a worthy family, loving Hari's name,
sits in solitude and weeps over His virtues.

**18.3.** By the rasa of love for Gauranga He has conquered the world —
even yavanas and chandalas were delivered;
the wretched Nayanananda's doubt of mind has not gone —
a heavy spear remains in his heart.[^28-50]

[^28-48]: PK: vol. 1, PDF p. 202 (printed p. 191), 3rd pallava, section "kevala rūpānurāga" (rupanuraga — gaura-chandrikas), no. 4
(mark "॥৪॥২৯১॥"), right after PK 290 (= Nayanananda's PK 787, no. 19); raga malar; in PK only 18.1–18.2, without signature. GPT1 —
p. 166, no. 31 (raga malar; scan PDF p. 425) — with a third couplet and the signature "pāmara nayanānanda"; GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 31
(catalogue: NN-013, "GPT only"; the PK number was found in preparing this chapter). Text 18.1–18.2 follows PK, 18.3 GPT1.
Attribution to Nayanananda by GPT only (C). On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-49]: PK: "look, O souls" (dekha jīva) — an address to all; GPT1: "look, friend" (dekha sai) — a townswoman's words. In the PK recension
there is no nagari motif at all, apart from the noble wife weeping over Gauranga (18.2) — and she loves Hari's name. GPT1: "a
garland that enchants the sages" (munimanoharā).
[^28-50]: "Yavanas and chandalas" — Muslims and outcastes: Gaura delivers all without distinction (cf. chapter 9, no. 1). "Doubt of
mind" and "a spear in the heart" are the poet's self-abasement (cf. note 4).

## 19. Nayanananda — "gaurāṅga-lāvaṇya rūpe ki kahiva eka mukhe…" (PK 787 = PK 290)
*Nagari-bhava. "How can one mouth tell of Gauranga's lovely form!" His smile and glance leave her no life; the Creator fashioned Him
in the mould of beauty, and her heart is in turmoil. The heroine laments: the Creator made her a daughter of a family, she is not free;
family, shame and fear are gone, she burns in the fire of her heart, but can tell no one. The poet: "Listen, charming one — you are
caught in the snare of love for Gauranga." Raga dhanashi.*[^28-51]

**19.1.** How can one mouth tell of Gauranga's lovely form —
and besides, the freshness of a flower!
The smile of the moon-face — I feel, friend, I shall not live —
and besides, the radiant glance![^28-52]

**19.2.** *(Refrain)* In the mould of beauty the Creator fashioned Him!
My heart feels strange, everything unsettles me,
the little doll of my soul weeps.[^28-53]

**19.3.** What shall I say to the Creator? He made me a daughter of a family,
and besides I am not free.
Gone are family, shame and fear; life will not stay —
I burn and perish in the fire of my heart.

**19.4.** To whom shall I tell it? Once told, love is broken;
my heart cannot keep its composure.
The word of Nayanananda: listen, listen, charming one —
you are caught in the snare of love for Gauranga.[^28-54]

[^28-51]: Signature: "Nayanananda." PK 787: vol. 2, PDF p. 124 (printed p. 111), 3rd shakha, 10th pallava, section "rūpānurāga"
(rupanuraga), "punashcha prakarantaram" — a gaura-chandrika of another kind, no. 11 (mark "॥১১॥৭৮৭॥"); raga dhanashi; MS P-R-Sa
no. 1277. The same pada is PK 290 (vol. 1, PDF pp. 201–202, printed pp. 190–191, 3rd pallava, "kevala rūpānurāga"; a duplicate with
minor variants). GPT1 — p. 166, no. 30 (raga dhanashi-dharatala); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 30 (catalogue: NN-012). Signature in PK — A.
On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-52]: "The freshness of a flower" (phulera kām̐cani) — the meaning of "kām̐cani" is uncertain (from kām̐cā, "fresh, young"?); MSS
"ka"–"cha" and GPT1: "kulera kām̐cani" (? "…of the family"). PK 290 and GPT1: "loving glance" (piriti-cāhani) instead of "radiant."
[^28-53]: "The little doll of my soul" (parāṇa-putali) — the inmost soul, the "pupil" of life. PK 290 and GPT1: "Friend, in what shapes
has the Creator fashioned Him!"
[^28-54]: "Charming one" (vinodinī) is usually a name of Radha; here the poet addresses the heroine (her name is not given; pronouns in
lower case). MS "kha" and GPT1: "lady" (ṭhākurāṇī). In PK the pada stands as a gaura-chandrika to Radha's rupanuraga: its frame — a
love that cannot be revealed, "a daughter of a family," "not free" — is taken from the padas on Radha. MS P-R-Sa: "life will not go
out" (vāhirāvāra), "in the fire of love" (prema anale).

## 20. Nayanananda — "kariva ki muñi kariva ki…" (PK 694)
*Nagari-bhava (a dream). "What shall I do? Secretly I am caught in love for Gauranga": in a dream Gorachand's face appeared to her —
long curling hair, eyes full of rasa; she, the daughter of a worthy family and the daughter-in-law of a worthy family, a faithful
wife, was lying in her husband's arms — and the waters of love for Gora swept all away. The poet: how will you now restrain your
heart? In PK, a gaura-chandrika to the section "telling of a meeting in a dream." Raga vibhasa.*[^28-55]

**20.1.** *(Refrain)* What shall I do, what shall I do?
Secretly I am caught in love for Gauranga.

**20.2.** Long, long curling hair, two eyes full of rasa;
I see a body as if anointed with beauty, virtue and love.

**20.3.** Suddenly it came and seized my breast:
in a dream I saw Gorachand's face.[^28-56]

**20.4.** In my father's family I am the daughter of the house,
in my father-in-law's family I am the daughter-in-law of the house.

**20.5.** I, a faithful wife, was lying in my husband's arms —
and the waters of love for Gora swept all away.[^28-57]

**20.6.** Says Nayanananda: I have understood this —
how will you now restrain your heart?

[^28-55]: Signature: "Nayanananda." PK: vol. 2, PDF p. 77 (printed p. 64), 3rd shakha, section "atha svapnarasodgāraḥ| śrīgauracandraḥ"
(gaura-chandrika to the telling of a meeting in a dream), no. 31 (mark "॥৩১॥৬৯৪॥"); raga vibhasa; MSS P-R-Sa no. 1169 and P-R
no. 10/39. GPT1 — pp. 165–166, no. 29 (raga vibhasa); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 29 (catalogue: NN-011). Signature in PK — A (MS P-R has
no signature). On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-56]: The subject is not named: "it came and seized my breast" we take as the sudden shock of the dream (in Bengali "vuka dharā" —
"the heart is gripped"); it can also be read "[He] came and embraced me." MS P-R puts this couplet before the signature; MS P-R:
instead of 20.1b — "I have fallen into the bhava of Gaurangachand."
[^28-57]: The sharpest nagari motif in Nayanananda's padas: a married woman, "a faithful wife," gives herself in a dream to love for
Gaura. This is a transfer of the plot of the padas on Radha (the parakiya-rasa of Vraja) to a townswoman of Nadia; translated exactly,
with nothing added. The tradition rejects such a depiction of Gaura (introductory note). MS P-R: "swept away by tears" (nayanera jale).

## 21. Yadu — "kaha nā upāya sakhi kaha nā upāya…" (PK 703)
*Nagari-bhava. "Do tell me, friend, what to do: Gora Raya ceaselessly rises in my heart!" Love for Gorachand cannot be forgotten, yet
Fate has made her a noble wife; His sweet speech is a stream of nectar, His form steals the hearts of faithful wives; the poet: "I have
sold myself to love for Gora for this whole life." In PK, a gaura-chandrika to the section "anuraga in the telling of a meeting."
Raga suhai.*[^28-58]

**21.1.** Do tell me, friend, what to do, tell me what to do:
ceaselessly Gora Raya rises in my heart.

**21.2.** Love for Gorachand cannot be forgotten —
what can I do? Fate has made me a noble wife.

**21.3.** What sweet speech — a stream of nectar!
What an enchanting form — it steals the hearts of faithful wives![^28-59]

**21.4.** Says Yadu: what can I say of all Gora's virtues?
I have sold myself to love for Gora for this whole life.[^28-60]

[^28-58]: Signature: "Yadu." PK: vol. 2, PDF p. 82 (printed p. 69), 3rd shakha, 6th pallava, section "rasodgārānurāgaḥ| prakārāntaraṃ|
tatra gauracandraḥ" (anuraga in the telling of a meeting — of another kind; here a gaura-chandrika), no. 40 (mark "॥৪০॥৭০৩॥"); raga
suhai; MS P-R-Sa no. 1176. Not found in GPT, KGC or BR (catalogue: YD-020; found in the full collation of PK, chapter 16, and
deferred to the nagari padas). The signature "yadu": Yadunatha Dasa (Kavichandra) or Yadunandana — not established (as with the
"Yadu" padas PK 2209, 2182 — chapter 16, note 1); C. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-59]: "Noble wife" (kulavatī), "faithful wives" (satī) — a nagari motif (cf. chapter 27, note 2): Gaura's beauty is such that even the
chaste lose their peace — a formula as in the padas on Krishna. MS P-R-Sa: "sweet form" (madhura) instead of "enchanting."
[^28-60]: In the signature the poet speaks of himself: "I have sold myself to love for Gora" — no longer as a townswoman, but as a
devotee who has given himself to Gaura. MS "kha": "what can I say" (ki kahiva) instead of "what can I do" (21.2).

## 22. Yadu — "gorācām̐de dekhiyā ki hailum̐…" (PK 859; GPT1 p. 169, no. 38)
*Nagari-bhava (reproaching the elders). "What has become of me since I saw Gorachand! I am caught in the snare of secret love": at
home she cannot bear the torment from the elders, her mother-in-law always scolds her because, remembering Gora's form, she goes mad;
she cannot stay at home. The poet: "Leave Gora — He will not leave you." In PK, a gaura-chandrika to the section "reproaches to the
elders." Raga varadi.*[^28-61]

**22.1.** What has become of me since I saw Gorachand!
I have been caught in the snare of secret love.

**22.2.** At home I cannot bear the torment from the elders:
the Creator made me a weak woman, and a family woman besides.

**22.3.** When Gora's form comes to mind, I go mad;
seeing it, my mother-in-law always scolds me.

**22.4.** I could not stay at home — what am I to do?
Says Yadu: leave Gora Raya — He will not leave you.[^28-62]

[^28-61]: Signature: "Yadu." PK: vol. 2, PDF p. 153 (printed p. 140), 3rd shakha, section "gurugaṇādīn prati ākṣepo yathā|
śrīgauracandraḥ" (reproaches to the elders; gaura-chandrika), no. 61 (mark "॥৬১॥৮৫৯॥"); raga varadi; MS P-R-Sa no. 1349. GPT1 —
p. 169, no. 38 (raga varadi); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 38. **Catalogue correction**: row YD-014 listed the pada as "GPT only"; it is
PK 859 (found in preparing this chapter). The signature "Yadu" — who exactly is not established (cf. note 58); C. On nagari-bhava see
the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-62]: "Leave — He will not leave" (chāṛile nā chāṛe): even if she tries to forget Gora, He will not go out of her heart. MS P-R-Sa:
"cannot be left" (chāṛite) — "Gora Raya cannot be left"; GPT1: "I shall go mad" (haive pāgalī). MSS "gha," P-R-Sa: "dei" instead of
"pāṛe" ("heaps abuse" — the same sense). The mother-in-law and the elders are figures of the padas on Radha (Jatila, Kutila); here
in the domestic life of Nadia.

## 23. Murari Gupta (signature in GPT only) — "sakhi he kena gorā niṭhurāi mohe…" (GPT1 p. 172, no. 48)
*Nagari-bhava. "Friend, why is Gora cruel to me? To the world He showed mercy, giving the shade of His feet — but me, unfortunate, He
has passed over." The woman who gave her life to love for Gaura finds no peace: had she known before, she would not have loved; what
joy is there in love if He does not look back? The poet answers: love for Gauranga burns; give up family honour, take shelter at His
feet — then you will attain Shachi's son. Raga suhai.*[^28-63]

**23.1.** *(Refrain)* Friend, why is Gora cruel to me?
To the world He showed mercy, giving the shade of His feet —
but me, unfortunate, He has passed over: tell me, why?[^28-64]

**23.2.** I gave my life to love for Gaura — my soul is restless,
I cannot stay calmly at home.
Had I known before, I would not have loved,
I would not have offered my life to another of my own accord.

**23.3.** He for whom I weep — if He does not turn to look,
what joy is there in such love?
The chataka begs the cloud for water — and if a thunderbolt is hurled at it,
will its breast not burst?[^28-65]

**23.4.** Says Murari Gupta: love is no easy thing,
least of all the burning of love for Gauranga.
Give up all family honour, take shelter at His feet —
then you will attain Shachi's son.[^28-66]

[^28-63]: Signature: "Murari Gupta." GPT1 — p. 172, no. 48 (raga suhai; scan PDF p. 431), right after PK 751 with the same signature
(GPT1 no. 47 — Radha's anuraga, without Gaura; catalogue: MU-002); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 48 (catalogue: MU-010). Not in PK, KGC or
BR. Majumdar considers most Bengali padas signed "Murari" doubtful (cf. chapter 13, nos. 11, 12); attribution by GPT only (C). On
nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-64]: "Tell me, why?" — we read "kahe" as "kāhe" ("why?", Vrajabuli); reading "kahe" ("says"), the sense is the same: the heroine
complains to her friend. "The shade of His feet" — shelter, the Lord's mercy to all.
[^28-65]: The chataka is a bird which, as the belief goes, drinks only rain water and waits for it from the cloud; if the cloud hurls
lightning instead of rain — an image of unrequited love from the padas on Radha. GPT1: "vāra" — a misprint for "yāra."
[^28-66]: The poet's counsel turns the nagari's complaint into an instruction on shelter: "give up family honour, take shelter at His
feet" — the path of surrender to Gaura (sharanagati), not of a love play. Some other padas of the section end in the same way (cf.
no. 21, note 60).

## 24. Dasa Murari — "eka dina mane ānanda vāṛhala…" (PK 2334)
*Nagari-bhava (the townswomen see Gaura and Nitai in the street). One day Nitai and Gaura, joyful and laughing, go alone to the
bazaar; the townswomen on their way to fetch water meet Them and cannot take their eyes off Gora: "It seems a dancer has come from
Gokula — let us go and see Him dance in the bazaar, let the water-fetching go hang!" Arm in arm the women fill both banks of the
Jahnavi. Raga dhanashi.*[^28-67]

**24.1.** One day, with joy in Their hearts, Nitai and Gaura Raya
go laughing to the bazaar — no one is with Them.

**24.2.** At that very time all the townswomen were going for water;
they met on the way — the beauty is beyond description — their eyes fell on Gora.

**24.3.** One says: "It seems a dancer has come here from Gokula!
Let us go and see — He will dance in the bazaar; let the water-fetching go hang!"[^28-68]

**24.4.** Arm in arm, all the women filled both banks of the Jahnavi;
gazing at Gora, they forgot themselves — says Dasa Murari.

[^28-67]: Signature: "dāsa murāri" (Dasa Murari). PK: vol. 3, PDF p. 316 (printed p. 305), 4th shakha, 23rd pallava, section
"śrīcaitanya-nityānandera rūpa-guṇa-varṇana" (the form and virtues of Chaitanya and Nityananda), no. 3 (mark "॥৩॥২৩৩৪॥"); raga
dhanashi; MS P-R-Sa no. 2408. GPT1 — p. 47, no. 71; GPT2 — sect. 1.3, no. 71 (catalogue: MU-005; in chapter 6 deferred to the nagari
padas). According to Majumdar, the signature "dāsa murāri" is not Murari Gupta; the author is not established (C). On nagari-bhava see
the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-68]: "A dancer from Gokula" — the townswomen, without knowing it, recognize Krishna in Gaura (cf. no. 4, note 12). Here the nagari
motif is mild: the women only crowd to see Gaura and Nitai; there is no love speech. MS P-R-Sa: "is coming" (āsiche); GPT1: "their eyes
filled [with tears]" (bharila nayāne) instead of "they forgot themselves" (24.4).

## 25. Balarama Dasa — "gaura-varaṇa maṇi-ābharaṇa nāṭuyā-mohana veśa…" (PK 2109)
*Nagari-bhava. Gaura's form — golden, in jewels, in the enchanting attire of a dancer: gazing at Him, the world forgot itself. "I am
dying, friend, seeing Gaura's figure: did not the Creator fashion, to slay young women, a Kama above Kama?" The townswomen lose their
composure and, disregarding their husbands, weep; the poet offers himself for the beauty of the nails of Gora's feet. In PK it opens the
pallava "Gaura's form." Raga mangala.*[^28-69]

**25.1.** Golden colour, jewelled ornaments, the enchanting attire of a dancer:
gazing and gazing, the world forgot itself, the whole land swayed.

**25.2.** *(Refrain)* I am dying, dying, friend, seeing Gaura's figure!
Did not the Creator fashion, to slay young women, a Kama above Kama?[^28-70]

**25.3.** Champaka, nageshvara, jasmine row upon row — the charming adornment of His hair;
seeing that form, young women are crazed: their composure and modesty are stolen.

**25.4.** Seeing that form, the townswomen of Nadia, disregarding their husbands, weep.
Says Balarama: I have offered myself for the beauty of the nails of Gora's feet.[^28-71]

[^28-69]: Signature: "Balarama." PK: vol. 3, PDF p. 233 (printed p. 222), 4th shakha, 18th pallava, section "atha śrīgauracandrasya
rūpādivarṇanaṃ" (the form of Gaurachandra etc.), no. 1 (mark "॥১॥২১০৯॥"); raga mangala; MS P-R-Sa no. 2217. GPT1 — p. 160, no. 7
(raga dhanashri; section 3.2 — the first in the series of nagari padas, before Vasu's PK 2149); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 7 (catalogue:
BD-017; PK 2109 was found in chapter 11 and deferred to the nagari padas). Under the signature "Balarama Dasa" PK has many padas of the
later Balarama Dasa (Majumdar; cf. chapter 11) — attribution to the contemporary is not established (C). On nagari-bhava see the
introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-70]: "A Kama above Kama" (kāmera upare kāma) — beauty surpassing the god of love himself (cf. Madana-mohana, note 9); "to slay young
women" is a formula of the poetics of beauty (chapter 27, note 6). MS P-R-Sa: "did not the Creator sculpt…" (gaṛhila ko).
[^28-71]: "Disregarding their husbands, they weep" is one of the sharpest nagari motifs (from the padas on the gopis who leave their
husbands for Krishna, *Bhag.* 10.29); translated as in the original; the tradition does not accept such a depiction of Gaura
(introductory note). The poet, however, speaks of himself as a devotee: he has "offered himself" (nichani — the nichhani rite, chapter
27, note 10) for the nails of His feet. MS "kha": "the moons of the nails" (cānde). MS "ka" and GPT1: "lovely jasmine" (mallikā
sundara); MSS "gha," "cha," P-R-Sa: "the whole land moved" (calila).

## 26. Chandrashekhara — "gaura-varaṇa heriyā vijurī…" (PK 2148)
*Nagari-bhava (only at the end). Gaura's form. Seeing His golden colour, the lightning hid in the sky; all the beauty of the three
worlds is defeated: the lion fled, ashamed before His waist, the elephant gave Him its gait, the does the play of their eyes, the yaks
went off into the forest, put to shame by His hair. Gaura in the midst of Nadia is a storm for the pride of young women. Raga tori.*[^28-72]

**26.1.** Seeing His golden colour, the lightning took up its abode in the sky;
all the expanse of beauty in the three worlds has lost and been defeated.[^28-73]

**26.2.** *(Refrain)* Look, look — the form that enchants Madana!
Abandoning its pride before the beauty of His waist, the king of the hills — the lion — has fled.

**26.3.** Hearing of His gait, the best of elephants surrendered its gait to His feet and went away;
the does, frightened, gave Him the play of their eyes.

**26.4.** Before the beauty of His hair the yaks gave up their pride,
went into the forest and lie there, ashamed and offended.

**26.5.** To make young women give up their pride — Gaura is in the midst of the town of Nadia.
Says Chandrashekhara: a thunderbolt has struck the modesty of young women.[^28-74]

[^28-72]: Signature: "Chandrashekhara." PK: vol. 3, PDF p. 248 (printed p. 237), 18th pallava, no. 40 (mark "॥৪০॥২১৪৮॥"); raga "tathā rāga"
(= tori, as for PK 2147); MS P-R-Sa no. 2255. GPT1 — p. 117, no. 19 (raga suhai; section 3.1, "form"); GPT2 — sect. 3.1 (catalogue:
ChSh-002; in chapter 6 deferred to the nagari padas; the GPT number was found in preparing this chapter). Chandrashekhara Acharya, the
Lord's maternal uncle, is the author of PK 2148 only by tradition (S. Ray; cf. PK 1854 — chapter 1); the attribution is not confirmed
(C). On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-73]: The whole poem is a chain of traditional comparisons: lightning (the colour of the body), lion (slender waist), elephant
(gait), doe (eyes), yak (the yak's tail, the chamara — the hair); all are "defeated" and "flee." MS "ka": "radiance" (vibhāta) instead of
"expanse" (vitati).
[^28-74]: The nagari motif is only in the last couplet: Gaura's beauty crushes the pride and modesty of young women (a general formula,
chapter 23, note 7). MS P-R-Sa and GPT1: "tejite gaurava" — a play on "gaura" / "gaurava" ("pride"): "to make young women give up their
pride — [their] pride…"; MS "ka": "having given up" (tejiyā).

## 27. Lochana Dasa — "āra śunyācha ālo sai gorā-bhāvera kathā…" (PK 2174)
*Nagari-bhava. "Have you heard, friend, what comes of love for Gora?" A young wife sat down to grind turmeric — and remembered
turmeric-coloured Gorachand: what cooking now! tears wet her breast and flooded the grinding-stone, the paste was ruined. The poet:
such an avatara as Gora has never been and never will be. Raga shri.*[^28-75]

**27.1.** Have you heard, friend, what comes of love for Gora?
In a corner of the house a young wife weeps, beside herself.[^28-76]

**27.2.** The fair one sat diligently to grind turmeric —
and turmeric-coloured Gorachand came to her mind.

**27.3.** What cooking now, what serving, what grinding of turmeric!
Tears wet her breast and flooded the grinding-stone.

**27.4.** The feeling for Gauranga welled up — she cannot restrain it:
the paste was soaked with tears, all went to ruin.

**27.5.** Says Lochana: hey, friend, what more can I say?
Such an avatara as Gora has never been and never will be.[^28-77]

[^28-75]: Signature: "Lochana." PK: vol. 3, PDF p. 259 (printed p. 248), 19th pallava ("Gauranga's form — the words of the nagaris"),
no. 7 (mark "॥৭॥২১৭৪॥"), between Vasu's padas PK 2173 and 2175 (chapter 27, nos. 12, 13); raga shri; MS P-R-Sa no. 2282. GPT1 —
p. 179, no. 66 (raga shri; with an extra couplet after 27.2: "her whole soul has died — the form draws mind and life to itself; the
heart is restless, friend, the soul finds no place"); GPT2 — sect. 3.2 (catalogue: new row LD-001). Lochana Dasa (c. 1520 — ?), author
of the *Chaitanya-mangala*, disciple of Narahari Sarakara, is a singer of nagari-bhava (introductory note); the pada is not part of the
*Chaitanya-mangala* (not found in our translation). Signature in PK — a recognized author (B). On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to
the section (chapter 27).
[^28-76]: "What comes of love for Gora" (gorā-bhāvera kathā) — lit. "the tale of Gora-bhava." "The fair one" (gorī) is the young wife; the
consonance gori — Gora — "turmeric-coloured" (haladi-varaṇa) is the play of the whole poem. MS P-R-Sa: "beside herself in heart" (hṛdaya
ākula); MS "ka": "Gora" (gorā) instead of "gori."
[^28-77]: "Such an avatara has never been and never will be" is Lochana's praise of Gaura as the highest incarnation; GPT1: "such an
avatara." Tears, confusion, inability to attend to work are signs of bhava (cf. CC on tears of prema), not of worldly passion; the
nagari motif here is only the domestic life of a young wife. MS P-R-Sa: "with tears" (lorete) instead of "lohete" (the same); MS
"gha": "flooded" (bhāsala).

## 28. Lochana Dasa — "nadīyā-nāgarī sāri sāri sāri…" (PK 2178)
*Nagari-bhava (the townswomen at the kirtana). The townswomen of Nadia walk in rows to the ghat of the Ganga — as if a host of moons had
come down from the sky onto the road — to see Shachi's son dance with His associates; one's garment slips, another's braid comes loose;
like painted figures they stand and gaze at Gaura; one, in bhava, falls into her friend's arms, another has tears, thrill, a swoon. The
poet: shame is struck down, Gora, the king of dancers, dances. Raga natika.*[^28-78]

**28.1.** The townswomen of Nadia walked in rows, rows, rows to the ghat of the Ganga —
such a radiance of beauty, as if a host of moons had left the sky and come down onto the road.

**28.2.** The son of Shachi dances together with His associates;
to see Him, they came eagerly to the bank of the Suradhuni.

**28.3.** One's garment slips — she does not set it right; another's braid comes loose;
like painted dolls they all stand together and gaze at Gaura, the jewel of virtues.[^28-79]

**28.4.** Seeing the sweetness of that form, all the townswomen are lost in rapture;
stirred by the fragrance of His body, they long to fly to Him.

**28.5.** One, overwhelmed by feeling, falls into another's arms, streams flow from her eyes;
on another's body the thrill is plain, another is as if in a swoon.[^28-80]

**28.6.** Says Lochana: gone is the fear for family honour, a thunderbolt on the head of shame!
Destroying steadfastness, dharma and all the rest, Gora, the king of dancers, dances.[^28-81]

[^28-78]: Signature: "Lochana." PK: vol. 3, PDF p. 260 (printed p. 249), 19th pallava, no. 11 (mark "॥১১॥২১৭৮॥"), right after
Nayanananda's PK 2177 (no. 17); raga natika; MS P-R-Sa no. 2286. GPT1 — p. 177, no. 61 (raga natika); GPT2 — sect. 3.2. The catalogue
had no row for it (**new row**: LD-002 — in the project's working catalogue, section "Lochana Dasa (nagari padas in PK)"). Lochana Dasa — see note 75; B.
On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^28-79]: The slipping garment and the loosened braid are images of self-forgetfulness (so in *Bhag.* 10.29 the gopis run to Krishna at
the sound of the flute, without finishing their dress); here they are the townswomen who have seen Gaura's kirtana. Translated as in the
original.
[^28-80]: Tears, thrill (pulaka), swoon are sattvika-bhavas, signs of prema; in Lochana the women of Nadia, seeing the Lord's dance,
experience ecstasy, like all who saw His kirtana (CB, Madhya-khanda). The nagari motif is in the frame (shame, family).
[^28-81]: "Destroying steadfastness, dharma" — as the sound of Krishna's flute made the gopis leave the dharma of family (*Bhag.* 10.29);
Vaishnavas understand this as the superiority of prema over worldly dharma, not as worldly passion. The tradition does not accept the
image of Gaura as a nagara (introductory note); Gaura Himself is here in kirtana with His associates, not in a love play.

## Summary of Chapter 28

*Chapter 28 completes the nagari padas of Vasu Ghosha: after the 25 padas from PK (chapter 27), here are 15 padas known from GPT (two
of them also have other witnesses: KGC — no. 1, the *Gita-chandrodaya* — no. 2; three are new to the catalogue: nos. 2, 5, 6).
Majumdar considers GPT unreliable for Vasu; one of these padas (no. 13) he explicitly calls a reworking of a pada on Krishna. Then
come the nagari padas of other poets from the same pallavas of PK ("Gauranga's form — the words of the nagaris," gaura-chandrikas to
purvaraga, anuraga, the dream, the reproaches to the elders): Nayanananda (5), Yadu (2), Murari (2), Balarama Dasa, Chandrashekhara,
Lochana Dasa (2). The padas of Yadunandana from the *Bhakti-ratnakara* (12th wave, pp. 904–910: the words of the "anuragavatis" —
women of Nadia in love with Gaura — in Narahari Chakravarti's narrative) are assigned to chapter 29, together with Narahari
Chakravarti's padas from the same cycle and from section 3.2 of GPT. The pada GPT1 4.4 no. 12 "…ḍākātera pirīti…" (signed Vasu) is
PK 2531, Radha's words without Gaura (excluded already in chapter 9); Lochana's pada PK 2219 is about the sannyasa, not nagari-bhava;
the pada KR-003 (PK 2018) is not nagari (translated in chapter 11).*

---

# Chapter 29. Nagari Padas — III: the cycle of the *Bhakti-ratnakara* (Yadunandana, Narahari Chakravarti) and the "Narahari" padas of GPT (sect. 3.2, nos. 39–45, 86–93)

*On what nagari-bhava is, the position of the tradition (Vrindavana Dasa, Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati) and the rules of translation, see the introductory note to the section of nagari padas in chapter 27; on the two poets named Narahari (Narahari Sarakara and Narahari Chakravarti) and on the attribution labels ("probably Sarakara", "probably Chakravarti", "not established"), see the introductory note to the "Narahari" appendix in chapter 17.*

## 1. Yadunandana — "gaurāṅga carita āju ki pekhalum̐ māi…" (BR 12, pp. 904–905; GPT1 p. 167, no. 34)
*Nagari-bhava. A woman of Nadia tells what she saw on the road: crying "Radha, Radha!", Gauranga weeps, embracing Gadai, rolls on the ground,
streams flow from His eyes; she herself loses all composure; Dasa Gadadhara smiles softly. Raga dhanashi.*[^29-1]

**1.1.** What have I seen today, mother — what Gauranga does!
Crying "Radha, Radha!" He weeps, embracing Gadai.[^29-2]

**1.2.** Unable to hold His heart, He rolls on the earth —
how much dust has clung to that golden body!

**1.3.** I look at that face — and do not know what my heart is doing;
how many streams, like the Suradhuni, pour from His eyes![^29-3]

**1.4.** I am dying, dying! Why did I go along that road!
There is no steadiness in my mind, my heart is bursting.

**1.5.** Seeing this, Dasa Gadadhara smiles softly, softly.
Yadunandana says: he floats in that rasa.[^29-4]

[^29-1]: Signature: "Yadunandana." BR, 12th wave: ed. 1913 (Murshidabad), pp. 904–905 (scan PDF pp. 912–913); ed. 1960, vv. 2803–2807. Narahari
Chakravarti, describing the places of Navadvipa, says that the Lord lingered by this tree and then went along the bank of the Ganga, "and here
women full of anuraga (anurāgavatī) joyfully and softly spoke with one another" — and gives their words in songs, "the first in a song of Sri
Yadunandana Chakravarti, disciple of Sri Dasa Gadadhara Thakura" (so in BR). Eleven more songs follow in BR (nos. 2–7 of this chapter; Narahari's
padas "nadīyāra mājhāre nācaye gorācām̐da" and "sai kivā aparūpa rūpa", translated in chapter 17; Yadunandana's pada "dekha dekha gorācānde" —
chapter 11, no. 12; Vasu's PK 2149 — chapter 27, no. 7; Devakinandana's pada "nadīyāra mājhāre onā rūpa" — the poet is outside the corpus).
GPT1 — p. 167, no. 34 (dhanashi; scan PDF p. 426); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 34 (catalogue: YN-002). Yadunandana Chakravarti was a disciple of
Gadadhara Dasa, a poet of the late 16th century; his padas in BR are B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-2]: "Mother" (māi) is an exclamation common in the speech of women in Vrajabuli ("ah, mother!"), here addressed to a friend. Gauranga, in the bhava
of Krishna, calls Radha and embraces Gadadhara Pandita: according to the *Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika* (147–153), Gadadhara is Radha Herself; cf.
chapter 11 (nos. 12–14) and Yadunandana's padas on Gaura and Gadadhara. The woman's words that she is "dying" express wonder and compassion
at the sight of the Lord's ecstasy; there is no desire in the text.
[^29-3]: "Streams like the Suradhuni" (suradhunī-dhārā) — the Lord's tears, abundant as the current of the Ganga.
[^29-4]: Dasa Gadadhara (Gadadhara Dasa), a companion of the Lord, was Yadunandana's teacher; he "smiles", understanding what is happening to the Lord.
"He floats in that rasa" may refer either to Gadadhara Dasa or to the poet himself; GPT: a "lahu lahu" (light, soft) smile.

## 2. Yadunandana — "dāsa gadādhara vadana heri…" (BR 12, p. 905)
*Nagari-bhava. The second of Yadunandana's two "gitas" at the beginning of the cycle: Gaura, looking at the face of Dasa Gadadhara, signals to him
with the corner of His eye, thrills, smiles; the woman saw Him on the bank of the Ganga — He steals the eyes of all young women. Raga kamoda.*[^29-5]

**2.1.** Looking into the face of Dasa Gadadhara,
He speaks with the corner of His eye, giving a sign.[^29-6]

**2.2.** Who knows why His body thrills;
in His smile nectar seems to rain.

**2.3.** On the bank of the Suranadi I saw Gora —
the thief of the eyes of all young women.

**2.4.** From the natural curve of His brows —
little friend, while I live, what shame is left?[^29-7]

**2.5.** The curve of His neck cannot be told:
the bird of the eye stays there, its wings outspread.

**2.6.** The beauty of His arms reaching to the knees —
seeing it, the hearts of young women crave.

**2.7.** At the soles of His reddish lotus feet
may Yadu's mind abide as a bee.[^29-8]

[^29-5]: Signature: "Yadu" ("yadu mana rahu…"). BR 12: ed. 1913, p. 905 ("punaḥ | kaścit kāmodaḥ", scan PDF p. 913); ed. 1960, vv. 2808–2814. The pada is
not in GPT1 or GPT2; in the catalogue — YN-005 (the second gita). Majumdar mentions both of Yadunandana's "gitas" at the beginning of the cycle as
songs of a disciple of Gadadhara Dasa. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-6]: The subject of 2.1 is not named in the original; in the sense of the cycle it is Gaura exchanging glances with Dasa Gadadhara (on Gaura and
Gadadhara Dasa in radha-bhava — chapter 11, no. 15). "Suranadi" (suranadī, "river of the gods") — the Ganga; so in the original.
[^29-7]: "Little friend" (ājuli) is a playful, affectionate address to a friend (cf. 7.5 below); the exact meaning of the word is not established. The
line can also be read: "in my heart, little friend, what shame is left?" — i.e., modesty is lost at the sight of Gaura. The nagari motif is rendered
as in the original.
[^29-8]: The image of the mind as a bee at the lotus feet is a common prayer formula of the signature (cf. "Narahari's mind is a bee" in the padas of
the appendix).

## 3. Narahari — "taruṇī-parāṇa-corā gorārūpa…" (BR 12, pp. 905–906; GPT1 p. 171, no. 46)
*Nagari-bhava. Gora's form steals the life of young women; blessed are those who drink it even once from the corner of the eye; Gaura, looking at
Pandita Gadai, calls him "Radhika!", holds Dasa Gadadhara by the hand, thrills and smiles — the depth of this rasa cannot be reached; He walks the
roads of Nadia, swaying like a nagara. Raga dhanashi. **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — the pada stands in the cycle of BR 12, in Vrajabuli.*[^29-9]

**3.1.** Gora's form, which steals the life of young women — its sweetness is a stream of nectar;
blessed, blessed, blessed are they who drink it even once from the corner of the eye!

**3.2.** *(Refrain)* Friend, to whom shall I tell this?
Gazing intently at Pandita Gadai, He calls him: "Radhika!"[^29-10]

**3.3.** Placing His hand in the hand of Dasa Gadadhara, He thrills with joy, His body bristling;
He smiles softly, softly — in what rasa does He float? I cannot reach the bottom.

**3.4.** With a nagara's airs He goes along the roads of Nadia, swaying;
His pose enchants Narahari's mind — Madana swoons at it.[^29-11]

[^29-9]: Signature: "Narahari." BR 12: ed. 1913, pp. 905–906 ("punaḥ kācit dhānaśī", scan PDF pp. 913–914); ed. 1960, vv. 2815–2818. GPT1 — p. 171, no. 46
(dhanashi; scan PDF p. 430); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 46 (catalogue: NG-079). The pada stands third in the cycle of the speeches of the "anuragavatis",
between two padas of Yadunandana, and, like all of Narahari Chakravarti's songs in BR, was written by him for this narrative (B). GPT1 readings:
"mādhurī amiñā dhārā", "kichui nā pāi thā", "helite dulite". Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-10]: Gaura calls Gadadhara Pandita "Radhika": Gadadhara is Sri Radha in Gaura-lila (GGD 147–153); the Lord, in the bhava of Krishna, recognizes
His beloved in him. This is the Lord's own confidential mood, which the townswoman sees but does not understand ("to whom shall I tell?").
[^29-11]: "A nagara's airs" (nāgarāli-ṭhāṭa) — a word from the language of the padas about Krishna ("nagara" — lover, gallant). The translation is
faithful to the author; the tradition does not accept the image of Gaura as nagara (introductory note, chapter 27): here it is the townswoman's
view, while the Lord Himself is absorbed in Krishna's bhava for Radha (3.2–3.3). "Narahari's mind" — genitive of possession: the Lord's pose
enchants the poet's mind.

## 4. Yadunandana — "sajani sai śuna gorā-aparūpa gāthā…" (BR 12, p. 906; GPT1 p. 169, no. 37)
*Nagari-bhava. "Friend, listen to the wondrous song of Gora": the tale of the secret play with the young wives of Vraja has flooded the world; the
fragrance of His body maddens the gods of love, the garland on His chest makes noble wives swoon; everything in Him is like the Moon of Gokula,
only the colour is golden; now He calls "Radha!", now laughs, now weeps aloud. Raga karnatika.*[^29-12]

**4.1.** *(Refrain)* Friend, listen to the wondrous song of Gora:
of the secret play with the young wives of Vraja —
that tale has flooded the world.[^29-13]

**4.2.** From the fragrance of His body how many Manmathas, maddened,
fly to Him in the guise of bees;
the garland of rangana flowers plays upon His chest —
and the noble wives swoon.

**4.3.** I see the golden colour — and all else, friend, is the same:
the speech, the gait, the radiance of the body;
the form of the Moon of Gokula, the plain snare of the brows —
a thorn to noble wives in both their families.[^29-14]

**4.4.** What woman, seeing the aim of His eyes
and the sweetness of the smile on His moon-face,
will keep her composure — and only then go home —
not driven mad by Manmatha?

**4.5.** Now He calls "Radha!" and sits with His eyes closed,
now laughs, overwhelmed by bhava,
now weeps aloud, His whole body bristling —
this is what Yadunandana loves.[^29-15]

[^29-12]: Signature: "Yadunandana." BR 12: ed. 1913, p. 906 ("punaḥ kācit karṇāṭikā", scan PDF p. 914); ed. 1960, vv. 2819–2823. GPT1 — p. 169, no. 37
(karnatika; scan PDF p. 428); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 37 (catalogue: YN-003). Readings: GPT1 "āra sava sei śākhī", BR 1913 "sei sakhi" (noting the
reading "sei sāthi"); BR 1960 "gorārūpa-gāthā". B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-13]: A tripadi; the refrain has three lines. The song is about Gora, while "the secret play with the wives of Vraja" is Krishna's lila: the
townswoman (and the poet) recognizes in Gaura Krishna of Vraja Himself; cf. 4.3 "the form of the Moon of Gokula" and the endings of nos. 5–7
("is He not the Moon of Gokula?").
[^29-14]: "Plain" (paratek, from pratyakṣa) — "evident", "in sight"; BR 1913 "payatek" is a misprint. "A thorn in both families" (dui kule kām̐ṭā) — the
ruin of one's good name in the father's and the husband's family; so the padas about Krishna speak of the gopis. The image is as in the original;
Manmatha, the "god of love", is Kamadeva.
[^29-15]: Weeping, laughter, closed eyes, bristling hair (pulaka) are the Lord's sattvika-bhavas in the bhava of Krishna longing for Radha (cf. no. 1).
The stanza turns from the townswomen to Gaura Himself: it is this bhava of His that the poet loves.

## 5. Yadunandana — "sai go nadīyā-jāhnavī-kūle…" (BR 12, p. 908; GPT1 p. 168, no. 36)
*Nagari-bhava (praise of His form). "Friend, on the bank of the Jahnavi in Nadia — what creator fashioned that body from golden shirisha flowers?"
His face a lotus, His lips bandhuli, His nose a kimshuka bud, His arms golden creepers; Gauranga cries "Hari!" and weeps on the lap of Dasa
Gadadhara; is He not the Moon of Gokula? Raga mallarika.*[^29-16]

**5.1.** *(Refrain)* Friend, on the bank of the Jahnavi in Nadia —
what creator, how, fashioned that body from golden shirisha flowers?

**5.2.** Who, seeing, would not believe?
His face a lotus, His lips bandhuli, His teeth — are they kunda?[^29-17]

**5.3.** To whom shall I tell it?
His lovely nose a kimshuka bud, His eyes red utpala lotuses.

**5.4.** I cannot say it in words:
His arms golden creepers, upon them lotuses, His nails blossoming jasmines.

**5.5.** His eyes — an ocean of bliss;
His soles — red land-lotuses, His nails put pearls to shame.

**5.6.** He bears the fragrance of love —
the people of the three worlds, seeing it, are intoxicated and do not return home.

**5.7.** "Hari, Hari, Hari!" He cries;
I do not know why Gauranga weeps on the lap of Dasa Gadadhara.

**5.8.** Why such bewilderment?
Yadunandana says: don't you know? — is He not the Moon of Gokula?[^29-18]

[^29-16]: Signature: "Yadunandana." BR 12: ed. 1913, p. 908 ("kācicca mallārikā", scan PDF p. 916); ed. 1960, vv. 2843–2850. GPT1 — p. 168, no. 36 (mallarika;
scan PDF p. 427; first line "soi lo nadīyā-jāhnavīkūle"); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 36 (catalogue: YN-006; Majumdar knew line 5.7). B. The nagari motif
is only in the address to a friend and in line 5.6; in substance this is praise of the Lord's beauty. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to
the section (chapter 27).
[^29-17]: Each stanza is a short opening line and a long line of comparisons (tripadi). Bandhuli — a red flower; kunda — white jasmine; kimshuka — the
red palasha flower; utpala — a lotus; shirisha — a delicate fragrant flower. GPT1 "daśana kunaki tāya" is probably a corruption of "kunda ki".
[^29-18]: "The Moon of Gokula" (gokulacanda) is Krishna: the friend's bewilderment as to why Gaura weeps is resolved by the poet: this is Krishna
Himself, and He weeps in the bhava of Radha (on the lap of Dasa Gadadhara; cf. chapter 11, no. 15). Cf. the endings of nos. 6 and 7.

## 6. Yadu — "dekha gorā-raṅga sai dekha gorā-raṅga…" (BR 12, pp. 908–909; GPT1 p. 138, no. 79)
*Nagari-bhava (praise of His form). "Look, friend, at Gora's play!" Through the town of Nadia walks a golden Ananga: His beauty surpasses a mirror
of gold and gems, His face is the full moon, His brows a bow, His eyes arrows; the young women lose their heads, and He does not even look back;
"He is that very Beauty of Gokula." Raga kamoda.*[^29-19]

**6.1.** *(Refrain)* Look at Gora's play, friend, look at Gora's play:
through the town of Nadia walks a golden Ananga.

**6.2.** His loveliness surpasses a mirror of gold and gems;
His reddish feet have lit up the earth.

**6.3.** His face has taken the splendour of the full moon;
the sky is bright with that radiance — for joy one cannot find the way.[^29-20]

**6.4.** His brows a bow, His eyes arrows, His aim sidelong:
His whole make is like the Madana of Vraja.

**6.5.** Arms to the knees, a broad chest —
who, seeing Him, does not feel the joy of a touch?[^29-21]

**6.6.** His gait is lovelier than that of an intoxicated king of elephants;
the young women are lost — and He does not even turn to look.

**6.7.** Yadu says: He is that very Beauty of Gokula;
you know and do not know — that is why you are afraid.[^29-22]

[^29-19]: Signature: "Yadu" ("yadu kahe"). BR 12: ed. 1913, pp. 908–909 ("kaścicca kāmodaḥ", scan PDF pp. 916–917); ed. 1960, vv. 2851–2857. GPT1 — p. 138,
no. 79 (sect. 3.1 "form", kamoda; scan PDF p. 397); GPT2 — sect. 3.1, no. 79 (catalogue: YN-011). In BR the pada stands in Yadunandana's cycle and is
his (B). Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-20]: "Ananga" ("the bodiless one") is the god of love; "a golden Ananga" is Gaura, beautiful as Kamadeva. 6.3b ("diśā nārī sukha", so in BR 1913, 1960
and GPT1) is understood as "diśā nā ri (pāri) — sukhe", "for joy one cannot find the way"; "the joy of the women of all quarters" is also possible.
The reading is obscure.
[^29-21]: "The joy of a touch" (paraśana-sukha) — from a mere glance: a delight as if one had touched Him. Rendered as in the original; this is an
image of the fullness of darshana, not of worldly desire.
[^29-22]: "The Beauty of Gokula" (gokulasundara) is Krishna. The friend "knows and does not know": she sees something extraordinary but does not
understand that before her is Krishna Himself — and fears for herself; the poet reveals the secret to her.

## 7. Yadunandana — "gauravaraṇa sonā chaṭaka cām̐dera jonā…" (BR 12, p. 910; GPT1 p. 168, no. 35)
*Nagari-bhava (only in the address "little friend" and in the words "destroying the composure of young women"). Golden Gaura, stirred by bhava,
weeps in streams, His whole body bristling, cries "Hari!", embraces Gadai and weeps: "What more, what more?…" — "is He not the Beloved of
Gokula?" Raga ashavari.*[^29-23]

**7.1.** Gaura's colour is gold, His radiance moonlight;
red as the young dawn, He stands motionless — His mind stirred by bhava.[^29-24]

**7.2.** From His reddish eyes flow streams, like the streams of the Suradhuni;
dense bristling covers His body — the burden of His feeling is heavier than the earth.

**7.3.** On His face a slight smile that destroys the composure of young women;
again and again, choking, He cries "Hari!" — and floods the world with weeping.

**7.4.** Embracing Gadai, He speaks sweetly, sweetly;
"What more, what more?" He says and weeps; I do not know in what rasa He is lost.

**7.5.** Whoever knows, knows it in the heart; my mind is immersed in that rasa.
Yadunandana says: little friend, is He not the Beloved of Gokula?[^29-25]

[^29-23]: Signature: "Yadunandana." BR 12: ed. 1913, p. 910 ("kācicca āśāvarī", scan PDF p. 918); ed. 1960, vv. 2870–2874. GPT1 — p. 168, no. 35 (ashavari;
scan PDF p. 427; the number is garbled in the recognized text); GPT2 — sect. 3.2 (catalogue: YN-012). GPT1 readings: "taruṇī dhairaja nāśi",
"nā jāni ki rase bhule". B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-24]: "Stands motionless" (caraṇe thira, lit. "firm on the feet") — the Lord stands still in bhava; it can also be read as "His feet are the young
dawn". "Heavier than the earth" (mahī jini bhāra bharā) — the fullness of feeling. The stanzas are tripadi.
[^29-25]: "The Beloved of Gokula" (gokula-piyā) is Krishna, the Beloved of Radha and the gopis; Gaura, embracing Gadadhara (Radha) and asking
"what more?", experiences the love of Radha and Krishna. "Little friend" (ājuli) — see note 7.

## 8. Narahari — "velā avasāne nanadinī sane…" (GPT1 p. 169, no. 39)
*Nagari-bhava. At dusk a young wife went with her sister-in-law to fetch water, saw Gaurangachand and came back having broken her pot; her body
trembles, her feet will not walk, in the ocean of His beauty there is no bottom; the poet: whoever has the sweetness of Gauranga awakened in the
heart, his family honour and good conduct sink in anuraga for Gorachand. Raga kamoda. **Attribution: probably Sarakara** — simple Bengali, brief;
not in BR, GCC, the *Gita-chandrodaya* or PK; the GPT2 index assigns the page to Sarakara; the preface of GPT2 quotes the pada as an example of
Narahari Sarakara's nagari padas.*[^29-26]

**8.1.** At the end of the day I went with my sister-in-law to fetch water;
I saw the form of Gaurangachand — and came back having broken my pot.[^29-27]

**8.2.** My body trembles, fever comes over me, my feet will not walk;
in the ocean of Gaurangachand's beauty I swim — and find no bottom.

**8.3.** His long, long eyes are fearful flower-arrows;
how can a woman keep her composure? — Madana himself trembles with fear.

**8.4.** Narahari says: whoever has the sweetness of Gauranga awakened in the heart —
his family honour and good conduct have all sunk in anuraga for Gorachand.[^29-28]

[^29-26]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — p. 169, no. 39 (kamoda; scan PDF p. 428); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 39 (catalogue: NG-075). GPT only: there are no
witnesses (BR, GCC, GCd, PK, KGC, PS checked). By the features that Majumdar takes as marks of Sarakara (simple Bengali without Vrajabuli, no
piling up of comparisons, correct metre, brevity) the pada is closer to Sarakara; but he considers padas known only from GPT unreliable — C. The
preface of GPT2 quotes the pada with an extra couplet (He stands by the river, lighting up both banks — cf. 12.4 below). Nagari-bhava — see the
introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-27]: The broken pot is a common motif of padas on purvaraga: so the gopis, seeing Krishna, drop their pots by the Yamuna. Cf. nos. 12 and 20 below.
[^29-28]: "Family honour and good conduct sink" (kulaśīla majila) is a formula of the supremacy of prema over worldly ties, known from the padas about
the gopis; so Vaishnavas understand it (cf. *Bhag.* 10.29: the gopis leave their homes on hearing the flute). The translation is faithful to the
author; the tradition does not accept worship of Gaura in the mood of the nagaris (introductory note, chapter 27).

## 9. Narahari — "śayane gaura svapane gaura…" (GPT1 pp. 169–170, no. 40)
*Nagari-bhava (only in the address to a friend). Gaura is in sleep and in dream, in life and in death; He is the pupil of the eyes and the necklace
on the neck; the poet wishes to keep Him in the heart and, in solitude, to gaze at Him; refrain: "Friend, speak to me of Gaura!" — His name is the
abode of nectar. Raga dhanashi. **Attribution: probably Sarakara** — simple Bengali; no witnesses; the GPT2 index — Sarakara; the preface of GPT2
quotes it as Sarakara's.*[^29-29]

**9.1.** In sleep — Gaura, in dream — Gaura, Gaura is the pupil of my eyes;
in life — Gaura, in death — Gaura, Gaura is the necklace on my neck.

**9.2.** Keeping Gauranga in my heart, I will sit in solitude
and to my heart's content hold that moon before me, eye to eye.

**9.3.** *(Refrain)* Friend, speak to me of Gaura!
Gora's name is the abode of nectar, the giver of love embodied.[^29-30]

**9.4.** He in whose heart the word "Gaura" ever sounds, the treasure "Gaura" ever lives —
says Narahari — at his feet he begs for shelter always.

[^29-29]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — pp. 169–170, no. 40 (dhanashi; scan PDF pp. 428–429; first line "śayane gaura"); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 40 ("emane gaura" —
probably a misreading of the recognized text; catalogue: NG-233, formerly NS-004 — the link with PK 103 is mistaken; PK 103 is the neighbouring
no. 41, translated in chapter 3, no. 2). GPT only — C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-30]: "The giver of love embodied" (pīriti-mūrati-dātā) can also be read as "Gora's name is love itself and the giver (of prema)". The ending (9.4)
is not a nagari motif but an ordinary Vaishnava prayer for shelter at the feet of a devotee in whose heart the name of Gaura lives.

## 10. Narahari — "marama kahiva sajani kāya…" (GPT1 p. 170, no. 42)
*Nagari-bhava. "To whom shall I reveal the secret of my heart, friend?" Wherever one looks there is Gauranga: He has entered the lake of the heart,
everything has become Gauranga; awake and asleep, at meals and on the way — only He; in the sky — He; Gauranga's feet are bound to the poet's
heart. Raga dhanashi. **Attribution: probably Sarakara** — simple Bengali; no witnesses; the GPT2 index — Sarakara.*[^29-31]

**10.1.** *(Refrain)* To whom shall I reveal my heart's secret, friend, to whom reveal my heart's secret?
Rising, sitting, looking about — I see Gauranga Raya.

**10.2.** Into the lake of my heart Gauranga has entered — everything has become Gauranga;
how much can I see with these two eyes? — if only I had a hundred thousand eyes!

**10.3.** Awake — Gauranga, asleep — Gauranga, always I see Gauranga;
at meals — Gauranga, on the way — Gauranga: what has become of me, friend?

**10.4.** I look at the sky — and there is Gauranga, always I see Gauranga;
Narahari says: Gauranga's feet are bound to the heart.[^29-32]

[^29-31]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — p. 170, no. 42 (dhanashi; scan PDF p. 429); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 42 (catalogue: NG-076). GPT only — C. Cf. no. 9: the same
motif, "Gaura everywhere". Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-32]: "Seeing the beloved everywhere" is a sign of the highest prema (so the gopis see Krishna everywhere; cf. CC Madhya 8, the conversation with
Ramananda Raya: the maha-bhagavata sees his Lord in everything moving and unmoving). The ending is the poet's prayer.

## 11. Narahari — "majilum̐ gaura-pīrite…" (GPT1 p. 170, no. 43)
*Nagari-bhava. "I have drowned in love for Gaura, friend": His incomparable form has dissolved into the whole world — the atasi and champaka
flowers have stolen His colour, the lotus His eyes, the palasha His ears, the sesame flower His nose, the aparajita buds His brows, the kunda His
teeth, the plantain His thighs, the lotus on its stalk His arms; "I know my Gaurahari in all the world." Raga dhanashi. **Attribution: not
established** — no witnesses; simple Bengali, but with a chain of comparisons that Majumdar does not find in Sarakara.*[^29-33]

**11.1.** I have drowned in love for Gaura, friend, drowned in love for Gaura:
seeing Gaura's form, incomparable in the world — it has dissolved into the world.

**11.2.** The atasi and champaka flowers, the red flowers have stolen Gauranga's form;
the lotus — His eyes, the palasha — His ears, the sesame flower — the curve of His nose.[^29-34]

**11.3.** The buds of the aparajita have stolen my Gauranga's brows;
the kunda buds steal the row of His teeth, the plantain tree His thighs.

**11.4.** The lotus on its stalk has stolen those arms, the lotus pond His chest;
Narahari says: I know my Gaurahari in all the world.

[^29-33]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — p. 170, no. 43 (dhanashi; scan PDF p. 429); GPT2 — sect. 3.2 (the number is not recognized in the GPT2 OCR). The
catalogue of stage 1 did not have this line (**new line**: NG-334). GPT only — C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-34]: The image of "the beloved's features stolen by flowers" is traditional: the woman in love sees the beloved's features in nature. Atasi is the
blue flax flower (Krishna's colour), champaka the golden one (Gaura's colour): both colours stand in one row; "śoṇa" — red (or: "the champaka that
glows red"). The nose — "nāsākūpa" (lit. "the nostrils").

## 12. Narahari — "ke āche emana manera vedana…" (GPT1 p. 171, no. 44)
*Nagari-bhava. "To whom shall I reveal my heart's pain, friend? — I will tell you": at dusk she went with her sister-in-law to fetch water, saw
Gauranga and broke her pot — shame is all she gained; the sister-in-law is a black serpent, evil-tongued; the tears cannot be held back; Gaura
shines on the bank of the Suradhuni like the autumn moon, lighting up both banks — but the sister-in-law did not let her gaze her fill. Raga pahida.
**Attribution: probably Sarakara** — simple Bengali; no witnesses; the GPT2 index — Sarakara; the ending is the same as in no. 8.*[^29-35]

**12.1.** Who is there to whom I could reveal my heart's pain, friend?
If I do not speak, my breast will burst and I will die; that is why I tell you.

**12.2.** At dusk I went with my sister-in-law to draw water;
seeing Gauranga, I broke my pot — shame is all I gained.

**12.3.** With me was my sister-in-law — a black serpent, wicked, crooked;
I cannot hold back my tears, my face has faded.[^29-36]

**12.4.** Gaura's body shines like the light of the autumn moon;
He stands on the bank of the Suradhuni, lighting up both banks.[^29-37]

**12.5.** A broad chest, and on it a garland of sandal flowers;
I could not gaze my fill — my sister-in-law was death to me.

**12.6.** Narahari says: whoever has the sweetness of Gauranga awakened in the heart —
his family honour and good conduct are all swept away by anuraga for Gauranga.

[^29-35]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — p. 171, no. 44 (pahida; scan PDF p. 430); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 44 (catalogue: NG-077). GPT only — C. The pada is an
expanded version of no. 8 (the same story and almost the same ending). Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-36]: The sister-in-law (nanadī), the mother-in-law, the husband are the "gurujanas", the elders who guard a young wife: the usual figures of padas
on purvaraga (with Radha — Jatila and Kutila). "Black serpent" is the heroine's own abuse; so in the original.
[^29-37]: "Lighting up both banks" (dukūla kariyā ālo): dukūla means both "both banks" and "both families" (the father's and the husband's); a pun is
possible.

## 13. Narahari Dasa — "ki herilāma gorārūpa nā yāya pāsarā…" (GPT1 p. 171, no. 45)
*Nagari-bhava. Gora's form cannot be forgotten: He has clung to the eyes like collyrium; if she dives into the water, she sees Gora in the water;
the three worlds have become Gorachand; Gora's form is an ocean of nectar, and the young woman's mind drowns in it, not knowing how to swim. Raga
shri (bara dashakushi). **Attribution: probably Sarakara** — simple Bengali, brief; no witnesses; the GPT2 index — Sarakara; GPT1 notes that in
some collections the pada is signed by Vasudeva Ghosha.*[^29-38]

**13.1.** What have I seen — Gora's form! — it cannot be forgotten:
Gora has clung to my eyes like collyrium.

**13.2.** If I dive into the water — in the water I see Gora;
the three worlds have become Gorachand — so it has come to be.

**13.3.** That is why I say: Gora's form is an ocean of nectar;
a young woman's mind drowns in it — she does not know how to swim.

**13.4.** Narahari Dasa speaks in fresh anuraga:
golden Gorachand awakens in the heart.[^29-39]

[^29-38]: Signature: "Narahari Dasa" (narahari dāsa). GPT1 — p. 171, no. 45 (shri — bara dashakushi; scan PDF p. 430); GPT1 below the line: "in some collections
this pada has the signature of Vasudeva Ghosha"; GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 45 (catalogue: NG-078). The pada is not in PK under either name. GPT only — C.
GPT1 readings: "pasarā", "añjala" (for "añjana", as in GPT2), "amiñā". Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-39]: "Fresh anuraga" (nava anurāga) — fresh, ever-growing attachment; so the first love of the gopis is called. The ending again speaks of the
poet's heart.

## 14. Narahari Dasa — "pīriti-mūrati śacīra dulāla…" (GPT1 p. 189, no. 86; GCC 7.2)
*Nagari-bhava. Shachi's son is love embodied, His fame fills the world; there is no one who, having once seen Him, would not forget himself; and
the love of the townswomen of Nadia for Gauranga is such that no one telling or hearing of it keeps composure: Gora is their japa, tapas and
meditation, without Him even for half a moment all is empty; His happiness is their happiness. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably
Chakravarti** — the pada is in the *Gaura-charita-chintamani* (kirana 7, pada 2).*[^29-40]

**14.1.** Shachi's son is love embodied; His fame fills the world;
there is no one who would not forget himself, having once seen the sweetness of that form.

**14.2.** Wholly wondrous is His art of rasa — I cannot understand what virtues are in Him;
without loving Gaurahari no one in the world lives.

**14.3.** And such is the love of these townswomen of Nadia for Gauranga —
who, telling of it or hearing, would keep composure?

**14.4.** Gora is their japa, tapas, meditation and contemplation; they know nothing else;
not seeing Gorachand even for half a moment, they count all as empty.

**14.5.** Gora is the treasure of their life, their life and their caste; Gora is the pupil of their eyes;
in sleep and in dream, saying "Gora, Gora", they have become as if mad.

**14.6.** Composure, dharma, shame, fear for their family — all they have given up for Him;
in Gora's happiness their happiness ever grows, sings Narahari Dasa.[^29-41]

[^29-40]: Signature: "Dasa Narahari" (dāsa narahari). GPT1 — p. 189, no. 86 ("yathārāga"; scan PDF p. 448); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 86 (catalogue: NG-080). Witness —
Narahari Chakravarti's *Gaura-charita-chintamani* (GCC; ed. 1947, p. 67): kirana 7 — "in the morning, the conversations among themselves of the
nagaris of Navadvipa, filled with that love", pada 2 (after an opening pada on the joy in Shachi's house at dawn). Kirana 7 of GCC is wholly a
"description of the nagaris of Navadvipa"; its padas form the greater part of section 3.2 of GPT (nos. 86–99, 124 and on; kiranas 8–11 — the dreams,
wishes and conversations of the townswomen) — a late (18th-century) poetic elaboration of the nagari motif by Narahari Chakravarti (B). Majumdar
says plainly that the long padas of GPT, uneven in metre, signed Narahari cannot be Sarakara's; the collation confirms it: they are padas of GCC.
Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-41]: "Their happiness lies in Gora's happiness" (gorā-sukhe sukha) is the mark of the gopis' love, which seeks only Krishna's happiness and not its
own (CC Adi 4: in the gopis' love there is not a trace of desire for their own enjoyment). Giving up "shame and family" is the same formula of the
supremacy of prema over worldly dharma (cf. note 28). The translation is faithful to the author; the tradition does not accept worship of Gaura in
the mood of the nagaris (introductory note, chapter 27).

## 15. Narahari — "mari mari hena nadīyā-nāgarīgaṇera…" (GPT1 pp. 189–190, no. 87; GCC 7.3)
*Nagari-bhava. The townswomen of Nadia spent the night in longing: some did not sleep, singing of Gorachand's deeds, others saw Him in a dream;
at dawn they come out of their houses on the pretext of work; skilled in stratagems, they do whatever pleases the elders and, with their leave,
go where they wish; they gather in a secluded place — the poet admires them. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC,
kirana 7, pada 3.*[^29-42]

**15.1.** Ah, ah! — I take upon myself all the misfortunes of such townswomen of Nadia:
this night they all spent in great longing.[^29-43]

**15.2.** Some stayed awake all night, singing of Gorachand's deeds;
others, sleeping sweetly, found the Moon Gaura in a dream.

**15.3.** Leaving their beds again, they rose at the end of the night
and came out of this house and that, as if on some errand.

**15.4.** The ways of these clever townswomen I cannot understand at all:
whatever work pleases the elders, that they do with care.

**15.5.** With the elders' leave they come and go — what more is there to say!
As their custom is day after day, so their happiness has no bounds.

**15.6.** Unseen, in a secluded place, sit the young women who captivate the world;
one by one they all gather there — and Narahari admires them.

[^29-42]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — pp. 189–190, no. 87 (scan PDF pp. 448–449); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 87 (catalogue: NG-081). GCC — kirana 7, pada 3 (ed. 1947,
pp. 67–68). GCC readings: "keha keha gorācāndera caritra gāiyā", "niśi parabhāta-kāle". B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section
(chapter 27).
[^29-43]: "I take upon myself their misfortunes" (vālāi laiyā) is a Bengali formula of admiring tenderness (lit. "taking their ills upon oneself"): the
poet blesses the townswomen.

## 16. Narahari — "ki kava yuvatī-janera yerūpa pīriti paraspare…" (GPT1 p. 190, no. 88; GCC 7.4)
*Nagari-bhava. The love of the young townswomen for one another is such that their bodies are different but their heart is one: one, laughing,
puts her arm round another's neck, another teases; "leave your pretence, tell us about yesterday — what stood in whose way, who saw Gaura the
jewel and how, how did you spend this night?" Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 4.*[^29-44]

**16.1.** What shall I say of the love of these young women for one another?
Their bodies are different, their heart is one — who has the power to understand this tenderness?

**16.2.** One, full of rasa, laughing and laughing, puts her arm round another's neck;
that one teases this one in a thousand ways.

**16.3.** Another says: "Leave your pretence, tell us — let us hear about yesterday:
what stood in whose way, who saw Gaura the jewel, and how?"

**16.4.** Another says: "Ah, tell me how you spent this night!"
Narahari says: it would be good to tell all these stories at length.

[^29-44]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — p. 190, no. 88 (scan PDF p. 449); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 88 (catalogue: NG-082). GCC — kirana 7, pada 4 (p. 68); GCC: "kare
parihāsa" (GPT1 "upahāsa"), "keha kahe ogo". The pada introduces the townswomen's stories that follow (nos. 17–21). B. Nagari-bhava — see the
introductory note to the section (chapter 27).

## 17. Narahari — "ki puchaha sakhi kālikāra kathā…" (GPT1 pp. 190–191, no. 89; GCC 7.5)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: in the evening she was sitting beside her mother-in-law and sister-in-law when she heard that Gaura was
passing along their lane; she did not know what to do, tears flowed; the mother-in-law kindly asked what was wrong — "I feel unwell" — and let
her go and lie down; on the pretext of sleep she went out of the gate and gazed her fill at His face. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably
Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 5.*[^29-45]

**17.1.** "Why do you ask, friend, about yesterday? — it makes me laugh to tell it;
casting off shame, I will tell how I saw the Moon of Nadia.

**17.2.** At the end of the day my mother-in-law, my sister-in-law and several other women —
I was sitting beside them, showing how well-behaved I am.

**17.3.** Just then the Lord of my life came along our lane;
hearing it, I started, looked all around — my mind was thrown into confusion.[^29-46]

**17.4.** I fell into a terrible fix, nothing came to my mind;
my soul was restless — what to do? — my eyes kept shedding tears.

**17.5.** Seeing me downcast, my mother-in-law says sweetly:
'Why are you like this, child? I don't know what pain you have.'

**17.6.** At these words I told her: 'I feel somehow unwell';
hearing this, she gave me leave: 'Go and lie down in the house.'

**17.7.** As if to lie down, I went out at once and stood outside the gate,
and, seeing once the sweetness of that face, refreshed my eyes and heart.

**17.8.** No one could notice — my body was filled with joy."
Narahari says: the stratagems of those full of rasa — who can understand them?[^29-47]

[^29-45]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — pp. 190–191, no. 89 (scan PDF pp. 449–450); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 89 (catalogue: NG-083). GCC — kirana 7, pada 5 ("kācidāha" —
"a certain one says", pp. 68–69). GCC readings: "dekhinu nadyāra śaśī" (GPT1 "dekhila"), "athira ati", "rasika janāra cāturī" (so also GPT1). B.
Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-46]: "The Lord of my life" (parāṇa-pati) is the heroine's word for Gaura, as the gopis in the padas speak of Krishna; the translation is faithful
to the author. The Lord Himself in this and the following padas only passes along the lane or stands with His companions at the ghat — He takes
no part in the townswomen's stratagems (cf. nos. 18, 20, 21).
[^29-47]: The heroine's ruse — deceiving her mother-in-law for the darshana of Gaura — and the poet's praise of "the stratagems of those full of rasa"
are rendered as in the original: this is a poetic convention of the padas on purvaraga (so the gopis deceive their elders for Krishna's sake).
The tradition does not accept worship of Gaura in the mood of the nagaris (introductory note, chapter 27), and the *Chaitanya-bhagavata* says
plainly that the Lord in Navadvipa did not look at women.

## 18. Narahari — "kālikāra kathā ki kava sajani…" (GPT1 p. 191, no. 90; GCC 7.6)
*Nagari-bhava. Another townswoman's story: yesterday she was sitting alone and heard that Gaura was passing; she hurried — and He with His
companions flashed by like lightning; she returned home in fear of the elders; someone told her mother-in-law, who came running in anger; the
young wife swore she had not seen Him and touched her feet — and the mother-in-law believed her. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably
Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 6.*[^29-48]

**18.1.** "What shall I say of yesterday, friend? — my soul weeps as I tell it:
I saw and yet did not see the Moon of Nadia, the life of my life.

**18.2.** Listen to how it was: I was sitting alone, in complete solitude;
suddenly I hear from people's lips: Gaura is coming.

**18.3.** I hurried — and saw Him with His dear companions;
flashing like lightning, He went on His way.

**18.4.** I was overcome, casting off shame and looking once at that face;
in fear of the elders I hurried home, more dead than alive.

**18.5.** I do not know who told my mother-in-law about it;
hearing it, she came running at me in anger, her face distorted.

**18.6.** How many harsh words she said! — I trembled with fear;
I said, 'I did not see Him', swore an oath and touched her feet.

**18.7.** Telling many untruths, I came out good — she believed me."
Narahari says: do not count this a fault — to think so is not right.[^29-49]

[^29-48]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — p. 191, no. 90 (scan PDF p. 450; the number is garbled in the recognized text); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 90 (catalogue: NG-084).
GCC — kirana 7, pada 6 (p. 69). GCC readings: "turite yāiyā dekhinu se nija priya parikara sāthe" (GPT1 without "priya"), "chum̐inu uhāra pā". B.
Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-49]: 18.7b (narahari kahe ithe doṣa ihā nā māna, e nahe bhāla) can be read in two ways: "do not count this a fault — to count it so is not good"
(the poet excuses the ruse for the sake of darshana) or "you do not count this a fault — but it is not good" (a gentle reproach). It is translated
by the first reading, more likely in the context of GCC, where the poet constantly praises the townswomen's "stratagems" (cf. 17.8, 20.16). The lie
and the oath are a poetic convention of the padas on purvaraga (cf. note 47).

## 19. Narahari — "nilaji haiyā vali ye sajani…" (GPT1 p. 191, no. 91; GCC 7.7)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: her husband's aunt came to visit for the first time in a long while; she joyfully sat beside her, but then
heard that Gaura was passing; she wanted to go out of the door — but the aunt, suspecting nothing, held her back by the end of her sari, adjuring
her "by my head", and asked about household matters; her kindness seemed like poison; the young wife did not know how to break away. Raga
"yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 7.*[^29-50]

**19.1.** "Casting off shame, I'll tell you, friend — listen to my story:
the pitiless Creator yesterday gave me cruel pain.

**19.2.** For the first time in many days my husband's aunt came to my house;
with joy in my heart I sat beside her, leaving everything.[^29-51]

**19.3.** And just then I hear: the nagara Gaura is passing;
I was all eagerness to go out of the door.

**19.4.** As soon as I think of getting up — ah! — she looks at me again,
catches the end of my sari and kindly sits me down, adjuring me by her head.

**19.5.** Understanding nothing of this, with a heart free of all guile,
she asks in every way, with care, about household matters.

**19.6.** My soul is restless — I listen to her and do not hear;
what is asked, what I answer — good or bad, I do not remember.

**19.7.** She is affectionate with me, as is proper, and to me it is like poison;
out of awkwardness I do not show it, but inside I am burning.

**19.8.** Seeing a terrible fix, I thought — let my body leave me!"
Narahari says: don't you know any stratagems — how to fool the aunt?[^29-52]

[^29-50]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — pp. 191–192, no. 91 (scan PDF pp. 450–451); GPT2 — sect. 3.2 (the number is not recognized in the GPT2 OCR). The catalogue of
stage 1 did not have this line (**new line**: NG-335). GCC — kirana 7, pada 7 (pp. 69–70); GCC readings: "nilaji haiyā valiye sajani śunaha āmāra kathā",
"mo'pāne cāya", "māthāra śapatha diyā". B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-51]: "The husband's aunt" (māsaisa, māsaśāśa) — the mother-in-law's sister, come on a visit. The plot is an obstacle to darshana: the same convention
as in nos. 17–18 (the elders prevent the heroine from seeing the beloved).
[^29-52]: The ending is a playful remark by the poet: "don't you know stratagems to get round your aunt?" Cf. 17.8 and notes 47, 49.

## 20. Narahari — "śuna go sajani suradhunī-ghāṭa haite…" (GPT1 pp. 192–193, no. 92; GCC 7.8)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: returning alone from the ghat of the Suradhuni, she met the Moon of Nadia on the road; at the sight of His face
she forgot composure and shame — the pot fell and broke; someone told her sister-in-law, who came running in fury; the young wife wept so that the
