sister-in-law's anger passed, and invented a story: the sister-in-law's friends abuse her at every corner, and she herself, unable to bear it,
broke the pot in anger; the sister-in-law, pleased, comforted her. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 8.*[^29-53]

**20.1.** "Listen, friend: I was coming alone from the ghat of the Suradhuni —
and on the road I met the Moon of Nadia.

**20.2.** What wondrous sweetness! His gait is lovelier than an elephant's;
I do not know who made this image of love embodied, and how.

**20.3.** To what shall I compare Him? I long to take Gora in His new attire
and either hide Him in my heart or make Him the pupil of my eyes.

**20.4.** As I looked at that face, composure, dharma and shame went far away;
the pot fell from my hip to the ground and broke into a hundred pieces.[^29-54]

**20.5.** What could I do? — having given my life and youth gladly to the Beloved of my soul,
in fear of the elders I came home and sat with grief in my heart.

**20.6.** I do not know who told my sister-in-law that the pot was broken;
in terrible anger, like a forest fire, she came rushing.

**20.7.** No trick would work, seeing her fearsome look —
I clutched my head with both hands and wept till my eyes were swollen.

**20.8.** Seeing my immoderate weeping, she let go of her anger;
calming down, she asks again and again — I gave no answer.

**20.9.** After a little while, having thought it over, she took my hand
and says softly, softly: 'Why don't you open your heart to me?'

**20.10.** With difficulty, in a faltering voice, I told her,
weeping, with grief in my heart: 'Why do you ask in vain?[^29-55]

**20.11.** Those whom you hold dear as life do terrible things:
at the ghat, in the field, on the road they slander you — I was ashamed to hear it.

**20.12.** I thought of tying the pot to my neck and throwing myself into the Ganga,
but could not — lest an ill name should spread about the family.

**20.13.** What could I do? I cannot quarrel with them;
all the ill they say of you — I heard it and was bewildered.

**20.14.** Whom could I call as a witness? No one was with me there;
in anger at them I broke the pot on the road.'

**20.15.** Hearing this, she was overjoyed, caressed me,
comforted me in every way and wiped my face with her own hand.

**20.16.** So yesterday I boldly escaped a terrible fix."
Narahari says: I take upon myself all the ills of your cleverness![^29-56]

[^29-53]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — pp. 192–193, no. 92 (scan PDF pp. 451–452); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 92 (catalogue: NG-085). GCC — kirana 7, pada 8 (pp. 70–71); GCC
readings: "dhīre dhīre kahe kisera lāgiyā nā kaha marama more", "śuniyā pāiye lāja", "paśiye gaṅgāra jale", "mukha mochāla āpana kare". B.
Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-54]: "Broke into a hundred pieces" — the motif of the broken pot (cf. nos. 8, 12 and note 27). "Composure, dharma and shame went away" — see note 28.
[^29-55]: After 20.10 GPT1 (p. 192, at the bottom) has an extra half-line "ki karili taila phelāli, valaye śāśuṛī" ("'What have you done — you've spilt the
oil!' says the mother-in-law"), which is not in GCC and does not fit the story (it is the sister-in-law who speaks); probably an insertion or a
printer's error. It is not included in the translation.
[^29-56]: "I take upon myself all the ills" (vālāi laiyā mari) is a formula of admiration (cf. note 43): the poet delights in the heroine's resourcefulness.
The invented story about the sister-in-law's friends is the same convention of "stratagems" (note 47).

## 21. Narahari — "ki kava sajani nanadera kathā…" (GPT1 pp. 193–194, no. 93; GCC 7.9)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: her sister-in-law, who thought herself the only faithful wife in Nadia and would not let her speak to anyone,
yesterday went for water herself and on the road to the ghat saw Gora with His companions — and lost all composure: the pot fell, her hair came
loose, her clothes slipped; coming to herself, she in embarrassment begged her brother's wife to keep the secret and promised to help her in
everything; "I did not spread it — a noble person guards another's shame." Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7,
pada 9.*[^29-57]

**21.1.** "What shall I say of my sister-in-law, friend? — it is laughable to tell:
she is a faithful wife, and all the women of Nadia, by her reckoning, are unfaithful.

**21.2.** And worse: she will not let me say a word to anyone,
she is forever scolding — I dare not go anywhere alone for fear.

**21.3.** With grief in my heart, day and night, I was dying, hearing her abuse;
I prayed to the Creator: let her pride be destroyed.

**21.4.** I do not know for what merit the merciful Creator heard my plea:
what I had in mind soon came true.

**21.5.** Listen to how it was: yesterday she went off, taking her pot;
and I followed behind her, with her leave.

**21.6.** On the road by which we both go to the ghat of the Suradhuni,
on that very road Gora stands with His dear companions.

**21.7.** Seeing the sweetness of that form, my sister-in-law could not keep her composure:
she began to shake all over, trembling under Madana's onslaught.[^29-58]

**21.8.** The pot fell from her hip to the ground, her hair came loose,
her clothes slip from her body of themselves — and there is not a trace of memory.

**21.9.** With difficulty she regained her composure, greatly embarrassed,
took me by both hands and says softly, softly, looking into my face:

**21.10.** 'Know for certain: you, my virtuous brother's wife, are dearer to me than life;
all I have said to you — do not hold it against me; I am in your power.

**21.11.** Whatever you do — tell me without embarrassment;
I will help you, even at the cost of my life,' she swears.

**21.12.** 'Only tell no one about this, keep it secret;
I have fallen into this rasa — what can I say? — Gaurahari has driven me mad!'

**21.13.** Thus she said much — hearing it, my joy knew no bounds,
and remembering what had gone before, much bitterness rose in me.

**21.14.** I thought: what is the use of spreading all this?"
Narahari says: one whose conduct is noble guards another's shame.[^29-59]

[^29-57]: Signature: "Narahari." GPT1 — pp. 193–194, no. 93 (scan PDF pp. 452–453); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 93 (catalogue: NG-086; "nadera" for "nanadera"). GCC — kirana 7,
pada 9 (pp. 71–72); GCC readings: "teṃha pativratā" (so also GPT1), "haila viṣama tharahari tanu" (GPT1 "narahari tanu" — a printer's error: a signature
is out of place here), "prāṇadhana diyā sahāya kariva valaye śapatha khā'yā". B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^29-58]: "Madana's onslaught" (madana-bhare) — attraction, of which the original speaks directly; translated precisely. 21.7–21.8 are signs of being
overwhelmed (trembling, the falling pot, loosened hair, slipping clothes, oblivion), usual in the padas about the gopis at the sight of Krishna
(cf. *Bhag.* 10.29 and note 79 of chapter 28). The tradition does not accept the image of Gaura as nagara (introductory note, chapter 27); the Lord
Himself here only stands with His companions by the road.
[^29-59]: The ending is a moral maxim of the poet: a noble person does not divulge another's disgrace. The translation is faithful to the author.

## Summary of chapter 29

*The chapter opens the nagari padas signed "Narahari" from section 3.2 of GPT. Before translating, section 3.2 of GPT1 (pp. 157–237, 180 padas) was
read through on the scan: 95 padas bear Narahari's signature, of which 32 were not in the catalogue (new lines NG-334…365); the witness of almost
all the long padas of this series is Narahari Chakravarti's *Gaura-charita-chintamani*, kiranas 7–11 ("the nagaris of Navadvipa"), which confirms
Majumdar's argument: the long padas of GPT with this signature are not Sarakara's. Translated: the cycle of the *Bhakti-ratnakara* (12th wave) —
the speeches of the "anuragavatis", the women of Nadia, by the tree on the bank of the Ganga (nos. 1–7: five padas of Yadunandana, a pada of Yadu
and a pada of Narahari Chakravarti; in them the townswomen see Gaura in the bhava of Krishna calling Radha and recognize in Him "the Moon of
Gokula"); the short padas of GPT1 3.2 nos. 39–45 in simple Bengali, which the GPT2 index assigns to Sarakara (nos. 8–13; "probably Sarakara" — C,
no. 43 — "not established"); the beginning of the 7th kirana of GCC — the townswomen's morning conversations and their stories of how, deceiving
their elders, they saw Gaura (nos. 14–21; "probably Chakravarti" — B). The padas of other poets of the section (nos. 49–60, Govinda Dasa, Jnanadasa)
were not translated; Lochana Dasa's padas (nos. 61–85, 116) are translated in chapters 28 and 34.*

# Chapter 30. Nagari Padas — IV: the "Narahari" padas of GPT (sect. 3.2, nos. 94–110, 120–123)

*On what nagari-bhava is, the position of the tradition (Vrindavana Dasa, Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati) and the rules of translation, see the introductory note to the section of nagari padas in chapter 27; on the two poets named Narahari (Narahari Sarakara and Narahari Chakravarti) and on the attribution labels ("probably Sarakara", "probably Chakravarti", "not established"), see the introductory note to the "Narahari" appendix in chapter 17.*

## 1. Narahari — "śuna śuna ago parāṇa soi…" (GPT1 p. 194, no. 94; GCC 7.10)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman complains to her friend about her household: whenever she sighs and murmurs "Gora", her mother-in-law burns with
anger, her sister-in-law is like poison, the neighbours taunt her day and night, she lives like a bird in a cage; but yesterday the Creator took
pity — at the close of day Gaura passed along their street, and she secretly saw Him from the window: His face, brows, eyes, garland, gait; and
the pain of her heart only doubled. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 10.*[^30-1]

**1.1.** Listen, listen, friend of my heart: I know you feel my pain — so to you I will tell it.

**1.2.** The ways of our house are unheard of in the land: as I tell them, my heart weeps.

**1.3.** If only I sigh, murmuring "Gora", the old woman hears and burns with anger.

**1.4.** My sister-in-law is like deadly poison: through her "virtues" my life is burnt away.

**1.5.** The neighbours are nothing but thorns to a good name: day and night they prick me with taunts.

**1.6.** Whom, friend, shall I call to witness this? I stay at home like a bird in a cage.

**1.7.** What more shall I tell of all this? There is no end to my sorrow.

**1.8.** But yesterday the Creator was kind to me — he put the moon of the sky into my hand.

**1.9.** At the close of day Gaura Raya was walking along our street.

**1.10.** Hurrying to the window, unseen, I saw Him.

**1.11.** How sweet is that moon of a face — a snare for the hearts of young women!

**1.12.** The curve of His brows is so graceful — who has the composure to bear it?

**1.13.** His eyes, outdoing wagtails, dance — I understood: from them no one escapes.

**1.14.** A garland of flowers sways at His throat — seeing it, many a Kamadeva swoons.[^30-2]

**1.15.** What more shall I say of that wondrous beauty? His gait enchants the world.

**1.16.** For only a moment could I see Him there — and the pain of my heart grew twofold.

**1.17.** Narahari says: sorrow will not remain — all will come to pass as your heart desires.[^30-3]

[^30-1]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 194, no. 94 (scan PDF p. 453); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 94 (catalogue: NG-336). GCC — kirana 7, pada 10 (ed. 1947,
p. 73; scan PDF p. 78). Nos. 94–99 of this chapter continue the 7th kirana of GCC — the townswomen of Navadvipa telling their friends in the morning
(beginning — chapter 29, nos. 14–21): GCC 7.10–7.12 = nos. 94–96, 7.14–7.16 = nos. 97–99; GCC 7.13 (how a townswoman remembered Gaura while cooking)
was not taken into GPT. GCC pp. 73–80 were checked against the scan (PDF pp. 78–85; re-OCRed with tesseract); pp. 81–88 (GCC 7.17–7.28) are missing
from the only available scan (see n. 18). GCC readings: "parāṇa sai" (so also GPT2), "deya e khom̐ṭā", "bhuruyuga vara bhaṅgima chānde". Metre — short payar (a couplet to a
line). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-2]: "Many a Kamadeva swoons" (mūrache kateka kāma) — the usual praise in the padas of the Lord's beauty, surpassing that of the god of love
(cf. Krishna's name Madana-mohana, "He who enchants Madana himself").
[^30-3]: The poet's consolation is a convention of the purvaraga padas; in the GCC padas the fulfilment of the wish is a darshan of Gaura seen from
afar (cf. nos. 2–3 and 5).

## 2. Narahari — "ki valiva ago gharera kathā…" (GPT1 pp. 195–196, no. 95; GCC 7.11)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: yesterday morning her mother-in-law went out, leaving her with her sister-in-law; the latter picked a quarrel
and went off in a huff to the neighbours; alone at the window, the townswoman saw Gaura passing and threw Him a withered kumuda bud; Gora, taking
it, said to the flower: "Do not grieve — the moon will rise"; at His glance she lost all strength; to her mother-in-law, on her return, she
complained of her sister-in-law and explained her agitation by fatigue and fear — and the mother-in-law comforted her and scolded the
sister-in-law. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 11.*[^30-4]

**2.1.** "What shall I say, friend, of what goes on in our house? If you hear it, it will pain you too.

**2.2.** Yesterday, as soon as night gave way to a bright morning, I secretly saw the Moon Gaura.

**2.3.** Perish shame now — what can it do to me? Something of it I will tell you.

**2.4.** Leaving me with my sister-in-law, my mother-in-law went off to the other end of the village.

**2.5.** And here my sister-in-law picked a quarrel and said many bad things to me,

**2.6.** and, to have her own way, she dropped everything and went off in a huff to someone else's house.

**2.7.** I stayed at home alone; I went and sat by the window.

**2.8.** Thinking of Gaura's beauty and virtues, I kept my eyes on the road.

**2.9.** And at that very moment Gauranga, the dear friend, appeared in our street.

**2.10.** Gazing unseen at that moonlike face, I forgot a little of the sorrow of my heart.

**2.11.** At once I threw a withered kumuda bud through the window.

**2.12.** Seeing it, Gora — and He is very quick-witted — took it in His hand and says, speaking to the kumuda:

**2.13.** 'Do not grieve: the moon will rise, and the heat of the sun will go far away.'[^30-5]

**2.14.** Having said this, smiling, He glanced just once from the corner of His eye towards me.

**2.15.** At once my body lost all strength, as if a deadly snake had bitten me.

**2.16.** Try as I might, I could not keep my composure: I longed to go and touch Him.[^30-6]

**2.17.** I tremble all over, my body sweats; I rise to walk — my feet will not move.

**2.18.** What shall I say? Trying to calm my heart, I remained in great agitation.

**2.19.** Just then my mother-in-law came home and asks me: 'Why are you like this?'

**2.20.** Very piteously I told her: 'My sister-in-law will not let me live in the house.

**2.21.** When you yourself are at home, she says nothing, but her heart burns like fire.

**2.22.** You left the house to go there — and here she picked a quarrel with me.

**2.23.** There is no end to the telling of it; and there was no fault of mine in it at all.

**2.24.** If you have any doubt in your mind, ask the neighbours here.

**2.25.** What shall I say! Leaving me alone, my sister-in-law went off to someone else's house —

**2.26.** judge from this how much sense she has. And why I am like this — listen:

**2.27.** besides being afraid all alone, I was also thinking of the housework;

**2.28.** whatever I did, I grew very tired, and that is why my head was spinning.'

**2.29.** Hearing my faltering words, my mother-in-law tenderly laid her hand on my head,

**2.30.** fanned me with the end of her own cloth, took my hands and comforted me at length.

**2.31.** Calling my sister-in-law, she scolded her — and hearing that, I was delighted."

**2.32.** Narahari says: you are truly fortunate — who else knows such tricks?[^30-7]

[^30-4]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 195–196, no. 95 (scan PDF pp. 454–455); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 95 (catalogue: NG-087). GCC — kirana 7, pada 11
(pp. 73–75; scan PDF pp. 78–80). GCC readings: "henai samaye gaurāṅga ekā" (GPT1 "gaurāṅgasakhā"; the GCC reading, "Gauranga alone", rhymes better with
dekhā), "nija kara dila āmāri māthe". Short payar. On 2.13 GPT1 has an editor's footnote with an interpretation (not reproduced). B. Nagari-bhava —
see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-5]: The kumuda is the white night-lily: it opens at moonrise and closes under the sun; in poetry it is an image of the loving woman pining for
her moon-beloved. The withered bud thrown from the window is the townswoman's mute sign ("I wither without my moon"); Gora answers the flower, not
her: "the moon will rise, and the heat of the sun will go." The moon (śaśī, cām̐da) is a constant name of Gaura in the GCC padas ("the Moon of
Nadia"), so the answer is both consolation and a promise of darshan; translated literally, without interpretation.
[^30-6]: The longing "to go and touch" and the signs of agitation (loss of strength, trembling, sweat) are stated plainly in the original; translated
exactly. These are formulas of purvaraga shared with the padas on the gopis; the Lord merely passes along the street and answers the flower. The
tradition does not accept worship of Gaura in the nagari mood (introductory note, chapter 27).
[^30-7]: The deception of the mother-in-law (the complaint against the sister-in-law, "fatigue" instead of the true cause) and the poet's praise of
the "tricks" are rendered as in the original — a poetic convention of the purvaraga padas (cf. n. 47 of chapter 29).

## 3. Narahari — "śuna go sajani valie tore…" (GPT1 p. 196, no. 96; GCC 7.12)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: putting on a new sari, she went alone to her brother's house and on the way met Gora; at His glance she lost
her composure and barely made it home; her mother-in-law, seeing tears in her eyes, asked what had happened — "I went out of the gate and saw a
terrible snake"; the frightened mother-in-law splashed water on her face. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7,
pada 12.*[^30-8]

**3.1.** "Listen, friend, I will tell you: I do not know what has come over me.

**3.2.** Hastily putting on a new sari, I set out alone for my brother's house.

**3.3.** On the way I met Gora — what shall I say? There is no measure to His beauty.

**3.4.** He glanced just once towards me — and I do not know what He did with the corner of His eye:

**3.5.** composure, dharma, modesty — all there was perished at that very moment.

**3.6.** My heart became I know not how — I reason with it and cannot calm it.

**3.7.** In agitation I walk — my feet will not move; my whole body trembles and trembles.

**3.8.** Again and again my clothes slip from my body — and He, seeing all this, smiles.[^30-9]

**3.9.** What could I do? For fear of the elders I somehow made my way home.

**3.10.** And there again my body languishes without the sight of that beautiful Gaura.

**3.11.** Just at that moment my mother-in-law came, sat down beside me and asks:

**3.12.** 'Why are you like this today? Your eyes are brimming with tears.

**3.13.** You speak so piteously — I do not know what pain has come to you.'

**3.14.** Hearing this, I told her: 'I had gone out of the gate,

**3.15.** and there I saw a terrible snake — my heart shook, all my courage was gone.

**3.16.** Then it slid away into the ditch — I was saved by the power of your feet.'

**3.17.** Hearing this, she grew very alarmed and herself splashed water on my eyes and face."[^30-10]

**3.18.** Narahari says: you fear nothing — you certainly know how to fool your mother-in-law!

p. 80). GCC has two extra couplets: after 3.15 — "se punaḥ mo pāne āila dhāiyā | palāinu mui vyākula haiyā ||" ("It rushed at me — I fled in
alarm"), after 3.17 — "nija kara dhari āmāra śire | māne śive kata manera ḍare ||" ("Laying her hand on my head, she in fear vowed many offerings to
Shiva"); the translation follows GPT1. Short payar. B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-9]: The slipping clothes are a sign of agitation, as in the padas on the gopis (cf. n. 58 of chapter 29); the original states it plainly, translated
exactly. The Lord's smile is the same as in no. 2 (2.14): He merely passes along the road. The tradition does not accept the image of Gaura as
nagara (introductory note, chapter 27).
[^30-10]: "A terrible snake" is an ambiguous answer: in no. 2 (2.15) Gaura's glance stung the townswoman "as if a deadly snake had bitten" her. The

## 4. Narahari — "nanadī vicāra kariyā garave…" (GPT1 pp. 196–197, no. 97; GCC 7.14)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: her sister-in-law, having planned mischief, dressed up and went for water, leaving her alone at home; on the
road she met Gaura with His companions and, forgetting all her schemes, followed Him with the pot on her hip; the mother-in-law caught her so and
snatched away the pot — while the daughter-in-law meanwhile saw Gaura on her own road; the mother-in-law praised her, and the sister-in-law was
put to shame. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 14 (second half).*[^30-11]

**4.1.** "Having thought it all out, my sister-in-law proudly put on a new sari
and went to fetch water, leaving me alone at home.

**4.2.** Gleeful, she hurried along her road —
and along that very road, with His companions, comes Gaura Raya.

**4.3.** Seeing the sweetness of that form, my sister-in-law quite lost her head:
all the schemes she had in mind she clean forgot.

**4.4.** Along that road came my mother-in-law — and, looking, sees her close by:
with the pot on her hip she is wandering after Gaurangachand.[^30-12]

**4.5.** 'Very good, very good!' she said in great anger, and snatched away the pot;
what could my sister-in-law say, and to whom? — she wished the earth would swallow her.

**4.6.** And I meanwhile, meeting beautiful Gauranga, my life, on my own road,
eased the pain of my heart gazing at that moonlike face.

**4.7.** A little later my mother-in-law came and praised me at length;
and what shall I say of my sister-in-law's shame — she is at home as if she were not there."

**4.8.** Narahari says: one who is a fool sees nothing:
tying her own fault in the end of her sari, she seeks to blame another.

[^30-11]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 196–197, no. 97 (scan PDF pp. 455–456); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 97 (catalogue: NG-089). GCC — kirana 7, pada 14
(pp. 77–79; scan PDF pp. 82–84). In GCC the pada is twice as long: GPT begins it from the middle (GCC "erūpa vicāra kariyā garave" — "having thus
thought it out…"; GPT "nanadī vicāra kariyā"). In the omitted first half (13 couplets, pp. 77–78) the townswoman tells how her sister-in-law and
her friends plotted to disgrace her: she told the mother-in-law that the bride would bring shame on the house with "a brahmana's son" (a hint at
Gaura); the mother-in-law replied that she would believe it only when she saw it with her own eyes; then the sister-in-law resolved to leave the
bride alone, on her way to fetch water to send a young man she knew to the house, and then to call the neighbours and expose her. The translation
follows GPT1; the omitted part is not translated (the text is that of GPT), only retold here. GCC readings in the second half: "prāṇa-gaurāṅgasundare",
"praśaṃsā karaye more". B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-12]: The strict sister-in-law who forgets her schemes at the sight of Gaura is a recurrent motif of GCC (cf. chapter 29, no. 21): even the
townswomen's adversaries lose their composure on seeing Gaura. The Lord here merely walks along the road with His companions.

## 5. Narahari — "ki valiva sakhi kakhana saphala…" (GPT1 p. 197, no. 98; GCC 7.15)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: her wish has never come true — the Creator has always put obstacles in the way; but yesterday, hearing that
Gaura was coming, she went up to the upper gallery and saw Him; the fragrance of His body reached her; Gora turned towards her — and just then her
mother-in-law called her; she went away, but the mother-in-law let her go for water. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** —
GCC, kirana 7, pada 15.*[^30-13]

**5.1.** "What shall I say, friend? Never has the wish of my heart come true:
to make me suffer, the pitiless Creator has put many obstacles in the way.

**5.2.** But yesterday, truly, along our road came the Beloved of my life;
hearing of it from people, I took courage, went up and stood on the upper gallery.[^30-14]

**5.3.** Seeing the sweetness of that form, both my eyes were drowned in it;
I thought: if only I could become a bird and fly to Him!

**5.4.** The fragrance of His graceful body came and entered my nostrils;
I lost all calm — what shall I say? There was no end to my joy.

**5.5.** Gora turned and looked towards me — and at that very moment the old woman
keeps calling and calling me; my heart shook — I came away, leaving that joy.

**5.6.** She gave me leave to go for water — I floated on waters of joy."
Narahari says: such a mother-in-law is found only by great good fortune.

[^30-13]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 197, no. 98 (scan PDF p. 456); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 98 (catalogue: NG-337). GCC — kirana 7, pada 15 (pp. 79–80; scan
PDF pp. 84–85); GCC readings: "loka mukhe śuni sāhase upara-dālāne dām̐ṛānu giyā", "bhāgyete mile". In letting her daughter-in-law go for water (to the
Ganga), the mother-in-law unknowingly lets her see Gaura again — hence the poet's playful praise. B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the
section (chapter 27).
[^30-14]: "The Beloved of my life" (parāṇa-piyā) — the heroine's word for Gaura, as in the padas on the gopis for Krishna (cf. n. 46 of chapter 29);
the translation is faithful to the author.

## 6. Narahari — "sajani, kata nā kahiva āmāra dukhera kāhinī kathā…" (GPT1 p. 197, no. 99; GCC 7.16)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: her mother-in-law, hearing that Gaura was coming, hurried home, bolted the door and sat in the courtyard on
guard; the daughter-in-law pressed her eyes to a tiny window and saw Gaura among His companions; with a look she let Him know how it was with her;
when the mother-in-law unbolted the door, the daughter-in-law was already sitting by the hearth. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably
Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 16.*[^30-15]

**6.1.** "Friend, however much I tell, there is no end to my tale of woe;
but yesterday the merciful Creator relieved my pain a little.

**6.2.** Leaving me at the cooking, my mother-in-law had gone out of the house;
hearing that Gaura was coming, she came back to me at once.

**6.3.** Glancing at me once more, she bolted the door of the house,
sat down in the middle of the courtyard and kept watching warily on every side.

**6.4.** And here my heart is in turmoil — I see no way out;
there was a tiny window — to it I pressed both my eyes.

**6.5.** Among His companions — the Crown of connoisseurs of rasa; who can fathom His ways?
Glancing about quite unobtrusively, He walks with the gait of an elephant.

**6.6.** Beholding but once the sweetness of that form, meeting His eyes with mine,
I, as if catching His sign, let Him know what state I was in.

**6.7.** Coming level with me, the Jewel of the clever smiled a little and spoke;
and I sat down again at the cooking — and then my one-eyed mother-in-law unbolted the door.[^30-16]

**6.8.** Squinting sideways, she looked at me with her left eye and was reassured."
Narahari says: if that calamity of an eye were gone too, all would be well![^30-17]

[^30-15]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 197, no. 99 (scan PDF p. 456); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 99 (catalogue: NG-090). GCC — kirana 7, pada 16 (p. 80; scan PDF
p. 85) — the last pada of GCC before the lacuna in the scan (pp. 81–88 are missing; the next surviving one is GCC 7.29 = GPT1 no. 124). GCC readings:
"āmāke randhane rākhiyā", "alapa gavākṣa āchila tāhāte sam̐pinu yugala ām̐khi", "calaye kuñjara-gati". B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the
section (chapter 27).
[^30-16]: "Crown of connoisseurs of rasa" (rasikaśekhara), "Jewel of the clever" (caturamaṇi), "the gait of an elephant" are epithets of Krishna
transferred by the poet to Gaura; what He said the pada does not tell. As in the other GCC padas, the Lord merely passes along the street among His
companions; all the rest takes place in the townswoman's heart.
[^30-17]: The poet's joke at the one-eyed (kāṇī) mother-in-law — literally "let that calamity of an eye be gone too, and it will be well"; translated
without softening.

## 7. Narahari — "ekadina āmi śāśuṛī nanadī vasiyāchi āṅgināya…" (GPT1 p. 198, no. 100)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's comic story: once she, her mother-in-law and her sister-in-law were sitting in the courtyard when Gauranga passed by;
the sister-in-law, gazing at Him, so forgot herself that her clothes fell from her; the daughter-in-law went to dress her — and forgot herself
the same way; the mother-in-law came to rebuke them — and the same befell her; coming to their senses, the mother-in-law told her daughter-in-law
to tell no one. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only; not in the surviving pages of GCC (it may have stood on the lost
pp. 81–88).*[^30-18]

**7.1.** "One day we — I, my mother-in-law and my sister-in-law — were sitting in the courtyard;
through the back gate I looked out and saw: Gauranga Raya is passing.

**7.2.** As befits a modest woman, I drew my veil and stayed seated;
but my sister-in-law, first of all, intoxicated by Madana, stood up, smiling and smiling.

**7.3.** Gazing and gazing through the window, she began to look at Gora;
seeing that her clothes had come loose, my mother-in-law shouted at her.

**7.4.** Overpowered, gazing at Gora's form, my sister-in-law did not hear that shout;
and as she gazed, her clothes fell from her — she was left quite naked.[^30-19]

**7.5.** Seeing this, I, laughing and laughing, went to dress her —
dress her, indeed! — looking at Gaura's form, I too was left naked.

**7.6.** To rebuke the two of us, my mother-in-law came over in anger —
what a deed of the Creator! — looking at Gauranga, the old woman too became naked.

**7.7.** Naked, the three of us gazed at Gora;
and as we gazed, He — the star of our eyes — went away, leaving us sightless.

**7.8.** Then all three of us came to our senses and bit our tongues;
my mother-in-law said: 'Daughter-in-law, tell no one of today's disgrace.'"

**7.9.** Narahari says: who will say what? — the plight of all three is the same:
keep quiet and carefully cover the cut-off ear with your hair.[^30-20]

[^30-18]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 198, no. 100 (scan PDF pp. 456–457); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 100 (catalogue: NG-338). **No witnesses.** GPT1 nos. 86–99
and 124–180 stand in the same order as the padas of Narahari Chakravarti's *Gaura-charita-chintamani* (GCC 7.2–7.16 and 7.29 onwards), so nos. 100–110
and 120–123, absent from the OCR text of GCC, were checked against the scan of GCC (ed. 1947; IA gaurcharitra-chintamani, the only available copy):
the scan (a 200-page PDF) **lacks printed pp. 81–88** — after p. 80 (PDF 85; end of GCC 7.16 = no. 99) comes p. 89 at once (PDF 86; beginning of GCC
7.29 = no. 124), and PDF pp. 94–98 repeat pp. 89–93. The lost pages held GCC 7.17–7.28 — 12 padas; in GPT this place holds 15 padas signed Narahari
(nos. 100–110, 120–123; between them — padas of Vasu, Lochana, Jnanadasa and no. 119 = GCC, kirana 2). Eight pages of GCC hold about 95 couplets of
the long metre, and the 15 GPT padas about 113; so most of them probably come from GCC, but all 15 cannot have stood there, and which ones did
cannot be established from the available sources. BR, *Gita-chandrodaya*, PK, KGC, PS, *Narottama-vilasa* — none of these padas. Hence nos. 100–110
and 120–123 are labelled "not established" (C), with a note on their probable origin in GCC. In tone — a rather coarse joke — this pada stands
out among the GCC padas. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-19]: 7.2–7.6: "intoxicated by Madana" (madane mātiyā) and the nakedness of the three women are as in the original; translated exactly, without
additions. It is a hyperbole of self-forgetfulness (in the *Bhagavata* the gopis running to Krishna put their clothes and ornaments on wrongly —
*Bhag.* 10.29), carried here to the point of a joke; the Lord merely passes by the house. The *Chaitanya-bhagavata* says plainly that in Navadvipa
the Lord did not look at women, and the Gaudiya tradition does not accept worship of Gaura in the nagari mood (introductory note, chapter 27); such
padas are a monument of late poetry, not an image of the Lord.
[^30-20]: "To cover the cut-off ear with one's hair" (cula diyā kāṭā kāṇa ḍhākā) — a proverb: to hide one's disgrace.

## 8. Narahari — "ki kava sajani āṅgināra mājhe…" (GPT1 p. 199, no. 101)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: hearing that Gora was approaching their house, she hastily finished the housework so as to go and look — but
her mother-in-law, guessing, shouted at her, and she could not take a single step. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only
(see n. 18).*[^30-21]

**8.1.** "What shall I say, friend? We were sitting in the middle of the courtyard —
and we heard: Gora, Shachi's son, is coming near our house.

**8.2.** To go there, I hastily finished the housework;
I was so impatient that no shame was left in me.

**8.3.** Guessing it, my mother-in-law shouted at me — my body trembled with fear;
it was as if a thunderbolt crashed on my head — I could not take a step.

**8.4.** So I remained, stricken with grief — no word would leave my lips."
Narahari says: while there is a mother-in-law, the pain of the heart will not go.

[^30-21]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 199, no. 101 (scan PDF p. 458); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 101 (catalogue: NG-339). No witnesses; probably from the lost
pages of GCC (pp. 81–88), but this cannot be established (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).

## 9. Narahari — "śuna śuna sai kālikāra kathā ki āra valiva tore…" (GPT1 p. 199, no. 102)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: yesterday her mother-in-law was instructing her in the dharma of a noble wife — when a wondrous sound of kirtana
arose; hearing the mridangas, the mother-in-law became as if mad, dropped her work and called her daughter-in-law to come along; to her excuses she
replied: "Look but once on that moonlike face — and your life will not be in vain." Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only
(see n. 18).*[^30-22]

**9.1.** "Listen, listen, friend, about yesterday — what more shall I tell you?
My mother-in-law set about teaching me the dharma of a noble, faithful wife.

**9.2.** And at that very moment a wondrous sound of kirtana arose —
hearing the voice of the mridanga, my mother-in-law became as if mad.

**9.3.** Dropping her own work, hurrying there, unable to keep still on the way,
she says to me impatiently: 'Come with me!'

**9.4.** But I told her: 'All the housework is lying here undone;
and besides, I am a wife of a noble family — how can I go there?'

**9.5.** Hearing this, she says: 'Doing the housework, you die every day;
look but once on that moonlike face — and make your birth fruitful.'

**9.6.** Hearing this, I joyfully hurried there and gazed to my eyes' content."
Narahari says: I take upon myself all the ills of your mother-in-law![^30-23]

[^30-22]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 199, no. 102 (scan PDF p. 458); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 102 (catalogue: NG-340). No witnesses; probably from the lost
pages of GCC (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-23]: The strict mother-in-law whom the sound of Gaura's kirtana makes "mad" is an image of the power of sankirtana, which even the elders of
Nadia could not resist (cf. *Chaitanya-bhagavata*, Madhya-khanda: the whole town gathers for the Lord's kirtana). Her words "make your birth
fruitful" are a call to the darshan of the Lord; the poet's praise is a formula of fond admiration (vālāi laiyā, cf. n. 43 of chapter 29).

## 10. Narahari — "śuna śuna sai divā avasāne…" (GPT1 pp. 199–200, no. 103)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: at the close of day, hearing that Gaura was coming, she joyfully went out of the gate — and, as ill luck would
have it, ran into her father-in-law there; he heaped abuse on her and in anger threatened to leave Nadia; at these words her heart sank. The poet's
consolation: who can leave Nadia? Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-24]

**10.1.** "Listen, listen, friend: at the close of day, full of joy,
hearing that Gaura was coming, I went out and stood by the gate.

**10.2.** The Creator mocked me: there I ran into my father-in-law;
how many harsh words he said to me, friend — there is no counting them.

**10.3.** In great anger he says: 'I will leave Nadia and live elsewhere — this very day!'
Hearing this, my heart stood still — all my hopes were gone.

**10.4.** So I remained, stricken with grief — who could console me?"
Narahari says: why worry? Who is able to leave Nadia?[^30-25]

[^30-24]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 199–200, no. 103 (scan PDF pp. 458–459); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 103 (catalogue: NG-341). No witnesses; probably from
the lost pages of GCC (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-25]: The poet's consolation means: no one will leave Nadia, where Gaura is (cf. no. 13: the father-in-law, on seeing Gaura, himself dances with
arms upraised). Translated literally.

## 11. Narahari — "śuna śuna ago mane chila āśā…" (GPT1 p. 200, no. 104)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: she had hoped to live in happiness, but the Creator settled her in a thicket of thorns: her father-in-law
coaches her kind mother-in-law — "Nimai's mridanga will soon sound to drive Nadia mad, and the young wives will run, heeding no one; go quickly and
bolt the door from outside"; how is she to see Him now? Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-26]

**11.1.** "Listen, listen, friend: I had a hope — to live in great happiness,
but the Creator has settled me in a forest of thorns — I am forever dying of this sorrow.

**11.2.** My father-in-law — a 'lord of virtues' — gives me much pain;
my mother-in-law is very kind, but he teaches her harsh words.

**11.3.** Sitting in private, he says to her softly: 'You stay at home,
and I will go there, settle the matter and come back quickly.

**11.4.** Soon Nimai's mridanga will sound to drive Nadia mad —
the young wives will run there, no one will heed anyone.

**11.5.** So go quickly and bolt the door of the house from outside.'
Much of this kind he says, and we hear it — and we are ashamed.

**11.6.** How then am I to see Him? The house has become unbearable."
Narahari says: one who is clever — would that frighten her?[^30-27]

[^30-26]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 200, no. 104 (scan PDF p. 459); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 104 (catalogue: NG-091). No witnesses; probably from the lost
pages of GCC (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-27]: The father-in-law calls the Lord by His household name — "Nimai" (nimāi); his fear of the kirtana that "drives Nadia mad" is an admission
of the power of sankirtana (cf. nos. 9 and 13). The poet's consolation is the same convention of the purvaraga padas as the praise of the
townswomen's tricks (n. 7).

## 12. Narahari — "dukhera kāhinī ki kava sajani…" (GPT1 pp. 200–201, no. 105)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: she burns in the taunts of the neighbours; her friend knows about her mother-in-law and sister-in-law, while her
father-in-law — a hunchbacked old man who can hardly walk — prays to Shiva with offerings that the young wives may not leave the house; and when Gaura
begins kirtana, the old man, hearing the mridangas, looks about in alarm, abuses everyone and sets a guard at the gate. The poet: who will forbid going
by the back gate? Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-28]

**12.1.** "What shall I tell of my woes, friend? I can bear it no longer:
I burn in the fire of the neighbours' taunts.

**12.2.** How my mother-in-law and sister-in-law treat me — do you not know, friend?
Of my father-in-law's 'virtues' it is not fit to speak — and yet I will tell you.

**12.3.** He sits at home — he has no strength even to walk, quite bent double —
and, gathering all sorts of things, he performs puja to Shiva in every manner.

**12.4.** With his cloth wound round his neck and both palms joined, he begs a boon:
'May the young wives keep still and not leave the house for a moment!'[^30-29]

**12.5.** Thus, with many prayers, he gets his way;
and I, standing behind the screen, hear it all — and am deeply ashamed.

**12.6.** And listen further: whenever the Jewel of virtues begins kirtana,
the old man, hearing the voice of the mridanga, is all alarm;

**12.7.** with eyes wide open he looks on every side — it is frightful to see —
and, twisting his face, speaks harsh words to everyone.

**12.8.** Guessing our intentions, he sets a guard at the gate."
Narahari says: but who forbids going by the back gate?

[^30-28]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 200–201, no. 105 (scan PDF pp. 459–460); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 105 (catalogue: NG-092). No witnesses; probably from
the lost pages of GCC (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-29]: A cloth wound round the neck and joined palms are a gesture of abject supplication. The old man prays to Shiva for a worldly end — that his
daughters-in-law stay at home; the poet sets his prayer against Gaura's kirtana (12.6), but does not disparage the worship of Shiva.

## 13. Narahari — "śuna go sajani śvaśurera kichu caritra…" (GPT1 p. 201, no. 106)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: her father-in-law instructed her at length and made her swear to guard the family's honour; but no sooner had
she sworn than the sound of the mridanga reached her — and she ran to where Gauranga was. The father-in-law chased her in a rage with a club — but,
glancing angrily at Gaurangachand, he could not take his eyes away, was caught in the net of prema, threw down the club and, raising his arms with
cries of "Hari, Hari!", broke into dance; afterwards he praised his daughter-in-law and himself begged her pardon. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution:
not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-30]

**13.1.** "Listen, friend, I will tell you something of my father-in-law's ways:
in private he instructed me at length, and then he says to me earnestly:

**13.2.** 'One thing troubles me greatly; and you are the daughter of good people:
touch my feet and swear that you will guard the honour of both families — otherwise what will become of us?'[^30-31]

**13.3.** Hearing this, I swore many oaths and dispelled his doubts —
and just then the nectar of the mridanga's sound entered my ears.

**13.4.** At once I ran off to where Gauranga Raya disports Himself;
learning of this deed of mine, my father-in-law became like fire.

**13.5.** He came running after me, seizing a fearsome club —
what could I do? — looking at my father-in-law, my heart stood still.

**13.6.** But with angry eyes he glanced just once at Gaurangachand —
and could not turn his eyes away: at once he fell into the net of prema.

**13.7.** In supreme joy he flung away the club from his hand
and, raising both arms and crying 'Hari, Hari!', he danced beside himself.

**13.8.** Having seen many such wonders, I went back home;
after a while he too came and praised me at length.

**13.9.** Taking my hand, he anxiously began to confess his fault;
seeing him so distressed, I bowed to his feet — and that made him glad."

**13.10.** Narahari says: now at last all awkwardness is gone;
by your grace the old man's hard heart has become good.[^30-32]

[^30-30]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 201, no. 106 (scan PDF p. 460); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 106 (catalogue: NG-093). No witnesses; probably from the lost
pages of GCC (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-31]: 13.2: "one thing troubles me greatly" (eka mora bahu bhrama; so GPT1 and GPT2) — the sense of the opening words is unclear; "both families"
(dudiga) — the father's family and the husband's.
[^30-32]: 13.6–13.7: the father-in-law who rushes at his daughter-in-law with a club and, at the sight of Gaura, breaks into dance crying "Hari!" is an
image of the transforming power of the Lord's darshan and of sankirtana; cf. the conversion of the opponents of kirtana in the
*Chaitanya-bhagavata* (Madhya-khanda). "By your grace" (tuyā kṛpāvale) — in the signatures of these padas the poet addresses the heroine; the words
can also be taken as addressed to Gaura.

## 14. Narahari — "rajanī divasa kakhana svapane…" (GPT1 pp. 201–202, no. 107)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's complaint: all her friends' hopes have been fulfilled, but she is "a wife in the corner": her mother-in-law abuses her
whenever she steps over the threshold, and to the ghat of the Suradhuni she is accompanied by her watchful sister-in-law, so that she dares not
even lift her veil. The poet advises her to outwit the wily one. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-33]

**14.1.** "Neither by day nor by night, nor even in dreams, do I know a trace of happiness;
my heart is worn out with longing, my body wasted away.

**14.2.** You will say: everyone's hopes have been fulfilled — why not yours?
What shall I say? Through the fault of my karma I have become a wife who sits in the corner.

**14.3.** If I step outside the house, my mother-in-law heaps abuse on me:
'Faithful? Unfaithful! No thought for your husband!' — I am a speck of grit in her eye.

**14.4.** And if some day I go to the ghat of the Suradhuni to bathe —
trusting no one else, my relentless sister-in-law goes along with me.

**14.5.** If on some pretext I wish to see Someone just once,
at her fierceness my body trembles — I dare not lift my thick veil.

**14.6.** She is very cunning, and to play tricks before her is frightening;
my heart is ill at ease — so, having bathed, I come straight home."

**14.7.** Narahari says: you, little friend, are a simpleton — why fear your sister-in-law?
To rob a thief you must throw dust in his eyes.[^30-34]

[^30-33]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 201–202, no. 107 (scan PDF pp. 460–461); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 107 (catalogue: NG-094). No witnesses; probably from
the lost pages of GCC (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-34]: "Someone" (kāhāke) — a bashful withholding of Gaura's name. "Little friend" (ājuli) — here, from the sense, "simpleton" (cf. n. 7 of
chapter 29: the exact meaning of the word is not established). "To rob a thief you must throw dust in his eyes" — a proverb (lit. "doing highway
robbery upon a thief, one must throw dust in his eyes"). The advice to outwit the elders is a poetic convention (n. 7).

## 15. Narahari — "ki kava sajani manera vedana kalaṅke pūrila deśa…" (GPT1 p. 202, no. 108)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's complaint: the whole neighbourhood is full of gossip about her, though she is in no way to blame — she has only heard
Gauranga's name from people, has never seen Him, and He does not know her; the neighbours sing of her "disgrace", for in youth every woman is to
blame. The poet does not believe her: there is no smoke without fire. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-35]

**15.1.** "What shall I say, friend, of the pain of my heart? The whole neighbourhood is full of talk about me,
though I am in no way to blame — not a trace of fault.

**15.2.** 'Gauranga, Gauranga' — I hear from people's lips, but what He is like I do not know;
I am a wife of a noble family, I sit in a corner of the house — who does not know me?

**15.3.** What beautiful Gauranga is like I have never seen, even from the corner of my eye;
I swear to you, I tell you truly: He does not even know me.

**15.4.** Dying of shame, I stay at home — I never go to other people's houses;
and still these neighbours of ours sing on and on of my disgrace.

**15.5.** Hearing and hearing empty slander, I burn twice over —
what can I say, and to whom? In youth one is just there to take the blame."

**15.6.** Narahari says: say what you will — the ear does not believe it:
if there were nothing, would anyone speak of another for no reason?[^30-36]

[^30-35]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 202, no. 108 (scan PDF p. 461); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 108 (catalogue: NG-095). No witnesses; probably from the lost
pages of GCC (n. 18). The last couplet is repeated in no. 123 (no. 21). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-36]: The townswoman's denial and the poet's disbelief are a game: in the padas of this series the very gossip about the "disgrace" of loving Gaura
is a sign of that love (cf. no. 16: "the whole world has gone mad with love of Him — why should I be the one to blame?"). Translated as in the
original.

## 16. Narahari Dasa — "ramaṇīramaṇa bhuvanamohana gaurāṅga-ratana sai…" (GPT1 pp. 202–203, no. 109)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman asks her friend: the whole world — children, old people, young men and women — has gone mad with love of Gauranga,
all float in joy seeing His dance and hearing the kirtana — why is she alone defamed? Better to drown herself than to live in Nadia; the poet: in
life and in death Gora will not forsake her. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-37]

**16.1.** "The Delight of women, the Enchanter of the world, Gauranga is a jewel, friend:
the whole world has gone mad with love of Him — why should I be the one to blame?[^30-38]

**16.2.** Children, old people, young men and young women weep at the sight of Gauranga —
why then am I alone disgraced? — words fail my lips.

**16.3.** That Gaurachandra is the joy of the world: everyone floats in joy;
but from my joyless eyes tears stream — through the fault of my karma, no doubt.

**16.4.** Whoever sees His dancing, whoever hears His kirtana — becomes intoxicated;
whom does it harm if I too, seeing and hearing, lose my senses?

**16.5.** I will live in Nadia no more — I will throw myself into the water and drown!"
In life and in death Gora will not forsake you, says Narahari Dasa.[^30-39]

[^30-37]: Signature — "Dasa Narahari" (dāsa narahari). GPT1 — pp. 202–203, no. 109 (misprinted "169"; scan PDF pp. 461–462); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 109 (catalogue:
NG-096). No witnesses; probably from the lost pages of GCC (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-38]: "The Delight of women" (ramaṇīramaṇa) — an epithet of Krishna transferred to Gaura (cf. n. 16); translated faithfully to the author. The
pada itself speaks of the whole world's love for Gaura — children, old people, young men (16.2) — and of His kirtana (16.4): the townswoman is
not alone in her love.
[^30-39]: "I will throw myself into the water and drown" is the usual formula of a loving woman's despair in the padas, not an intention; the poet's
answer reverses it: Gora will not forsake the one who loves Him, either in life or in death.

## 17. Narahari — "vidhātāra mane nā jāni ki āche…" (GPT1 p. 203, no. 110)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's complaint: yesterday she went to see Gorachand, and her husband, learning of it, heaped abuse on her; her
brother-in-law, unable to bear her distress, himself rebuked his brother. How then is the wish of her heart to be fulfilled? The poet: do not
grieve — folly will be destroyed. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-40]

**17.1.** "I do not know what the Creator had in mind when he gave me a human birth:
what shall I say? — in a fierce wildfire of sorrow my heart is ever burning.

**17.2.** Yesterday I went there to see Gorachand, the treasure of my life;
hearing of it, my senseless husband heaped hundreds of abuses on me.

**17.3.** My husband's younger brother was near — he cannot bear to see me unhappy;
hearing the reproach and the abuse, he at once rebuked his brother soundly.

**17.4.** Tell me, tell me, friend: how then will the wish of my heart be fulfilled?"
Narahari says: grieve no more — folly will be destroyed.[^30-41]

[^30-40]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 203, no. 110 (scan PDF p. 462); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 110 (catalogue: NG-097). No witnesses; probably from the lost
pages of GCC (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-41]: "The treasure of my life" (prāṇadhana) — the townswoman's word for Gaura (cf. n. 14). "Folly will be destroyed" (kumati haive nāśa) — from the
sense of the pada, the folly of the husband who abuses his wife for taking darshan of Gaura: the poet promises not a meeting in defiance of the
husband but a change in the husband himself (cf. GCC 7.29 = GPT1 no. 124: "my husband is very good" — the husband himself praises Nimai and does
not forbid the wives to see Him). On the motif "disregarding their husbands" see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).

## 18. Narahari — "śuna śuna ogo parāṇa sajani kahie tomāra prati…" (GPT1 pp. 205–206, no. 120)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: in her house she is loved — and yesterday she went with her husband's aunt to the house of Ai (Shachi); Ai
was very affectionate to her, but she did not see Gaurangachand, and her pain doubled; on the way back, envying Shachi's neighbours, she suddenly
saw Gora with His companions on her own road, lifted her veil a little — and lost her composure; the aunt too could not stand firm. Raga
"yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-42]

**18.1.** "Listen, listen, friend of my heart, to what I tell you:
my father-in-law and mother-in-law — I know not for what virtues — love me very much;

**18.2.** my sister-in-law holds me dear as life and never scolds me —
so yesterday I went with my husband's aunt to the house of Ai.[^30-43]

**18.3.** Ai was very affectionate to me — what need to tell it all!
But I did not see Gaurangachand — and the pain of my heart doubled.

**18.4.** After staying a little while, I took my leave and set off, sad at heart,
and I saw that the young wives who live in that quarter are in great happiness.

**18.5.** I thought: if only we all lived in this quarter,
then the hope that was in my heart would easily come true.

**18.6.** With quick steps I head for home, friend — and on the very road by which we go
Gora stands with His dear companions.

**18.7.** My husband's aunt beside me — I was in a fix: no word would leave my lips;
lifting my veil a little, I saw that moonlike face.

**18.8.** My clothes slip from my body, my whole body trembles;
somehow, slowly, slowly, I began to move my feet.

**18.9.** Turning back and back I gazed — my heart grew utterly bewildered;
it resolved for certain: neither shame, nor fear for the family, nor dharma will remain.[^30-44]

**18.10.** On that road my husband's aunt stopped too: seeing Him, she could not stand firm."
Narahari says: seeing that form, who would not lose herself?

[^30-42]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 205–206, no. 120 (scan PDF pp. 464–465); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 120 (catalogue: NG-099). No witnesses; probably from
the lost pages of GCC (n. 18): in its structure (a visit with the husband's aunt to another quarter, a meeting with Gora on the way back) the pada
is close to GCC 7.30 = GPT1 no. 125 (with the aunt — to the house of Murari Gupta). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section
(chapter 27).
[^30-43]: "My husband's aunt" (pisesa, pisi-śāśuṛī — the father-in-law's sister). "Ai" (āi, "mother") — Shachi-devi: the townswoman had gone to the house
of the Lord's mother.
[^30-44]: 18.8–18.9: the slipping clothes, the trembling, the resolve to cast off "shame, fear for the family and dharma" are stated plainly in the
original (cf. n. 9, and n. 41 of chapter 29: the formula of the supremacy of prema over worldly dharma); the Lord merely stands with His
companions on the road. The tradition does not accept worship of Gaura in the nagari mood (introductory note, chapter 27).

## 19. Narahari — "ki valiva ogo nanada āmāra, kevala viṣera phala…" (GPT1 pp. 206–207, no. 121)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's story: her sister-in-law is a veritable poison fruit, and no trick can be played before her; but she trusts the
friends and lets her brother's wife go to them at any time — and on this pretext she went yesterday to see Gaurangachand; there follows a
description of His form from head to foot. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-45]

**19.1.** "What shall I say, friend? My sister-in-law is a veritable poison fruit:
she is very cunning — before her we cannot play any trick.

**19.2.** But she trusts you very much — the pretence cannot be seen through:
morning, evening, night — she does not forbid me to come here.

**19.3.** On this pretext I went yesterday to see Gaurangachand:
is there a young woman who, seeing Him, could keep her composure?

**19.4.** How the weight of curling locks sways upon His back!
How lovely on His brow are the curls and the tilaka — to what shall I compare them?

**19.5.** How the brows curve, what a glance, what a signal of the eyes!
How wondrous the smile on His lips — His speech flows in a stream of nectar!

**19.6.** How the earrings sway in His ears, how beautiful His cheeks!
What a pearl in His nose, what a radiance of the lovely chin!

**19.7.** What a curve of the arms, what a garland of flowers at His throat!
How slender the waist, and the thighs like inverted plantain stems!

**19.8.** How the radiance of the nails of His lovely feet steals away the heart!"
Narahari says: having seen that form, how did you ever get home?[^30-46]

[^30-45]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 206–207, no. 121 (scan PDF pp. 465–466); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 121 (catalogue: NG-100). No witnesses; probably from
the lost pages of GCC (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^30-46]: 19.4–19.8 — a description of the Lord's form "from head to foot" (rupa-varnana) in the usual images of the padas on Krishna and Gaura (curling
locks down the back — Gaura before sannyasa; a slender waist, thighs like "inverted plantain stems", the radiance of the nails) — this is
contemplation of the Lord's beauty, not a worldly description. "A pearl in His nose" (nāsāra mukutā) — so in the original.

## 20. Narahari — "śuna śuna ogo parāṇa sajani nivedi tomāra āge…" (GPT1 p. 207, no. 122)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman's complaint: her sister-in-law is hard-hearted and knows nothing of another's pain; whenever she hears that Gauranga has
come to someone's house, she, on some pretext and unbeknown to the old woman, runs there herself — but forbids her brother's wife. The poet: such
is the way of sisters-in-law. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-47]

**20.1.** "Listen, listen, friend of my heart, to what I confide to you:
day and night I am dying with longing — my own home feels like a stranger's.

**20.2.** My sister-in-law is hard — what shall I say of her? It is bitter even to tell:
of another's pain she knows nothing at all — she knows only her own pleasure.

**20.3.** If she hears from anyone that Gauranga has come to someone's house,
she thinks up so many tricks — and the old woman of the house does not see through them —

**20.4.** and off she runs there, — but me, and this is the unfair part, she forbids!"
Narahari says: what is wrong in that? She is showing what a sister-in-law is.

[^30-47]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 207, no. 122 (scan PDF p. 466); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 122 (catalogue: NG-101). No witnesses; probably from the lost
pages of GCC (n. 18). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).

## 21. Narahari — "sajani to save dekhe sukha pāi…" (GPT1 p. 207, no. 123)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman whose friends question her about yesterday laughs and denies it: such talk does not become her. The poet does not
believe her. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: not established** — GPT only (see n. 18).*[^30-48]

**21.1.** "Friend, seeing you all I am glad — that is why I come here;
and you ask me about yesterday — it is simply laughable!

**21.2.** Tell me, tell me: how would such talk befit me?
Knowing me, you say such things — it pains me."

**21.3.** Narahari says: say what you will — the ear does not believe it:
if there were nothing, would anyone speak of another for no reason?

[^30-48]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 207, no. 123 (scan PDF p. 466); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 123 (catalogue: NG-342). No witnesses. A short pada (3 couplets);
the signature (21.3) repeats word for word the signature of no. 108 (no. 15, 15.6) — perhaps the answer of another townswoman in the same
conversation, or a fragment. In tone it continues no. 15 (denial and the poet's disbelief; see n. 36). C. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to
the section (chapter 27).

## Summary of chapter 30

*The chapter continues the padas signed "Narahari" from section 3.2 of GPT — the townswomen of Nadia telling their friends in the morning how,
despite the strictness of their mothers-in-law, sisters-in-law, fathers-in-law and husbands, they saw Gaura. Nos. 94–99 (nos. 1–6) were found in
Narahari Chakravarti's *Gaura-charita-chintamani* (kirana 7, padas 10–12, 14–16; "probably Chakravarti" — B; no. 97 in GPT is only the second half of
the GCC pada 7.14). Nos. 100–110 and 120–123 (nos. 7–21) stand in GPT in the place of GCC 7.17–7.28, but those pages (pp. 81–88) are lost in the
only available scan of GCC, and there are no other witnesses: they are labelled "not established" (C), with a note on their probable origin in GCC
(n. 18). In several padas the strict elders — a mother-in-law, a father-in-law, the husband's aunt — themselves lose their composure on hearing the
kirtana or seeing Gaura and become His devotees (nos. 9, 13, 18); the direct motifs of attraction and of deceiving the elders are rendered
exactly, with notes on the position of the tradition (introductory note, chapter 27).*

# Chapter 31. Nagari Padas — V: the "Narahari" padas of GPT (sect. 3.2, nos. 119, 124–145): the townswomen's dreams

*On what nagari-bhava is, the position of the tradition (Vrindavana Dasa, Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati) and the rules of translation, see the introductory note to the section of nagari padas in chapter 27; on the two poets named Narahari (Narahari Sarakara and Narahari Chakravarti) and on the attribution labels ("probably Sarakara", "probably Chakravarti", "not established"), see the introductory note to the "Narahari" appendix in chapter 17.*

## 1. Narahari — "ghumaka-ghore bhora śacīnandana…" (GPT1 p. 205, no. 119; GCC 2.13)
*Gaura asleep. At the end of the night Shachi's son, deep in sleep, as if immersed in a sleep of long ago in the kunja, softly says: "Wake,
crown-jewel of women, beautiful one! Without the song of your words My hearing has no joy; open your eyes, give Me a smile; rise — I Myself will
adorn you." This is not a townswoman's speech: GPT placed the pada in the section of nagari padas, but in GCC it stands in the account of the
last part of the Lord's night. Raga lalita. **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 2, pada 13.*[^31-1]

**1.1.** Shachi's son, held by deep sleep — who can fathom His play of prema? — as if immersed in a sleep of long ago in the kunja, speaks thus, sweetly and softly:

**1.2.** "Wake, wake, crown-jewel of women, beautiful one — how long will you sleep at the end of the night? Without drinking the song of the nectar of your words, My restless hearing is bereft of the least joy.

**1.3.** Leave your closed eyelids: with the tremulous corners of your eyes, with a graceful movement, do Me honour. My heart is bound — I say it without fear: smile and give Me joy.

**1.4.** Understand My wish — rise and sit up: with My own hands I will adorn you." So speaks Narahari's Lord — and says it again, lost to Himself.[^31-2]

[^31-1]: Signature — "Narahari" (narahari pahum̐ — "Narahari's Lord", i.e. the poet's Lord). GPT1 — p. 205, no. 119 (raga lalita; scan PDF p. 464); GPT2 — sect. 3.2,
no. 119 (catalogue: NG-098). GCC — kirana 2, pada 13 (ed. 1947, p. 30; scan PDF p. 35), "lalita-rāga". The second kirana of GCC describes the last part
of the Lord's night: the bedchamber, the bees flying into the house, the birds that wake Him at dawn; in the next pada (GCC 2.14, not taken into GPT) these
words spoken in sleep are heard by Gadadhara Pandita, who wakes and then keeps watch by Gaura's bed (2.15–2.16). Thus in the author Gaura in sleep speaks
the words of Krishna waking Radha in the kunja at the end of the night (cf. the padas on the waking of Radha and Krishna, nishanta-lila): this is a
remembrance of Vraja, not nagari-bhava; on Gadadhara as the embodiment of Radha's bhava in Gaura-lila — GGD. The pada is in Vrajabuli (tachu, mohe, tohe,
majhu). B. The pada stands in the GPT section of nagari padas — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-2]: 1.2: "the song of the nectar of your words" (vacanāmṛta-saṅgīta) — so GPT1 and GPT2; GCC has "the nectar of your sigh" (sītkṛta, "sitkara" — a sigh from descriptions of a lovers'
meeting), a more explicit reading; the GPT text is translated. 1.3: "do Me honour" — after the GCC reading "kari kara sammāna" (GPT: "kari mana māna", sense
unclear); "My heart is bound" — GPT "mana mana vandha" (probably a misprint for GCC "mama mana bandhaka" — "My heart is in pledge [to you]"); "give Me joy"
(GPT "rabhasa") — GCC "give Me the jewel of a smile" (hāsi ratana). 1.4: "says it again, lost to Himself" (GPT "vahuri nigadata kakhana viśāri"; GCC "bahu
vinigadata kathana visāri" — "speaks much, forgetting what He says") — the sense of the last words is conjectural.

## 2. Narahari — "mora pati ati sujana sajani…" (GPT1 pp. 207–208, no. 124; GCC 7.29)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman tells her friend: yesterday her husband, alone with his father, said that Nimai Pandita has the power of God, has
mastered His senses, is righteous, merciful to wicked people and full of the joy of kirtana; therefore the young wives should not be forbidden
to see Him — His darshan destroys all that is inauspicious; as in Vraja Krishna was not recognised by the brahmanas but by their wives, so it is
here. Hearing this she rejoiced, and when Gaura passed along the street with Gadadhara, Nityananda and His companions, she went out and gazed
on Him to her heart's content: the other women were held back by their mothers-in-law, but no one held her back. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution:
probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 29.*[^31-3]

**2.1.** "My husband, friend, is a very good man: listen to what he is like. Yesterday, sitting alone with his father, he said to him:

**2.2.** 'In the town of Nadia is Nimai Pandita: in Him is the power of God. Who created such a wonder I do not know; there is no end to His virtues.

**2.3.** One so master of His senses and so righteous I have never seen with my own eyes. To wicked people He is boundlessly merciful; He floats in the joy of kirtana.

**2.4.** Therefore I say: never, not even by oversight, forbid your daughters-in-law [to go to Him]. I know for certain: by His darshan all that is inauspicious perishes.

**2.5.** Fortunate are all our young wives — what more can I say? I cannot even express it. Therefore blessed is this birth as a woman — I take upon myself all its ills.

**2.6.** But we, drunk with false pride, live day and night like the blind: such a Wonder in the midst of Nadia — and we cannot recognise Him.

**2.7.** In Vraja the brahmanas did not know the Lord of Vraja — the brahmanas' wives attained Him. So it is here, there is no doubt of it — I have understood, having reflected.'[^31-4]

**2.8.** So father and son talked long in many ways; hidden nearby, I listened and listened — and my heart rejoiced.

**2.9.** I thought: if only I could see Gorachand right now — with the corners of my eyes I would tell Him all this.

**2.10.** Just then, from the direction of our quarter, joyful cries rose again and again; knowing that Gaura was coming, I hurried out and stood by the road.

**2.11.** From afar I gazed my fill — what wondrous beauty! The radiance of His body, outshining gold, blazes in every direction.

**2.12.** On His left is Gadadhara, on His right Nityananda, bliss itself; all around are His other companions: all gaze at that moon of a face.

**2.13.** With His own companions the Crown of connoisseurs of rasa comes, overflowing with rasa; who, seeing that lovely glance, can keep hold of her heart?

**2.14.** Smiling, as if in conversation, the Moon of Nadia showers streams of nectar; the grace of His form has captivated the world — like the snare of Madana.

**2.15.** Knowing that the Lord of their life was coming, the young women of our quarter came running; their harsh mothers-in-law and sisters-in-law held them back with many words.[^31-5]

**2.16.** But no one held me back — I fulfilled my heart's desire." Narahari says: she whose husband is so gracious — what obstacles has she?

[^31-3]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 207–208, no. 124 (scan PDF pp. 466–467); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 124 (catalogue: NG-102). GCC — kirana 7, pada 29 (ed. 1947,
pp. 89–90; scan PDF pp. 86–87; the pada begins with the first line of p. 89 — directly after the lost pp. 81–88, see n. 18 of chapter 30). GPT nos. 124–126 are
the last padas of the 7th kirana of GCC (7.29–7.31). GCC readings: "seirūpa hethā", "hema jiniyā" (2.11; GPT1 and GPT2 "hena", a misprint; translated after
GCC), "āise dhāyā … nivāre aneka kaiyā" (2.15), "pāinu manera sādhā" (2.16). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-4]: The husband's speech is praise of the Lord from the lips of a householder of Nadia: Nimai Pandita has "the power of God" (īśvara-śakati), has mastered the
senses (jitendriya), is merciful to the wicked — cf. in CB (Madhya) the deliverance of Jagai and Madhai and the words that the Lord's kirtana purifies even
sinners. 2.7 — the story of the wives of the sacrificing brahmanas (Bhag. 10.23): the brahmana priests did not recognise Krishna and refused Him food, while
their wives left everything, came to Him and received His mercy. So in this pada the rightness of the women who long to see Gaura is affirmed by a husband
in conversation with his father.
[^31-5]: "The Lord of their life" (prāṇanātha) — the townswoman's word for Gaura, as in the padas of the gopis about Krishna (cf. n. 14 of chapter 30); translated
faithfully to the author. The townswoman herself in this pada only gazes at Gaura from afar, standing by the road.

## 3. Narahari — "śuna śuna sai vidhi arasika…" (GPT1 pp. 208–209, no. 125; GCC 7.30)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman laments that the Creator has not settled any of Gaura's companions in her street — then He would come there too;
yesterday she went with her husband's aunt to the house of Murari Gupta, where the young wives were preparing sandal paste and garlands for
Gauranga's coming, but the aunt took her away; on the road, looking back, she saw Gaura with His companions — lips, smile, brows, sandal on His
brow, necklace, gait; then her husband's elder brother appeared with his students, but he too was looking at Gora, and she, covering her face,
slipped away. The poet teases her about her shame. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 7, pada 30.*[^31-6]

**3.1.** "Listen, listen, friend: the Creator has no taste for rasa — I have understood how he goes about his work; otherwise why would he give me such pain day and night?

**3.2.** Had he settled one of Gaura's companions here, then the Moon of Nadia would come to our street too and dispel our grief.

**3.3.** That is why I tell you: yesterday, leaving all the housework, I went with my husband's aunt to that quarter — to the house of Murari Gupta.[^31-7]

**3.4.** There the young wives were rejoicing — their happiness had no bounds: for the Beloved of their life they were grinding sandal paste and stringing garlands of flowers.

**3.5.** From them I heard that Gauranga would come there; but the aunt, her business done, set off home — and I could not stay.

**3.6.** Lost in thought, having gone some way, I looked back at the road: the young crown prince of Nadia, finely dressed, was coming with His companions.

**3.7.** What wondrous beauty of the lips! The teeth — a gleam of pearls; the smile showers streams of nectar; the face — the splendour of the autumn moon.

**3.8.** And the curve of His brows, the glances of His curving eyes — in so many ways! The sandal on His brow is so lovely — at one look all young women are drowned.

**3.9.** At His throat sways a necklace of gold and gems, lighting up the world; His gait is so enchanting — who in the world, seeing it, would not forget himself?

**3.10.** In the ocean of that beauty I bathed in joy, standing by my husband's aunt; turning round, I saw: behind us, with his students, came my husband's elder brother.

**3.11.** By good luck he did not see me — he was looking at Gora; covering my face with my veil, lowering my eyes, I carefully hurried away."

**3.12.** Narahari says: your shame before your husband's elder brother — do I not know it? Were I to tell it all, you could not stay in this land.[^31-8]
