pp. 90–91; scan PDF pp. 87–88). It is followed in GCC by a short concluding stanza (7.31, metre "surata-surati": the townswomen, recalling the past day, each tell
their own) and the colophon of the 7th kirana: "the morning doings… the description of the doings of the nagaris of Navadvipa"; stanza 7.31 was not taken
into GPT. GCC readings: "prāṇapriyā" (3.4), "gaurāṅga āsive hethā", "rahite nā pālum̐ tathā" (3.5), "daśana tāraka-chaṭā" — "the teeth — a gleam of stars"
(3.7), "majaye yuvatī jāti" (3.8), "dekhilum̐" (3.10). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-7]: Murari Gupta — a physician from Shrihatta, the Lord's companion from childhood, author of a Sanskrit life of Him (Murari's "Kadacha"; our translation);
his house in Navadvipa is one of the places of the Lord's kirtanas (CB, Madhya).
[^31-8]: "The husband's elder brother" (bhāsura) — before him a young wife by custom covers her face and does not show herself. He himself, walking with his
students (paṛuyā), was also "looking at Gora". The last line is the poet's joke: the whole street would know at whom she was gazing; translated as in the
original.

## 4. Narahari — "śuna śuna sai niśira kāhinī…" (GPT1 pp. 209–210, no. 126; GCC 8.2)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. A townswoman tells her friend about the night: in the evening, thinking of Gaura, she went with her mother-in-law to
the house of Srivasa Pandita, where Gora sat among His companions and talked smilingly with Gadadhara; for fear of her mother-in-law she
could not stay and returned home, lay down without supper and fell asleep only late at night; in her dream she came again to Srivasa's house,
anointed Gora with sandal paste, put garlands on Him — and on some pretext He embraced her. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably
Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 2.*[^31-9]

**4.1.** "Listen, listen, friend: what happened at night I will carefully tell you. At dusk, my work done, I was sitting at home.

**4.2.** Thinking and thinking of Gora's beauty and virtues — I do not know what came over me — I went with my mother-in-law to the house of Srivasa Pandita Thakura.

**4.3.** There, among His peerless companions, Gora is seated — the thief of the precious composure of young women, well-born and chaste.

**4.4.** His golden body shines, anointed with lovely sandal paste — as if Mount Sumeru had been smeared with the ground-up autumn moon.

**4.5.** A garland of malati sways at His throat — like a snare enchanting the world; hundreds upon hundreds of Madanas swoon at the sight of the shape of His face.

**4.6.** Smiling, He holds sweet converse with Gadadhara; showering nectar in streams, He soothes the ache of the ears.

**4.7.** Ah, ah! At the sight of such beauty, what becomes of the heart! What shall I say — not for one moment could I gaze my fill of Him with both my eyes.

**4.8.** Wretched me, what could I do? The Creator made woman dependent. For fear of my mother-in-law I could not stay and came home, dying at heart.

**4.9.** In grief I lay down; when my sister-in-law asked, I told her: 'I am not hungry, do not wake me — I feel somehow unwell.'

**4.10.** She, a simple soul, went away, and I lay there distraught; my body was restless, friend — sleep came only deep in the night.

**4.11.** In my dream I went to the house of Srivasa Thakura and saw Him; with all the longing of my heart I anointed Gora's body with fragrant sandal paste.

**4.12.** Carefully I put on His neck garland after fresh garland of many flowers; and the life of Narahari, the Crown of connoisseurs of rasa, on some pretext embraced [me]."[^31-10]

[^31-9]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 209–210, no. 126 (scan PDF pp. 468–469); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 126 (catalogue: NG-343). GCC — kirana 8, pada 2 (ed. 1947,
p. 92; scan PDF p. 89), "kācidāha — yathā[rāga]" ("one of them said"). The 8th kirana of GCC (colophon: "…the description of the tales of dreams") continues the
nagaris' "morning": it opens with pada 8.1 (raga vibhasa, not taken into GPT) — at dawn the friends gather, laughing, and each without shame tells her dream;
GPT nos. 126–144 are these tales. GCC readings: "vasiyā āchilum̐", "gorā rūpa-guṇa", "śarada śaśī" (4.4), "bhuvana-mohana-phānda", "vadana-chānda" (4.5),
"mākhālum̐ gaura gāya" (4.11). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-10]: The townswoman's dream (4.11–4.12): the embrace (āliṅgana) is a direct motif of sambhoga; translated exactly, adding nothing. The dream is her imagination:
the Lord in His lila did not touch women and in Navadvipa did not look at them (CB, Adi; introductory note, chapter 27), and the Gaudiya tradition does not
accept the worship of Gaura as a nagara ("gaura-nagari" is counted by Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati among the apasampradayas). Majumdar regards the long GPT padas
signed Narahari as late, not Sarakara's; these padas indeed belong to Narahari Chakravarti (18th c.). The signature merges with the townswoman's speech:
"the life of Narahari" (narahari-prāṇa) is an epithet of Gaura (cf. "Narahari's Lord"). Srivasa's house is the place of the Lord's night kirtanas (CB, Madhya;
there the doors were barred and outsiders not admitted) — here only the backdrop of the tale.

## 5. Narahari — "śuna śuna ohe parāṇa sajani…" (GPT1 pp. 210–211, no. 127; GCC 8.3)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. A townswoman tells her dream: adorned, she sat in a kunja, pining; suddenly at the entrance there appeared a youth, a
kishora the colour of a rain-cloud — with a peacock feather on His crown, a flute at His lips, a pearl necklace; He came near, jested, beckoned
her with His glance; and as she watched, the Dark One became Gora; He sat beside her, she turned away in feigned anger, He begged forgiveness —
and the dream ends with their meeting. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 3.*[^31-11]

**5.1.** "Listen, listen, friend of my heart, to you I will tell it: a dream such as tonight's I have never seen.

**5.2.** I was sitting in a kunja bower, adorned in every way; thinking and thinking, my body had wasted away, there was not a trace of joy in it.

**5.3.** With restless eyes I looked in every direction — I do not know what had come over me; and suddenly I saw: someone had come to the outer door.

**5.4.** What wondrous youth — a kishora, as if rasa itself in bodily form! What shall I say of the majesty of that nagara? His body is the colour of a rain-cloud.

**5.5.** His palms and soles outshine the dawn, His nails are a cluster of moons; the curls and the tilaka on His brow are lovely — like a snare enchanting the world.

**5.6.** His crown is gracefully tilted, a peerless peacock feather flutters; to the fragrance of its fine flowers bees come swarming — there is no counting them.

**5.7.** Holding the flute to His lower lip, He plays it again and again: who in the world, hearing it, can keep composure?

**5.8.** On His neck — a double string of pearls, like the streams of the Suradhuni; as He walks, the belt of bells on His hips tinkles, and lovely anklets on His feet.

**5.9.** With a graceful play of His brows He came up to me — and in how many ways He jested: who could understand it?

**5.10.** Smiling, looking at me, He signals with the corners of His eyes; with a trick He lifts away my veil — what is He doing! — He draws my very life to Himself.

**5.11.** And another wonder: as I watched, that Dark One became Gora. With what shall I compare Him — the thief of the life of so many chaste young wives?

**5.12.** Slowly, slowly He came near and sat beside me; with sweet, sweet words He soothes me, longing to touch.

**5.13.** In feigned anger I turned my face away — yet my joy had no bounds; 'Forgive My offence,' He said, and again caught the end of my sari.

**5.14.** At the touch of His body I grew helpless and was lost in Him." The Lord of Narahari's life, the great Connoisseur of rasa, did what was in His heart.[^31-12]

is from the middle of the pada). GCC — kirana 8, pada 3 (ed. 1947, pp. 93–94; scan PDF pp. 90–91), "anyā ca — yathārāga" ("and another"). GCC readings:
"dekhiye nāi" (5.1), "nakhara-nicaya cānda" (5.5), "uṛaye mayūra pākhā" (5.6; GPT1 and GPT2 "ubhaye", probably a misprint; translated after GCC), "muralī"
(5.7), "kaṭi taṭe", "sundara nūpura" (5.8), "majila uhāra sane" (5.14). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-12]: The townswoman's dream (5.12–5.14): the longing to touch, the touch, and "was lost in Him" (majilum̐ uhāra sane) are a direct motif of sambhoga; translated
exactly, adding nothing and softening nothing. The dream is her imagination: the Lord in His lila did not touch women and in Navadvipa did not look at them
(CB, Adi; introductory note, chapter 27); the Gaudiya tradition does not accept the worship of Gaura as a nagara ("gaura-nagari" is counted by Bhaktisiddhanta
Sarasvati among the apasampradayas); according to Majumdar such GPT padas signed Narahari are late (here — Narahari Chakravarti, 18th c.). The Dark One
becoming Gora in the dream (5.11) is a poetic image of the identity of Gaura and Krishna (CC Adi 1.5; cf. the Lord's revealing of Shyamasundara to Ramananda
Raya — CC Madhya 8). "The Lord of Narahari's life" (narahari-prāṇapati) — a signature merged with the speech: Gaura is the Lord of the poet's life.

## 6. Narahari — "ājuka rajanī sukhamaya svapana…" (GPT1 pp. 211–212, no. 128; GCC 8.4)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. A townswoman tells her friends a dream about themselves: adorned, they sat together and sang of Gaura for a watch of the night,
then sent a messenger to Gauranga; hearing of Him, they ran to the kunja; He seated them, jested, wounded them with His glance, embraced them. The
poet: why be ashamed to tell of yourself? Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 4.*[^31-13]

**6.1.** "Tonight I saw a blissful dream, friends: you are the most fortunate in the world; listen, I will tell it.

**6.2.** Each adorned in her own way, eager, you sat together in a secluded place; singing and singing songs of Gora's virtues, you passed a watch of the night.

**6.3.** Choosing the moment, you sent a messenger to where Govinda was; she went very quickly and told Gauranga everything.[^31-14]

**6.4.** Just as quickly she came back to you, herself agitated; hearing from her lips the news of the Beloved of your life, you all ran.

**6.5.** From afar, seeing the sweetness of Gora's form, you were enchanted; entering the kunja bower, you came up to the Lord of your life.

**6.6.** With great tenderness He seated you, taking each by the hand; smiling, how many jests He and you exchanged with one another!

**6.7.** Most clever Gora shot a fearful arrow from the corners of His eyes; by it you were overcome and could not keep the pride of youth.

**6.8.** The serpents of all your brows bit Him again and again — and the composure the Moon of Nadia had seemed at once to leave Him.

**6.9.** Opening both arms, He embraces — peerless is His love; in great joy I made a sign — and, understanding it, He grew still more intoxicated.

**6.10.** The desire that was in your hearts the King of connoisseurs of rasa fulfilled." Narahari says: why are you ashamed to tell of yourself?[^31-15]

[^31-13]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 211–212, no. 128 (scan PDF pp. 470–471); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 128 (catalogue: NG-105). GCC — kirana 8, pada 4 (ed. 1947,
p. 94; scan PDF p. 91), "anyā ca — yathārāga". GCC readings: "sukhamaya sava svapana" (6.1), "gorā-guṇagaṇa … gom̐āilā" (6.2), "karilā paraspare" — "jested with
one another" (6.6; adopted in the main text: GPT1 and GPT2 "paraśa pare" — "touching", a misprint, as in 22.7), "tā yena takhani gela" (6.8; GPT1 and GPT2 "mena"), "tomādera mane ye chila tā yena karila rasikarāja" (6.10; the OCR is uncertain). B.
Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-14]: "To where Govinda was" (govinda āchena yathā): the messenger speaks with Gauranga — Govinda here is apparently Krishna's name given to Gaura (cf. "the Moon
of Gokula", chapter 29); another understanding is also possible — the house of Govinda (Ghosha or another companion) where the Lord was. The messenger (dūtī)
is an image from the padas on Radha and Krishna.
[^31-15]: The dream (6.6–6.10): touches, embrace, the "composure leaving" the Moon of Nadia are direct motifs of sambhoga and attraction; translated exactly, adding
nothing and softening nothing. The dream is the townswoman's imagination, not the Lord's lila: the Lord did not touch women (CB, Adi); the tradition does not
accept gaura-nagari (n. 10 and the introductory note, chapter 27). 6.9: "I made a sign — and, understanding it, He grew still more intoxicated" (subahu haraṣe
ṭhārinu vujhiyā adhika mātila seha) — the sense of the line is unclear ("seha" may mean "he" or "that love"). The poet's signature (6.10) is a joke: under the
guise of a dream about her friends the teller is telling her own.

## 7. Narahari — "śuna śuna sai svapane dekhinu nikuñjakānane gorā…" (GPT1 p. 212, no. 129; GCC 8.5)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. A friend tells the heroine her dream: Gora in a kunja grove was gazing at her path and weeping; learning from the friend
that she would come, He begged her to hasten; the heroine, adorned, came, and the King of connoisseurs of rasa embraced her; then on some
pretext she became manini — and He entreats her to relent; at this the teller woke. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** —
GCC, kirana 8, pada 5.*[^31-16]

**7.1.** "Listen, listen, friend: in a dream I saw Gora in a kunja grove — gazing at your path, in anguish He was shedding tears.

**7.2.** Hearing from me that you were coming, how He pleaded with me! Seeing His state, I came in haste and told you.

**7.3.** Hearing it, you joyfully adorned yourself and met Him in the kunja; welcoming you from afar, the King of connoisseurs of rasa took your hand and drew you into His embrace.

**7.4.** How much merry jesting there was! — and on some pretext you became manini. Narahari's Lord entreats you — and I woke in distress."[^31-17]

[^31-16]: Signature — "Narahari" (narahari pahum̐ — "Narahari's Lord"). GPT1 — p. 212, no. 129 (scan PDF p. 471); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 129 (catalogue: NG-344). GCC — kirana 8,
pada 5 (ed. 1947, p. 95; scan PDF p. 92), "anyā ca — yathārāga". GCC readings: "locana lorā" (7.1), "bheṭilā nikuñjamājha" (7.3), "māninī hailā tumi" (7.4). B.
Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-17]: The pada is built on the pattern of the padas on Radha and Krishna: the friend as messenger, the Beloved waiting in tears in the kunja, the meeting and
the heroine's mana (manini — "full of mana", the lover's pique). Gaura here — in a townswoman's dream — plays the part of Krishna; in His own lila He wept not
for the women of Nadia but for Krishna, in the bhava of Radha (CC Adi 4). The embrace (kore karila, 7.3) is a direct motif of sambhoga; translated exactly. The
dream is the townswoman's imagination; the Lord did not touch women (CB, Adi); the tradition does not accept gaura-nagari (n. 10 and the introductory note,
chapter 27).

## 8. Narahari — "śuna śuna ogo tomāre valie niśira svapanakathā…" (GPT1 pp. 212–213, no. 130; GCC 8.6)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. In her dream a townswoman went to Srivasa's house, where the companions were singing to mridangas and karatalas and
Gaura was dancing among them; suddenly bhava seized Him — trembling, streams of tears; He fell and rolled on the ground like a golden lotus;
forgetting shame, she sobbed aloud and woke; the household ran to ask why she was weeping; falling asleep again, she saw that Gora had come to
her courtyard — she seated Him on a couch, fanned Him with the end of her sari, offered betel. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably
Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 6.*[^31-18]

**8.1.** "Listen, listen, friend, I will tell you the night's dream: I went to the house of Srivasa Pandita Thakura, where Gauranga was.

**8.2.** How lovely is Srivasa's courtyard — I saw it, and my eyes were soothed; with joy in my heart I stood in a secluded spot, keeping composure and dharma.

**8.3.** There the companions, happy at heart, with mridangas and karatalas, quite mad with joy, sing sweet, nectarean melodies.

**8.4.** In the midst of that circle Shachi's son shines — what wondrous attire! His curling, glossy hair is adorned with lovely flowers of every kind.

**8.5.** At His ears graceful earrings sway, the glow of His cheeks is peerless; on His brow are drops of fine sandal paste, like the splendour of the autumn moon.

**8.6.** On His broad chest sway many necklaces, light as down; new ornaments shine on Him — with what shall I compare Him?

**8.7.** Swaying His arms, the Most Clever One dances, stepping gracefully; "Hari, Hari!" He cries; hearing it, no one keeps composure.

**8.8.** I do not know what bhava rose in Him: His body trembles again and again; from both eyes streams flow without cease — like the current of a river.

**8.9.** Heaving a deep sigh, in agitation He fell to the ground — He rolls like a golden lotus; no one can hold Him.

**8.10.** Seeing this, my heart trembled; I gave shame its last libation of water; "What has happened, what has happened?" I cried, and sobbed aloud, beside myself.[^31-19]

**8.11.** Then my sleep broke; waking, I sat up in bed; "What is it, what is it?" — everyone came running to ask why I wept.

**8.12.** What could I tell anyone? With grief in my heart I fell asleep again, like a chataki bird; and again I dreamed: Gora had come to my courtyard.

**8.13.** "Come in, come in, friend!" I said, and quickly seated Him on the couch; seeing He was tired, I carefully fanned Him with the end of my sari.

**8.14.** Preparing fresh betel, I offered it to that moon-like face; and with the Lord of Narahari's life I sat, happy at heart."[^31-20]

pp. 95–96; scan PDF pp. 92–93), "anyā ca — yathārāga". GCC readings: "gelāma gaura yathā" (8.1), "dām̐ṛāinu" (8.2), "nānā jāti" (8.4), "śarada śaśīra ghaṭā" (8.5),
"hainu" (8.10), "ghumāinu cātakī-pārā" (8.12), "tāmbūla hāsiyā dilāma" (8.14), "laiyā śutinu manera sukhe" (8.14; see n. 20). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory
note to the section (chapter 27).

in Srivasa's courtyard; CC Adi 17). "I gave shame its last libation of water" (lāje tilāñjali dinu; tilanjali — the offering of water with sesame to the dead) — a
saying: I abandoned shame for good. "Like a chataki bird" (8.12) — the chataka, by poetic tradition, drinks only rain-water from the clouds and ever waits for it:
an image of longing.

of sambhoga is more direct; the GPT text is translated, the GCC reading is noted here. The dream is the townswoman's imagination; the Lord did not touch women
(CB, Adi); the tradition does not accept gaura-nagari (n. 10 and the introductory note, chapter 27).

## 9. Narahari — "śuna śuna ogo rajani-svapana…" (GPT1 pp. 213–214, no. 131; GCC 8.7)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. First the townswoman dreams that the whole world has gone mad with the virtues of Gaurangachand, and even the wicked and
the slanderers have become His followers; falling asleep again, she sees: as Shyama held the rasa on the bank of the Yamuna, so Gora on the bank
of the Suradhuni has made an abode of rasa; the women of Nadia, casting off shame, go there in crowds; her husband bolts the door, but her
husband's brother's wife slyly opens it; she runs, sees Gaura Raya in a circle of young women amid music and song, dances — and He, laughing,
presses her to His breast. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 7.*[^31-21]

**9.1.** "Listen, listen, friend, I will tell the night's dream that is in my heart: the people of the whole world went mad with the virtues of Gaurangachand.

**9.2.** All who were — the foolish, the crooked, the deceitful, the slanderers — giving up their perverse nature, became followers of Gaura.

**9.3.** Seeing this and much else, once I woke, friend; and when I fell asleep again, I saw another wonder — I will tell you all of it.

**9.4.** As Shyama on the bank of the Yamuna held the rasa and other pastimes, so Gora on the bank of the Suradhuni made an abode of rasa.[^31-22]

**9.5.** Casting off shame and fear for their families, all the nagaris of Nadia, mounted on the chariot of desire, go crowd after crowd, passing by hundreds of thorns.

**9.6.** Leaving the housework, I was in great eagerness to go there; suddenly my husband came and quickly bolted the door of the house.

**9.7.** I was in a fix — whom could I tell what? — and lost all strength; I thought: I shall not live if I do not see the Beloved again.

**9.8.** At that moment my clever sister-in-law, my husband's brother's wife, on some pretext unbolted the door; carefully, carefully, softly, softly I stepped outside.

**9.9.** Blossoming with joy, I ran, looking back at no one — as a young bird escapes from an iron cage.

**9.10.** Arriving quickly, I gazed my fill on Gaura Raya: in the midst of a circle of young women He shines — with what shall I compare Him?

**9.11.** On every side all kinds of instruments sound — there is no end of joy; women sing sweet melodies, showering streams of nectar.

**9.12.** Drunk with the honey of that lotus face, I danced again in joy; Narahari's Lord, seeing this, laughed and pressed me to His breast."[^31-23]

(9.9), "yuvatī-maṇḍalī" (9.10), "cāridige", "sura nārīgaṇa" (9.11). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).

[^31-23]: "My husband's brother's wife" (jā). Deceiving the husband and fleeing the house (9.6–9.9) is a motif of the padas on the gopis running to the call of the flute
(Bhag. 10.29); pressing to the breast (9.12) is a direct motif of sambhoga; translated exactly. The dream is the townswoman's imagination; the Lord did not touch
women (CB, Adi). "Women sing sweet melodies" (madhura sura-nārīgaṇa) may also be understood as "celestial women" (suranārī); GCC separates "sura" ("melody").

## 10. Narahari — "rajanī-svapana śuna go sajani…" (GPT1 p. 214, no. 132; GCC 8.8)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. A townswoman, casting off shame, tells: in her dream Gora quietly entered her chamber, looking around, sat at the head
of her bed, touched her lips, jested, embraced her, weeping with joy — as if He had found a treasure He could not let go of even for a moment.
Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 8.*[^31-24]

**10.1.** "Listen to the night's dream, friend — I tell it, casting off shame: softly, softly Gora enters my chamber, warily looking all around.

**10.2.** Smiling, He sat, moving close to the head of my bed; with His own hand He touched my lips — and floats in an ocean of joy.

**10.3.** Intoxicated, jesting, He speaks the sweetest words in every way; twining His arms, holding [me] to His heart, He bathes [me] with the tears of His eyes.

**10.4.** In His own heart He deems He has found a treasure — it is hard for Him to let it go even for a moment." The Beloved of Narahari's life is love itself embodied; what more shall I say?[^31-25]

[^31-24]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 214, no. 132 (scan PDF p. 473); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 132 (catalogue: NG-107). GCC — kirana 8, pada 8 (ed. 1947, p. 97; scan PDF
p. 102), "anyā ca — yathārāga". GCC readings: "caudige cāyā" (10.1), "śithāna-pāśe" (10.2), "pirītera mūrati" (10.4). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the
section (chapter 27).
[^31-25]: The whole dream (10.1–10.4) is a direct motif of sambhoga: Gora enters the townswoman's chamber, touches her lips, embraces her; translated exactly, adding
nothing and softening nothing. This is the townswoman's imagination, not the Lord's lila: the Lord did not touch women and in Navadvipa did not look at them (CB,
Adi); the Gaudiya tradition does not accept the worship of Gaura as a nagara (Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati; introductory note, chapter 27); according to Majumdar
such GPT padas signed Narahari are late (here — Narahari Chakravarti). Gaura's tears (10.3) in His own lila are tears of prema for Krishna (CC Adi 4).

## 11. Narahari — "śuna śuna niśi-svapana sai…" (GPT1 p. 214, no. 133; GCC 8.9)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream, on the pattern of the khandita padas. In a dream at dawn the finely dressed Gaura came to the townswoman; she asked why He
had come and told Him to go where He had spent the night — the traces of a sleepless night cannot be hidden; He swore hundreds of oaths, pleaded
with her — and then the dream broke. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 9.*[^31-26]

**11.1.** "Listen, listen, friend, to the night's dream — I tell it to you, leaving shame aside.

**11.2.** At dawn, in fine attire, Gaura came to me.

**11.3.** Looking at that moon-like face, I said: 'Why have You come running?

**11.4.** Where You happily spent the night — go there quickly and meet there.

**11.5.** What is hidden does not stay hidden — it is all plain: with her You stayed awake, passing the night.'

**11.6.** Hearing this, He swears hundreds of oaths — and, longing to touch, pleads with me.

**11.7.** Then the dream broke." Narahari knows what became of her.[^31-27]

[^31-26]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 214, no. 133 (scan PDF p. 473); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 133 (catalogue: NG-346). GCC — kirana 8, pada 9 (ed. 1947, p. 98; scan PDF
p. 103), "anyā ca — yathārāga". Metre — short payar (a couplet to a line). Readings: 11.3 "valinu" — "I said" (so GPT2 and GCC; GPT1 "calinu" — "I went", probably a
misprint; translated after GPT2 and GCC); GCC: "prabhāta-samaye" (11.2), "se candravadana-pānete cāyā" (11.3), "henakāle" (11.7). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory
note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-27]: The pada repeats the scheme of the khandita padas — the heroine to whom the Beloved comes at dawn bearing the traces of a night spent with another (in the
Krishna padas — with Chandravali); the reproach, the oaths and the longing to touch come from there. Transferring this image to Gaura is a convention of the nagari
padas, not the Lord's lila (n. 25; introductory note, chapter 27). "Narahari knows what became of her" — the poet's signature; translated as in the original.

## 12. Narahari — "śuna śuna ogo sajani rajanī-svapana…" (GPT1 pp. 214–215, no. 134; GCC 8.10)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. In a dream the Moon of Nadia came to a townswoman's house; her harsh sister-in-law at the door accused her of a liaison
with a strange man and threatened to tell her brother in the morning; the townswoman feared not for herself — let them revile her — but that
wicked people would slander the Beloved and He would never again come to their street; she wept, repeating His name, and woke. Raga
"yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 10.*[^31-28]

**12.1.** "Listen, listen, friend, I will tell you the night's dream: with great effort the Moon of Nadia came and met me in the house.

**12.2.** Just then my harsh sister-in-law, standing at the door, says: 'You are dallying with a strange man and are not afraid!

**12.3.** Very well: in the morning my brother will come — I will tell him everything; and I will take my own honour and go — I will not stay in this sinful house.'

**12.4.** Hearing this, I thought in fear: when the night is over — I do not know what my husband will do when he comes home.

**12.5.** Let everyone revile me as much as they like — that does not pain me; but what if wicked people should slander the Beloved of my life!

**12.6.** If the Creator makes this known, then it will be dreadful: for the rest of my life I shall never again see the Moon of Nadia.

**12.7.** He will never come to our street, will never think of me; wretched as I am, I know it for certain — otherwise why should things be so?

**12.8.** Saying this, I sobbed in distress, repeating His name again and again. Narahari knows: I saved my life by waking up quickly."[^31-29]

[^31-28]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 214–215, no. 134 (scan PDF pp. 473–474); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 134 (catalogue: NG-347; in GPT2 no. 134 is printed after no. 135).
GCC — kirana 8, pada 10 (ed. 1947, p. 98; scan PDF p. 103), "anyā ca — yathārāga". GCC readings: "āsiyā sāmbhāila ghare" — "entered the house" (12.1), "para puruṣera sane
vilasaha, ithe nā vāsaha bhaya" (12.2), "bhaya pāyā pohāile niśi" (12.4), "prāṇe vām̐cāinu turite cetana pāyā" (12.8). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to
the section (chapter 27).
[^31-29]: The sister-in-law's accusation ("you are dallying with a strange man", para-puruṣera sane vilasaha) is rendered exactly. The heart of the pada is 12.5–12.6: the
townswoman is ready to bear any abuse, so long as rumour does not touch Gaura and she is not deprived of His darshan. This is a dream, not an event (n. 10;
introductory note, chapter 27). The signature merges with the townswoman's speech ("Narahari knows: I saved…"); "waking up" — lit. "regaining consciousness"
(cetana pāiyā).

## 13. Narahari — "sajani rajanī-svapana śunaha…" (GPT1 pp. 215–216, no. 135; GCC 8.11)
*Nagari-bhava; a comic dream. To guard the townswoman, her sister-in-law slept on her bed; at night the Moon of Nadia came and by mistake sat on
the sister-in-law's couch and touched her chin; she woke crying "Thief!", chased Him, caught Him and brought Him back with abuse, but Gora looked
at her — and conquered her; then, not finding the townswoman, He left dejected; and the sister-in-law, with downcast face, confessed that she had
"fallen into the hands of a terrible thief" and begged her to keep silent. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8,
pada 11.*[^31-30]

**13.1.** "Friend, listen to the night's dream — what a laugh! To guard me, my sister-in-law lay down where my bed is.

**13.2.** The Moon of Nadia came, entered, trembling with joy — and, taking her for me, sat on my sister-in-law's couch.

**13.3.** Softly, softly, in delight, He touched her chin with His tendril-like hand; my sister-in-law awoke, started up in alarm, looking all around.

**13.4.** She says to me: 'Wake up, wake up, quick — a thief has got into the house!' Hearing this, Gora fled in fear and stood some way off.

**13.5.** The harsh sister-in-law ran after Him with threats; going a little way, she caught up — and the Beloved of my life could not escape.

**13.6.** Drunk with the pride of youth, she seized Him firmly by both hands — and, abusing Him in every way, stopping again and again, she leads Him into the house.

**13.7.** Youthful Gora, full of rasa, looked at my sister-in-law — bound her in the noose of His arms, conquered her, and did what was in His heart.[^31-31]

**13.8.** Not finding me, the Jewel of virtues went away dejected; and my sister-in-law, all limp, came to me again.

**13.9.** Looking at her, I asked: 'What is this — why are you so glad at heart?' She, with downcast face, says: 'I fell into the hands of a terrible thief.

**13.10.** Keep it secret, or in the morning the smoke of scandal will rise.'" Narahari is the witness: as I began to console her, sleep left my eyes.[^31-32]

[^31-30]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 215–216, no. 135 (scan PDF pp. 474–475); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 135 (catalogue: NG-348). GCC — kirana 8, pada 11 (ed. 1947, p. 99;
scan PDF p. 104), "anyā ca — yathārāga". GCC readings: "praveśila adhika madana-bhare" — "entered, overflowing with Madana" (13.2; GPT "athira ānanda bhare", "trembling
with joy"; the GPT text is translated), "vasilena nanadinīra pālaṅka-pare" (13.2), "kara-pallave cibuka paraśe haraṣa haiyā" (13.3), "kata dūre yāi pāila, palāite
nārila parāṇapiyā" (13.5), "yauvana-garave" (13.6), "tem̐ha adhomukhe" (13.9), "parabhāte haibe kalaṅka-dhūma" (13.10). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to
the section (chapter 27).
[^31-31]: 13.7 is a direct motif of sambhoga (bound her in the noose of His arms, "conquered", "did what was in His heart" — kaila ye āchila mane); translated exactly,
adding nothing. The pada is a farce: the strict sister-in-law who guards the young wife is herself "conquered" by Gaura; this is the motif running through GCC (the
strict elders, on seeing Gaura, lose their severity; cf. nn. 12, 23 of chapter 30) carried to a coarse joke. Such a depiction of the Lord is precisely what the
Gaudiya tradition rejects: the Lord did not touch women and in Navadvipa did not look at them (CB, Adi); the worship of Gaura as a nagara is an apasampradaya
(Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati; introductory note, chapter 27). This is a townswoman's dream told for laughter (13.1: "what a laugh!").
[^31-32]: "The smoke of scandal" (kalaṅka-dhūma) — evil rumour. The signature is "Narahari the witness" (narahari sāthī): the poet brings himself into the dream as a
witness; the last words
(āśvāsite bhāṅgila ām̐khira ghuma — "as [I] began to console her, sleep left the eyes") are understood thus: the teller herself consoles her sister-in-law and at once
wakes up (cf. the ending of 12.8: "I saved my life by waking up quickly"); the subject is not named in the original, and the reading "as he began to console her" is also possible.

## 14. Narahari — "svapanera kathā śuna go sajani…" (GPT1 pp. 216–217, no. 136; GCC 8.12)
*Nagari-bhava; a comic dream. In a dream the Beloved entered the townswoman's house wrapped in a blanket, so that her sister-in-law would not
recognise Him; she seated Him on a couch and threw off His blanket — and His face shone like the moon from behind the clouds; her mother-in-law
asked what the light in the house was, and the townswoman answered that it was Chandra, the moon god, who had appeared, pleased with her vow, and
asked the mother-in-law to name a boon; she wished everyone wealth, long life and well-being; returning, the townswoman wiped her Beloved's body
with the end of her sari, He embraced her — and then she woke. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 12.*[^31-33]

**14.1.** "Listen to the dream, friend: yesterday the Connoisseur of rasa, the Beloved of my life, entered the house unseen, wrapped in a blanket.

**14.2.** Seeing this, I laughed softly and asked: 'Why have You dressed up like this?' The Beloved says: 'In case your sister-in-law should recognise Me later [tomorrow].'[^31-34]

**14.3.** Much like this He said; hearing it, I covered my face with the end of my cloth, took the Lord of my life by His lovely hand and joyfully seated Him on the couch.

**14.4.** What sweetness His face had at that moment — what can I say of what was in my heart? As if a mass of golden lotuses had blossomed in the waters of the Kalindi.

**14.5.** Seeing this, I took heart and threw off that blanket from Him — as if the autumn moon had come out from behind thick clouds.

**14.6.** At that very moment my mother-in-law asks: 'What is that light in the house?' Hearing this, my whole body trembled — my soul simply flew away.

**14.7.** Hurrying out, I stood at the door, looking with fear in my heart, and, taking courage, began to speak cunningly with her:

**14.8.** 'You know my vow to Chandra — I keep it with care; so by his grace he has appeared today, pleased with my worship.

**14.9.** He wishes to give a boon — but what boon to ask I do not know; whatever you say, that I will take; only do not come in here yourself.'

**14.10.** Hearing this, softly, softly, delighted, she says with great earnestness: 'Ask for wealth, long life, prosperity and well-being for all — all of this.'

**14.11.** Hearing this, I quickly went into the house in great joy; sitting by my Beloved, I wiped His body with the end of my sari.

**14.12.** The Lord of Narahari's life with great tenderness took me in His embrace; then my sleep broke — and in separation I was drowned in tears."[^31-35]

[^31-33]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 216–217, no. 136 (scan PDF pp. 475–476); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 136 (catalogue: NG-108). GCC — kirana 8, pada 12 (ed. 1947, pp. 99–100;
scan PDF pp. 104–105), "anyā ca — yathārāga". GCC readings: "parāṇa rasika rāya" (14.1), "kanaka-kamala-rāśi" (14.4), "khasāyā phelinu mena" (14.5; "mena" — so also GPT1,
= "yena"), "tem̐ho dekhā dila" (14.8), "ethā nā āsiha tumi" (14.9), "āyuvṛddhi śubha savāra eteka leha cāyā" (14.10), "bhāsinu ām̐khira jale" (14.12). B. Nagari-bhava —
see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-34]: Bengali kāli means both "yesterday" and "tomorrow": in 14.1 — "yesterday" (the night being told of), in 14.2 — "tomorrow", "later". The blanket (kambala) under which Gaura hides the radiance of His body, and the
"light in the house" (14.6), play on the image of Gaura as the moon: the townswoman passes Him off as Chandra, the moon god — and this is true in a poetic sense: He is "the
Moon of Nadia". The deceiving of the mother-in-law is rendered as in the original (cf. n. 7 of chapter 30).
[^31-35]: The embrace (14.12) is a motif of sambhoga, translated exactly; the dream breaks off, and the townswoman is left in separation. The dream is her imagination; the Lord
did not touch women (CB, Adi); the tradition does not accept gaura-nagari (n. 10 and the introductory note, chapter 27).

## 15. Narahari — "śuna śuna ogo valiye tomāre svapane nadyāra śaśī…" (GPT1 p. 217, no. 137; GCC 8.13)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. In a dream the Moon of Nadia sat beside the townswoman and asked her to adorn Him with her own hands; she oiled and
decked His hair with flowers, drew sandal on His brow, put on earrings, a pearl in His nose, bracelets, necklaces, a belt of bells and anklets —
and then woke before she had gazed her fill. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 13.*[^31-36]

**15.1.** "Listen, listen, friend, I will tell you: in a dream the Moon of Nadia, smiling, came and sat beside me — like a mass of golden lotuses.

**15.2.** He says to me: 'Today adorn Me with your own hands.' Hearing those clever words — what joy I felt, how can I tell?

**15.3.** The merriment grew: His hair — the young women of Nadia are mad for it — I anointed with many fragrant oils, dressed in many styles and decked with flowers.

**15.4.** On His brow I drew lovely drops of sandal, like bright moons; at His ears I fixed earrings — they flash like the sun; with what can I compare them?

**15.5.** Wiping the smiling lotus of His face, I saw His brows — like a row of bees; looking into His eyes, drunk with joy, I set a pearl in His nose.

**15.6.** His lovely arms, outdoing an elephant's trunk, steal away composure and dharma; on them I put many ornaments and lovingly bracelets on His wrists.

**15.7.** On His broad chest I arranged necklaces — peerless is the beauty of His waist; on His hips I put a belt of bells — His knees shine.

**15.8.** On the feet of Narahari's Beloved I carefully put anklets; then my sleep broke — and I could not gaze my fill of Him."[^31-37]

[^31-36]: Signature — "Narahari" (narahari priya — "Narahari's Beloved"). GPT1 — p. 217, no. 137 (scan PDF p. 476); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 137 (catalogue: NG-109). GCC — kirana 8,
pada 13 (ed. 1947, pp. 100–101; scan PDF pp. 105–106), "anyā ca — yathārāga". GCC readings: "nava yuvatī bhule ye cule" (15.3), "vām̐kā chānde vāndhinu" — "tied it
aslant" (15.3), "candanabindu" (15.4), "bhṛṅga-pām̐ti" (15.5), "gaja-śuṇḍa" (15.6), "henakāle nim̐da bhāṅgila" (15.8). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the
section (chapter 27).
[^31-37]: The heroine adorning the Beloved with her own hands (veśa racanā) is a motif of the padas on Radha adorning Krishna; the nose-pearl (gajamuktā), the belt of
bells and the anklets are Krishna's ornaments in the padas. In Gaura-lila the Lord was adorned and anointed by His companions (cf. Gaura's abhisheka and adornment
at Srivasa's — CB, Madhya; chapter 14); here the service is transferred into a townswoman's dream. There is no motif of sambhoga in the pada.

## 16. Narahari — "śuna śuna ogo parāṇa-sai…" (GPT1 pp. 217–218, no. 138; GCC 8.14)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. A townswoman tells her friends without shame: in her dream Gora embraced and kissed her; she teased Him about the traces
of kajal, kumkum and sindur on His face, but then her harsh sister-in-law sat down at the door — the Beloved hid, and she woke; falling asleep
again, she saw Him adorning her — putting sindur in her parting, braiding her hair, putting on a bodice and a nose ornament — and laying her on
His breast. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 14.*[^31-38]

**16.1.** *(Refrain)* "Listen, listen, dear friends: before all of you, casting off shame, I will tell the night's dream.

**16.2.** Smiling, floating in joy, how tender that Playful One is with me! Opening both arms, in every way, He quickly takes me in His embrace.

**16.3.** He cannot be still — His body quivers, trembles like lightning; like a greedy bee, drunk with joy, He kisses the honeyed face.

**16.4.** That moon-like face was prettily adorned with kajal, kumkum and sindur; seeing this, I teased Him — hearing it, my Friend was abashed.[^31-39]

**16.5.** Lovingly, smiling a little, I wiped that moon-like face again; and just then my harsh sister-in-law came and sat down at my door.

**16.6.** My soul flew away — what could I do? The Friend of my life hid in fear; then my sleep broke — waking, I feel my heart pounding.

**16.7.** When I fell asleep again, that young Nagara is adorning me: He puts sindur in my parting and with what care He braids my hair!

**16.8.** When He began to put a bodice on my breast, I said: 'Why are You putting a bodice on me?' The Beloved, laughing, says: 'And the man's attire — do you not remember it?'

**16.9.** What more shall I say? Eagerly setting an ornament in my nose, He at once lays me on His broad chest.

**16.10.** In every way He tells tales of rasa — as if pouring nectar." Narahari's Lord is love embodied, the Enchanter of young women.[^31-40]

scan PDF pp. 106–107), "anyā ca — yathārāga". The first stanza is a refrain (dhru; so GPT1). GCC readings: "nilajī haiyā" (16.1), "cumbaye madane māti" — "drunk with

## 17. Narahari — "ki kava svapane kata parihāsa kare go…" (GPT1 p. 218, no. 139; GCC 8.15)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. A townswoman tells how in her dream Gora jested with her, embraced her, trembling, and spoke of rasa; the poet: "How
shameless is Narahari's Beloved — the thief of the dharma and vows of young wives!" Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC,
kirana 8, pada 15.*[^31-41]

**17.1.** "What shall I say! In the dream how He jests, my Gora, the Crown of connoisseurs of rasa! And what eyes He has — fearful are the curving glances that steal the treasure of life and youth.

**17.2.** Smiling sweetly, sweetly, floating in joy, He puts His face to my face and takes me in His embrace; His body thrills in the waves of Madana — how many words of rasa He brings up!

**17.3.** Lovingly swinging the ornament in my nose, He is — I know not by what rasa — enraptured." How shameless is the Beloved of Narahari's life — the thief of the dharma and vows of young wives![^31-42]

p. 107), "anyā ca — yathārāga". Metre — a long line with the address "go" in the middle. In GCC the pada is a line longer: in place of GPT's last line there are two
lines with more explicit details of the dream and the signature "narahari-prāṇa-priya nilaja emana go, yuvatī-varata kare bhaṅga" ("so shameless is the Beloved of

clothes", "the breaker of dharma"); transferring it to Gaura is a convention of the nagari padas which the tradition rejects: the Lord did not touch women (CB, Adi; n. 10
and the introductory note, chapter 27).

## 18. Narahari — "svapane vandhuyā mora pālaṅke vasila go…" (GPT1 p. 218, no. 140; GCC 8.16)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. In a dream the Beloved sat on her couch, called her dearer than life, embraced her, offered her betel, touched her lips;
the poet: Narahari's Beloved is the only one who enchants young women. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8,
pada 16.*[^31-43]

**18.1.** "In the dream my Friend sat on the couch, and once I glanced at Him from the corner of my eye; Gora, love embodied, with such tenderness deems Himself in my power.

**18.2.** With His moon-like lips He tells me again and again: 'You are dearer to Me than life'; saying this, He embraces me and floats in joy, while I die of shame.

**18.3.** Preparing betel, He puts it into my mouth and gazes, beside Himself with joy; then with His tendril-like hand He touches my lips — and offers His life for them.

**18.4.** Smiling sweetly, sweetly, He showers nectar — what art of a connoisseur of rasa!" The Beloved of Narahari's life, the darling of the heart, is the One who enchants young women.[^31-44]

[^31-43]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — p. 218, no. 140 (scan PDF p. 477); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 140 (catalogue: NG-112). GCC — kirana 8, pada 16 (ed. 1947, pp. 102–103; scan PDF
pp. 107–108), "anyā ca — yathārāga". GCC readings: "ām̐khi-koṇe" (18.1), "madane vibhora hayā cāya" — "gazes, drunk with Madana" (18.3; GPT "haraṣe vibhora", "beside Himself with
joy"; the GPT text is translated), "variṣe" (18.4), "narahari-prāṇa-priyā … eka janā" (18.4). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-44]: The embrace and the touching of the lips are direct motifs of sambhoga; translated exactly. "Offers His life for them" (parāṇa nichiyā deya tāya) — the rite of
nichani: giving oneself in exchange "for" the beloved (cf. the glossary). "The darling of the heart" (hiyāra putali, lit. "the doll of the heart") — an endearment.
The dream is the townswoman's imagination; the Lord did not touch women (CB, Adi); the tradition does not accept gaura-nagari (n. 10 and the introductory note,
chapter 27).

## 19. Narahari — "śunaye svapana āmā pāne cāñā cāñā go…" (GPT1 pp. 218–219, no. 141; GCC 8.17)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. In a dream Gora, gazing at the townswoman, sat down beside her, lifted away her veil, touched her chin, gazed at her face,
embraced her; the poet: where did Narahari's Beloved learn so many plays of rasa? Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC,
kirana 8, pada 17.*[^31-45]

**19.1.** "Listen to the dream: gazing and gazing at me, Gora, the thief of the life of young women, plays His pair of eyes that outdo the wagtails — enraptured by I know not what rasa.

**19.2.** Smiling, He came, sat beside me and with His own hand lifts away my veil; 'Ah, ah!' He says, touching my chin, and gazes at my face again and again.

**19.3.** What love! — in His mind there is one thing: to wear me at His neck like a necklace; when body touches body, how the play increases — young Madana is His companion.

**19.4.** How much art there is in His laying lips to lips — what shall I say? I have never heard of such a thing." Where did the Beloved of Narahari's life learn it — He knows so much of rasa?[^31-46]

(ed. 1947, p. 103; scan PDF p. 108), "kācicca — yathārāga". GCC readings: "cāyā cāyā go yuvatī-parāṇa-corā gorā", "jiniyā khañjana yuga nayana nācāya go" (19.1), "vadana

introductory note to the section (chapter 27).

softening nothing. The dream is the townswoman's imagination; the Lord did not touch women and in Navadvipa did not look at them (CB, Adi); the Gaudiya tradition does
not accept gaura-nagari (Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati; introductory note, chapter 27); according to Majumdar such GPT padas are late (here — Narahari Chakravarti).

## 20. Narahari — "ogo sai rasera bhramara mora gorā…" (GPT1 p. 219, no. 142; GCC 8.18)
*Nagari-bhava; a dream. "My Gora is a bee of rasa, the stealer of the honey of the lotus faces of young women": in the dream He sat beside her,
spoke nectarean words, touched her chin, laid His lips to hers, embraced her. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC,
kirana 8, pada 18.*[^31-47]

**20.1.** *(Refrain)* Friend, my Gora is a bee of rasa: who knows the secret heart of young women? — He is the stealer of the honey of their lotus faces.

**20.2.** "In the dream He came, sat beside me and, smiling, talks with me; I know not what nectar of rasa He pours — and the ache of ears and heart is gone.

**20.3.** With what tenderness He touches my chin — what grace in His wiles! Laying lips to lips, He does not turn His eyes away and covers my face with His palm.

**20.4.** He holds heart to heart — what more shall I say? — and His golden body trembles again and again." What does the Friend of Narahari's life know! — His love is an ocean of joy.[^31-48]

## 21. Narahari — "svapanera kathā kahite kahite uṭhila premera ḍheu…" (GPT1 pp. 219–220, no. 143; GCC 8.19)
*Nagari-bhava. As the townswomen told their dreams, a wave of prema rose: one laments that the Creator made her a woman for sorrow — she can never
gaze her fill on Gorachand; another is ready to rid herself by cunning of the fear of the elders; a third — to leave home for Gaurasundara; one
complains of the wicked tongues of Nadia, another wishes her name to be linked by rumour with Shachi's son; one calls them to go to Him at once;
and the last one's left eye twitches — a good omen, says the poet. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8,
pada 19.*[^31-49]

**21.1.** As they told their dreams, a wave of prema rose: their love is so peerless that none of them can keep composure.

**21.2.** One says: "Oh, the Creator made me a woman to suffer sorrow: never can I gaze my fill on such a Gorachand!"

**21.3.** Another says: "Oh, born a woman, one cannot fulfil the heart's desire; with all kinds of cunning I will rid myself of this fear of the elders."

**21.4.** A third says: "Let these elders perish — what have I to fear? For the treasure of my life, Gaurasundara, I will surely leave my home."[^31-50]

**21.5.** One says: "Oh, the people of Nadia are very wicked: I have never even seen the Lord of my life, and still they say so many evil things."

**21.6.** Another says: "Oh, there will be talk throughout the town of Nadia; heedless of it, I will keep the Beloved in my heart and soothe my pain."

**21.7.** Yet another says: "Oh, day and night there is one desire in my heart: let my name surely be slandered together with Sri Shachinandana!"

**21.8.** One says: "Oh, say what you will — I can bear it no longer: without Him my soul is restless; tell me, what shall I do?"

**21.9.** Another says: "Oh, let us throw fire on the brow of this family shame — come, come quickly, let us go and meet the Lord of our life right now!"

**21.10.** Yet another says: "Look, what is happening to me? — my left eye is twitching!" Narahari says: why worry? — all these are witnesses of good fortune.[^31-51]

scan PDF pp. 108–109), "yathārāga". GCC readings: "nārī haile nā pūre manera āśa" (21.3), "keha vale ogo maruka e gurujanere kisera ḍara" (21.4), "tāhā nā māniye … ghucāva

is a good omen (for a man — the right); the poet's reply: "why worry (bhāva ki lāgiyā)? — all these are witnesses of good fortune" (the sense is conjectural).

## 22. Narahari — "rajanīprabhāte aneka maṅgala…" (GPT1 p. 220, no. 144; GCC 8.20)
*Nagari-bhava. At dawn the townswomen, seeing many good omens, forgot a little the pain of their hearts; each tells whom she worships in order
to attain Gauranga: one — Ganga-devi, another — Gauri, a third — the Sun, a fourth vows to honour Old Shiva if today she sees the Beloved
without hindrance. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 8, pada 20.*[^31-52]

**22.1.** At the dawn of the night the young women, seeing many good omens, forgot a little the pain of their hearts, and joy grew in their minds.

**22.2.** One says: "Oh, I have understood: today the Creator has been gracious; whatever desire anyone has — all will be fulfilled."

**22.3.** Another says: "Oh, every day I worship this Jahnavi: by her boon I will surely attain the Lord of my life — know it."

**22.4.** A third says: "Oh, with great care I worship Gauri every day: so I will end my sorrow, meeting Gauranga, the Lord of my life."

**22.5.** Yet another says: "Oh, I worship the Sun in many ways: by his grace and boon I will soothe my heart — do not worry."

**22.6.** One says: "If today I see the Beloved of my life without hindrance — then I will worship Old Shiva with care, offering many gifts."[^31-53]

**22.7.** Another says: "I feel I shall meet Him right now." Thus, in the rapture of prema, they talk with one another.

**22.8.** All their hearts are trembling — if only they could see Sri Gaurasundara. Narahari says: ah, ah! — I take upon myself all the ills of such prema.

pp. 109–110), "yathārāga". It is followed in GCC by the short pada 8.21 (in tripadi metre: the nagaris know only Gora, He is their life and wealth; the poet prays that
the doings of the nagaris may always appear in his heart; not taken into GPT) and the colophon of the 8th kirana: "…the description of the tales of dreams". GCC
readings: "savāra" (22.2), "jāhnavī", "tāra vare" (22.3), "tem̐ha dukha dūra kariva miliyā" (22.4), "tām̐ra kṛpāvale" (22.5), "dekhiye" (22.6), "kahaye paraspare" (22.7;
GPT1 "paraśa pare" — a misprint; translated after GCC). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).

Nadia worship the demigods, praying to meet Gaura — as the gopis of Vraja worshipped Katyayani, praying for Krishna as their husband (Bhag. 10.22): the aim of their vows
is the Lord; translated as in the original.

## 23. Narahari — "rajanī prabhāte āju nava nava nāgarī yata…" (GPT1 pp. 220–221, no. 145; GCC 9.1)
*Nagari-bhava. At dawn the young nagaris, longing to see Gaura, devise stratagems — one plans tricks, another laughingly rejects them, a third
considers her mother-in-law's temper; and she, pleased by an astrologer's good words, had slept with the door unbarred and, waking at daybreak,
came to the young wives: "What are you doing here, children?" — "We are learning the tale of Lakshmi for the Lakshmi-puja," answers one; and the
mother-in-law praises them. The poet: there is nothing in the world but the desire for wealth. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably
Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 9, pada 1.*[^31-54]

**23.1.** At daybreak today all the young nagaris, in the hope of seeing Gaura, dear to their life, devise so many stratagems!

**23.2.** All of them are most clever, versed in rasa, floating in an ocean of rasa: one plans all kinds of tricks, another laughingly rejects them.

**23.3.** A third, setting aside many fears, considers her mother-in-law's temper; and she, meanwhile, is greatly pleased by an astrologer's good words.

**23.4.** In her contentment the old woman had slept with the door of the house unbarred; starting up again and again, she jumped up: "The night is over!"

**23.5.** Waking, she sees: in the east the dawn has risen; hastily leaving her bed, she came to her daughters-in-law.

**23.6.** Sweetly she asks: "Children, what are you sitting here doing?" One says: "Oh, for the Lakshmi-puja we are learning the tale of Lakshmi."

**23.7.** Hearing this, saying "good, good", she praised them many times. Narahari says: in the world there is nothing but the desire for wealth.[^31-55]

scan PDF pp. 110–111), without a raga mark; the 9th kirana opens with the heading "Again in the morning — of the goings of the nagaris of Navadvipa, their desires, darshan
and the rest". GCC readings: "prāṇapriya gaura daraśana āse" (23.1), "keha vā khaṇḍaye hāsi" (23.2), "śubha daivajña vacane haiyāche adhika prīta" (23.3), "rajanī pohāila
bali" (23.4), "nāhika kāra" — "who has it not?" (23.7). The next GPT pada (no. 146 = GCC 9.2) — the mother-in-law's account of that very astrologer, who told her to send
the young wives to Shachi-devi — opens chapter 32. B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^31-55]: The Lakshmi-puja (worship of the goddess of prosperity) and "the tale of Lakshmi" (lakṣmīra kathā, "Lakshmi-katha" — a ritual story read by women at the puja) are
the pretext with which the young wives reassure their mother-in-law; the deceiving of the elders is rendered as in the original (cf. n. 7 of chapter 30). The signature is
the poet's smile: the mother-in-law, hearing of Lakshmi, that is, of wealth, is at once content; GCC has "who in the world has no desire for wealth?".

## Summary of chapter 31

*The chapter continues the padas signed "Narahari" from section 3.2 of GPT. All 23 padas were found in Narahari Chakravarti's "Gaura-charita-chintamani"
and checked against its scan ("probably Chakravarti" — B): no. 119 (no. 1) = GCC 2.13 — Gaura in sleep speaks the words of Krishna waking Radha (not
nagari-bhava; GPT placed it in the section of nagari padas); nos. 124–125 (nos. 2–3) = GCC 7.29–7.30 — the end of the townswomen's morning tales (the
husband praising Nimai Pandita; the house of Murari Gupta); nos. 126–144 (nos. 4–22) = GCC 8.2–8.20 — the 8th kirana, "the tales of dreams": at dawn the
townswomen tell their friends their dreams of Gaura and then speak of their love and of good omens; no. 145 (no. 23) = GCC 9.1 — the beginning of the 9th
kirana. Dreams with a direct motif of sambhoga (embrace, kiss, "He did what was in His heart") are translated exactly, without additions and without
softening, each with a note: the dream is the townswoman's imagination, the Lord in His lila did not touch women and in Navadvipa did not look at them (CB,
Adi), the Gaudiya tradition does not accept the worship of Gaura as a nagara (introductory note, chapter 27). Where GCC is more explicit than GPT ("drunk with
Madana", "lay down" instead of "sat", the extra lines in no. 17), the GPT text is translated and the GCC reading noted.*

# Chapter 32. Nagari Padas — VI: the "Narahari" padas of GPT (sect. 3.2, nos. 146–168): the townswomen's daydreams and the talk of the heavenly women

*On what nagari-bhava is, the position of the tradition (Vrindavana Dasa, Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati) and the rules of translation, see the introductory note to the section of nagari padas in chapter 27; on the two poets named Narahari (Narahari Sarakara and Narahari Chakravarti) and on the attribution labels ("probably Sarakara", "probably Chakravarti", "not established"), see the introductory note to the "Narahari" appendix in chapter 17.*

## 1. Narahari — "śuna śuna vadhū eta dine vidhi…" (GPT1 pp. 221–222, no. 146; GCC 9.2)
*Nagari-bhava (a mother-in-law's speech). An elderly woman tells her daughters-in-law: yesterday an astrologer came to their house who knows what is in
everyone's mind; when she asked how good fortune might come, he told her to honour Shachi-devi, Nimaichand's mother: the dust of her feet removes the
threefold miseries, whoever sees her face at dawn knows no sorrow, and whoever reviles her is destroyed by the goddess Ugrachanda; so every morning she
should send her daughters-in-law to her house. The mother-in-law hurries the young wives off to Shachi — and they, covering their faces, make a show of
pleading their household work. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 9, pada 2.*[^32-1]

**1.1.** "Listen, listen, daughters-in-law: at last the Creator has become gracious to me! Yesterday, at the time of the day-watch, an astrologer came to our house.

**1.2.** What shall I say of his virtues — such a one, truly, I have never seen here: whatever anyone asks, he tells it all — he knows what is in a person's mind.

**1.3.** 'How will good fortune come?' I said, and clasped his feet. Seeing my anxiety, he says: 'Do not worry at all, mother.

**1.4.** In your village lives Shachi-devi — do you not know her greatness? She is supremely honoured in the world; her deeds are known to all.

**1.5.** Very easily had is the dust of her feet: whoever places it on his head will have wealth and kin — but what is great in that! — at once it removes the threefold miseries.

**1.6.** Whoever rises at dawn and sees her face floats in happiness birth after birth and never knows sorrow.

**1.7.** Whoever reviles Mother Shachi burns to death in the fire of sorrow; know for certain: the goddess Ugrachanda destroys him.

**1.8.** Therefore, instructing your daughters-in-law and giving up all guile of heart, send them with care at daybreak to the house of Sri Shachi-devi.

**1.9.** She will be gracious and bless them — and the heart's wish will be fulfilled: prosperity will grow, there will always be much happiness, misfortunes will be destroyed.

**1.10.** Know for sure: Nimaichand's mother grieves at others' grief.' Saying much like this, the worthy astrologer went on to another house.[^32-2]

**1.11.** Hearing all this I was very glad: I felt in my heart as if all ill fortune had gone.

**1.12.** So go quickly: she is my own — she calls me 'elder sister', treats me fondly, and never regards anyone as a stranger.

**1.13.** When you get there, bow to her and speak humble words: by her grace all happiness will come — this I know for certain.

**1.14.** She will say to you all: 'Stay here this morning,' — then come back early on some pretext: for I myself shall be going there."

**1.15.** Hearing the mother-in-law's most eager words, [the young wives] are overjoyed; and, to be coaxed a little more, one says very softly, covering her face with her cloth:

**1.16.** "How can we go in the morning, leaving the household work?" Narahari says: "You will come back and do it; now there must be no delay."[^32-3]

[^32-1]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 221–222, no. 146 (scan PDF pp. 480–481); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 146 (catalogue: NG-117). GCC — kirana 9, pada 2 (ed. 1947,
pp. 106–107; scan PDF pp. 111–112), "vṛddhāha — yathārāga" ("the old woman said"). The ninth kirana of GCC ("Again in the morning — the outings of the nagaris of Navadvipa,
their wishes, their darshan and so on"; it opens with GCC 9.1, no. 23 of chapter 31) tells how the mothers-in-law themselves send their daughters-in-law to Shachi-devi;
GPT omits GCC 9.3–9.5 — the mother-in-law coaxes the young wives again, they dress, bow to her and set out (9.3), the joyful procession of the young women (9.4, Vrajabuli,
raga lalita) and the first of their "wishes" — to bow to Shachi and steal a glance at Gauranga (9.5). Before 9.5 the author has a Sanskrit rubric, "their wishes
(manoratha) he relates in order": the following padas (nos. 2–12 of this chapter) are these wishes. GCC readings: "parama ānanda" (1.11), "yāha śīghra kari" (1.12),
"āsiyā karive" (1.16). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^32-2]: The astrologer's speech is a praise of Shachi-devi, the Lord's mother: so the Vaishnava biographies too honour her (CB, Adi and Madhya — Shachi as the mother of the
Lord, worthy of the whole world's reverence). The "threefold miseries" (tritāpa) — those caused by one's own body and mind, by other beings and by the forces of nature.
Ugrachanda (ugracaṇḍā) is a fierce form of Durga (Chandi); the threat to those who revile Shachi is the village astrologer's word, rendered as in the original. The
promise "will have wealth and kin — but what is great in that" (1.5) the poet puts in the astrologer's mouth so that the mother-in-law, mindful of prosperity, will
gladly let the young wives go (cf. the end of no. 23 of chapter 31: "there is nothing in the world but the craving for wealth").
[^32-3]: 1.15–1.16: the young wives, longing to see Gaura, make a show of pleading their household work "to be coaxed" — the poet's smile; rendered as in the original.
The last line can be understood either as the mother-in-law's answer or as the poet's own word ("Narahari says…"); it is left as in the original.

## 2. Narahari — "sakhīsaha sukhe śrīśacīdevīra…" (GPT1 p. 222, no. 147; GCC 9.6)
*Nagari-bhava; a daydream. On the way to Shachi's house a townswoman dreams: she will stand with her friend in Shachi-devi's courtyard and steal a
glance at Gaura; He will answer with a sly look — and she will have neither composure nor dharma left, she will tremble at Madana's arrow and strain
to embrace Gaurangachand, but her friend will hold her back by the end of her sari; the others will laugh, she will be abashed and turn away, covering
her face — and Gaura will smile. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 9, pada 6.*[^32-4]

**2.1.** "Gladly, with my friend, I shall go and stand in the courtyard of Sri Shachi-devi; unnoticed, I shall glance at Him once — and cool my eyes and heart.

**2.2.** He in turn will look at me — with the sly signal of His eyes; I shall have neither composure nor dharma left — I shall tremble at Madana's arrow.

**2.3.** My body will be wet with sweat, my hair will keep coming loose; my cloth will slip again and again — not a trace of shame will remain.

**2.4.** I shall be all too eager to embrace Gaurangachand — my friend will hold me back by the end of my sari; I shall heed her word.

**2.5.** Seeing me so, the others will laugh a good deal among themselves; understanding all that, I shall grow calm at heart, a little abashed.

**2.6.** Turning away, I shall stand again, covering my face with my cloth; the Lord of Narahari's life, seeing this, will smile with joy of heart."[^32-5]

PDF p. 114), "kācicca — yathārāga" ("and another [said]"). This is the second of the "wishes" (manoratha) of the townswomen on their way to Shachi's house (note 1):
all the padas nos. 2–12 are in the future tense ("I shall stand", "I shall glance", "He will say"), i.e. not an account of what happened but what each one pictures to
herself on the way. GCC reading: "kām̐piva madana-bhare" — "I shall tremble under Madana's weight" (2.2). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section
(chapter 27).

attraction; rendered exactly, adding nothing and softening nothing. It is the townswoman's daydream, her imagination: in the pada itself she is held back, and Gaura
only smiles. According to the biographies, in Navadvipa the Lord did not look at women or touch them (CB, Adi); the Gaudiya tradition does not accept the worship of
Gaura as a nagara (introductory note, chapter 27; Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati counts "gaura-nagari" among the apasampradayas). The padas of this cycle belong to
Narahari Chakravarti (18th c.); Majumdar regards the long GPT padas signed Narahari as late, not Sarakara's.

## 3. Narahari — "saiyera samīpe dām̐ṛāiva punaḥ…" (GPT1 pp. 222–223, no. 148; GCC 9.7)
*Nagari-bhava; a daydream (feigned mana). A townswoman dreams: at her friend's sign she will stand beside her, turned away from Gaura; unable to see
her face, He will be troubled and with the corner of His eye will ask her friend: "Why such anger? Forgive — one's own are not blamed; tell her to lift
her veil just once." The friend will entreat her, she in feigned anger will go and stand far off; Gauranga will be bathed in tears, the friend will
clasp her feet — and then, smiling, she will lift her veil and glance sidelong, giving Him supreme joy. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably
Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 9, pada 7.*[^32-6]

**3.1.** "At my friend's sign I shall stand beside her again; I shall not look at Gaura the nagara — I shall stay turned away.

**3.2.** Unable to see my face, He will be much troubled; glancing unnoticed at my friend, He will say to her with the corner of His eye:

**3.3.** 'I do not understand at all: why such cruel anger? Forgive — no one holds it against one's own.

**3.4.** Tell her to lift her veil just once, adjuring her by Me: let My eyes and heart be cooled by beholding the sweetness of that face.'

**3.5.** Understanding this, my friend will entreat me: 'Take the cloth from your face and stand there — let Gaurahari see.'

**3.6.** Hearing this, I shall pretend not to hear; then she will lift it with her own hand — but I shall stop her and in great anger go and stand far off.

**3.7.** Seeing this, Gauranga Raya will be bathed in tears; seeing that, my friend, distressed, will clasp my feet.

**3.8.** Then, smiling, I shall lift my veil and glance sidelong — I shall give the Lord of Narahari's life, the Friend, supreme joy."[^32-7]

[^32-6]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 222–223, no. 148 (scan PDF pp. 481–482); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 148 (catalogue: NG-119). GCC — kirana 9, pada 7 (ed. 1947,
pp. 109–110; scan PDF pp. 114–115). GCC readings: "keha nā laoye doṣa" (3.3), "juṛāuka nayāna hiyā" (3.4), "terachha nayāne rava" — "I shall remain [standing],

poet's signature about Gaura (cf. note 5 of chapter 31).

## 4. Narahari — "gaura nāgara rasera sāgara…" (GPT1 p. 223, no. 149; GCC 9.8)
*Nagari-bhava; a daydream. A townswoman dreams: looking at Gaura the nagara, the ocean of rasa, she will smile and talk with her friend about rasa;
seeing her wondrous grace, He will float in joy; she will signal to Him with a curved glance, bite her lip and draw her veil, and with the aim of her
brows steal away His composure; the King of connoisseurs of rasa will long to embrace her — and Narahari will restrain Him, reminding Him of what
people would say. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 9, pada 8.*[^32-8]

**4.1.** "Looking at Gaura the nagara, the ocean of rasa, with a faint smile I shall tell my friend tales of rasa.

**4.2.** Seeing my wondrous grace, He will float in joy; smiling ever so slightly, I shall signal to Him with a curved glance.

**4.3.** Understanding that, I shall bite my lip and draw my veil; unnoticed, by the aim of my brows, I shall steal away the Friend's composure.

**4.4.** The King of connoisseurs of rasa will long to embrace me — and Narahari will carefully restrain Him, reminding Him of what people would say."[^32-9]

women (CB, Adi; cf. nos. 19–20 of this chapter, where Narahari's own heroines say the same).

## 5. Narahari — "saiyera nikaṭe dām̐ṛāva ghuṅaṭe…" (GPT1 p. 223, no. 150; GCC 9.12)
*Nagari-bhava; a daydream. A townswoman dreams: she will stand beside her friend with half her face veiled and steal glances; when the Friend looks
at her with a half-smile, she will look away; out of shyness He will lower His eyes — and then from the corner of her eye she will look at the moon of
His face; He will not be able to meet her eyes, and she will keep gazing. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 9,
pada 12.*[^32-10]

**5.1.** "I shall stand near my friend, half my face covered by my veil; glancing little by little, unnoticed, I shall fulfil my heart's desire.

**5.2.** When the Friend looks at me with a half-smile, I shall understand, at once turn my eyes away and keep looking elsewhere.

**5.3.** The Beloved of my life, out of shyness, will charmingly lower His eyes; seeing that, I shall again look from the corner of my eye at the moon of His face.

**5.4.** The Restless One will not be able to meet my eyes — and I, seeing that, shall keep gazing." Narahari's Lord will float in joy as eyes meet eyes.

scan PDF pp. 117–118), "anyā ca — yathārāga" ("and another"). In GCC this pada comes after GCC 9.11 (= no. 153, no. 8 of this chapter); the compiler of GPT moved it.
"The Restless One" (cañcala, 5.4) refers to Gaura. The last line (signature) is the poet's word; it can also be read as continuing the townswoman's daydream ("…will
float in joy, His eyes meeting [mine]"). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).

## 6. Narahari — "āi more vahu yatana karive…" (GPT1 p. 224, no. 151; GCC 9.9)
*Nagari-bhava; a daydream. A townswoman dreams: Ai (Shachi) will be kind to her, but she will not stay by Ai — she will stand behind her friend and
gaze her fill at Gaura while remaining unseen; He will grow anxious and ask her friend with a sign of the eyes: "Where is your companion?"; the friend
will draw her forward and lift her veil; the Crown of connoisseurs of rasa will say with the corner of His eye: "Where did you learn these tricks? How
shall I live without seeing you?" — and Narahari will make peace between them. Raga "yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC,
kirana 9, pada 9.*[^32-11]

**6.1.** "Ai will be very kind to me — but I shall not stay by Ai: quite unnoticed, I shall stand behind my friend.

**6.2.** Supremely joyful, I shall still the hunger of many days: I shall give the chakora birds of my eyes the nectar of that moon of a face to drink.

**6.3.** I shall look my fill, but He will not be able to see me; growing anxious, He will say to my friend by a sign of the eyes:

**6.4.** 'You have come alone — where has your companion stayed? Not seeing you two together, I am pained at heart.'

**6.5.** Understanding this, my friend will take me by the hand and draw me in front of her; feigning anger, smiling slightly, I shall not go forward.

**6.6.** Even so my friend will hold me in front of her and with her own hand lift my veil, teasing me no end.

**6.7.** By a sign of the eyes she will say to the Friend: 'Look at Your own,' — and the Crown of connoisseurs of rasa, looking at me, will say with the corner of His eye:

**6.8.** 'Well, well! Where did you learn these tricks? Tell Me now: how shall I live without seeing you?'

**6.9.** He will convey much like this; understanding, I shall own my fault — and yet the Crown of connoisseurs of rasa, Gora, will still be cross with me.

**6.10.** Then Narahari will make it up: he will bring [me], show the necklace on the neck — and [He], smiling slightly, will say: 'Never do so again.'"[^32-12]

scan PDF pp. 115–116). In GCC the second line of couplet 6.6 is omitted: in its place the edition has a row of asterisks (a mark of omission); otherwise there are minor
differences ("parama ānanda haiyā", 6.2; "antare pāiye vyathā", 6.4; "vandhu prati", 6.7). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^32-12]: Ai ("mother") is Shachi-devi (cf. note 1); the townswoman dreams of being received kindly by Shachi. The silent conversation of the eyes (6.3–6.8) is what she
imagines (cf. note 5). 6.9–6.10 are understood conjecturally: who is "cross" and whose necklace Narahari will "show" (perhaps as a token of reconciliation) is not
clear from the text; GCC has "will make it up, yielding, will show the necklace on the neck" (mānāva māniyā dekhāve). The verb forms in -ba (niva, kariva) are used
here by the poet for the third person as well (the friend, Gora), for the sake of rhyme.

## 7. Narahari — "gaurāṅgacām̐dera pāne nirakhite…" (GPT1 pp. 224–225, no. 152; GCC 9.10)
*Nagari-bhava; a daydream. A townswoman dreams: gazing at Gaurangachand she will fall into a daze, be overcome, and her earring will roll on the
ground; she will hastily cover herself with her sari-end — and the jingle of her bangles will delight Him; with a glance He will ask: "Remove the cloth
— let Me see your hair"; her friend will tell her to turn away, and then herself throw the cloth off her head; Gora, enraptured, will gaze without
blinking, while she, abashed, will pull up her veil, scold her friend as "shameless" and step aside — to Gauranga's delight. Raga "yatharaga".
**Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 9, pada 10.*[^32-13]

**7.1.** "Gazing at Gaurangachand, I shall fall into a deep daze: I shall be overcome, an earring will slip and roll on the ground.

**7.2.** I shall quickly cover myself with my sari-end — with that my hand will move: hearing the jingle of the bangles on my wrist, He will be delighted.

**7.3.** With the corner of a sidelong glance Gauranga, the allure of the world, will convey: 'Remove the cloth for a moment — let Me see how beautiful your hair is.'

**7.4.** Understanding this, I shall smile slightly and cover my face with my veil; seeing me shy, He will be delighted and again convey something to my friend.

**7.5.** My clever friend will say to me: 'Stand turned away — otherwise, looking at Gauranga, you will lose all calm.'

**7.6.** At these words I shall forget myself and stand with my back to Gora — and my friend with her own hand will quickly throw the cloth off my head.

**7.7.** At that moment Gora, rapt in rasa, quite overcome, will remember nothing — He will keep gazing with unblinking eyes.

**7.8.** I, much abashed, shall hastily pull the cloth up over my head and, with outward anger, scold my friend, calling her shameless.

**7.9.** I shall go and stand a little way off from my friend — and she, owning her fault, will draw me back and hold me, swearing by my head.

**7.10.** Seeing this play of mine, Gauranga, lover of play, will again float in merriment," — and in the depths of his heart Narahari, the Friend's companion, will laugh.[^32-14]

[^32-13]: Signature — "Narahari". GPT1 — pp. 224–225, no. 152 (scan PDF pp. 483–484); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 152 (catalogue: NG-121). GCC — kirana 9, pada 10 (ed. 1947,
pp. 111–112; scan PDF pp. 116–117). Two places in GPT1 are corrected after GCC (noted in VAR): 7.2 "jhām̐piva" ("I shall cover myself"; GPT1 "kām̐pila" — "trembled",
a misprint) and 7.6 "pichu kariyā" ("turning my back"; GPT1 "kichu kariyā"). B. Nagari-bhava — see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^32-14]: Gora, enraptured and oblivious at the sight of the townswoman's uncovered head (7.7), is her daydream, as in all the padas of this cycle (note 5); rendered
exactly. A married woman's uncovered head before a strange man was by custom immodest; hence "shameless" (7.8) and the heroine's feigned indignation.

## 8. Narahari — "gaurāṅgacām̐dere nirakhi sakhīre…" (GPT1 p. 225, no. 153; GCC 9.11)
*Nagari-bhava; a daydream. A townswoman dreams: gazing at Gaurangachand and signalling to her friend, she will smile sweetly and talk with her;
swaying her head, she will loosen her hair-knot, her nose-pendant and earrings will swing; the nagara will say with a glance that He cannot see the
ornament on her back — and she, on some pretext, will lift the cloth and show it to Him; at once the Connoisseur of rasa will be overcome. Raga
"yatharaga". **Attribution: probably Chakravarti** — GCC, kirana 9, pada 11.*[^32-15]

**8.1.** "Gazing at Gaurangachand, signalling to my friend with a sidelong glance, smiling sweetly, sweetly, I shall happily make sweet talk.

**8.3.** The swinging of the jhapa on my back He will not be able to see — and the nagara, signalling with the corner of His eye, will say [so] with a slight smile.

**8.4.** On some pretext I shall lift the cloth with my left hand and show it to Him — at once the Connoisseur of rasa, the life of Narahari, will be overcome."[^32-16]

## 10. Narahari — "saiyera samīpe dām̐ṛāva nāgara…" (GPT1 p. 226, no. 155; GCC 9.14)

**10.3.** Hearing this, my friend will say: 'The fault is yours: the nagara wants to see your dear face, and you are cross at that.'

**10.4.** Hearing this, I shall speak [to Him] by a sign and smile like nectar," — Narahari will not be able to calm Him: Gora will lose all composure.

*Nagari-bhava; a daydream (reproach). A townswoman dreams: seeing Gaurangachand's smiling face, she will put her cloth round her neck, join her palms

**11.3.** What more is there to say — not once do You come and show Yourself on the road. The Creator made me a woman — hence the grief; otherwise I would stay with You.'

**11.4.** Hearing this, the Friend of Narahari's life will be abashed and, saying 'I will surely come', will swear with the corner of His eye."[^32-21]
