# Chapter 34. Nagari Padas — VIII: Lochana Dasa (22 padas from GPT, sect. 3.2, nos. 62–85, 116); concluding note to the section of nagari padas

*On what nagari-bhava is, the position of the tradition (Vrindavana Dasa, Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati) and the rules of translation, see the introductory note to the section of nagari padas in chapter 27.*

*Chapter 34 is the last of the section of nagari padas: the padas signed by Lochana Dasa in section 3.2 of the *Gaura-pada-tarangini* (GPT). There are 26
of them: nos. 61–85 (GPT1 pp. 177–189, scan PDF pp. 436–448, in one continuous block) and no. 116 (p. 204, PDF p. 463). All have been checked against the
scan of GPT1 (text and signatures), against GPT2 (same numbering, same text), the *Padakalpataru* (PK), the *Padamrita-samudra*, the
*Kshanada-gita-chintamani*, Lochana's *Chaitanya-mangala* (our translation) and the anthologies of the early twentieth century. Four
padas are not translated anew here: **no. 61** "nadīyā-nāgarī sāri sāri sāri…" = PK 2178 and **no. 66** "āra śunecha ālo sai…" = PK 2174 were translated
in chapter 28 (nos. 28 and 27); **no. 80** "ānanda nadīyāpure ṭalamala premabhare…" = PK 2088 is a passage of the *Chaitanya-mangala* itself
(Madhya-khanda: the Lord in kirtana, raga sindhura, with the refrain "The town of Nadia rejoices…"; our translation — *Chaitanya-mangala*, Madhya-khanda, part 4, vv. 110–118;
GPT gives vv. 110–114 and 118, without vv. 115–117), in content a praise of the Lord in kirtana, not nagari-bhava; **no. 84** "niravadhi gorārūpa mane
jāgiyāche go…" = PK 777, signed by **Vasu Ghosha** (translated in chapter 27, no. 16): in GPT1 the same pada also stands as no. 17 with Vasu's
signature, so Lochana's signature in no. 84 contradicts both PK and GPT itself. The remaining 22 padas are translated below (nos. 1–22).*

*Lochana Dasa (c. 1520 — ?) is the author of the *Chaitanya-mangala*, a disciple of Narahari Sarakara Thakura of Shrikhanda, a younger contemporary of
the Lord's associates; he himself did not see the Lord. The nagari motif is present in the *Chaitanya-mangala* too (the women of Nadia, forgetting
shame, hurry to look at Gaura — see our translation, *Chaitanya-mangala*, Adi-khanda, part 1, note 9; *Chaitanya-mangala*, Adi-khanda, part 10, notes 5–6); Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati,
publishing the *Chaitanya-mangala* (1922), refuses in his preface to ascribe to it "the doctrine of gaura-nagari" (the translator's preface to our translation of the *Chaitanya-mangala*). The padas
of this chapter are of two kinds: (1) padas in the literary language of the padas, in payar and tripadi metre (nos. 1–4, 15–17, 21); (2) padas in
colloquial Bengali, in short rhymed feet, with colloquial forms ("dekhalāma", "halo", "ka're") and kirtana singers' insertions in brackets (nos. 5–14,
18–20, 22) — in the manner of the playful songs traditionally connected with Lochana's name (dhāmālī, "dhamali"). The padas of the second kind are
known only from GPT (two of them — nos. 16, 17 — are also in the anthology *Prachina-vaishnava-padavali*, 1922, with Lochana's signature); their
language was probably renewed in oral transmission. None of the 22 padas is in PK or in the *Chaitanya-mangala*; Lochana's signature does not
compete with any other (except in no. 84, excluded above). The attribution rests only on the signature in GPT: Lochana is a recognized
author, but these padas have no independent witnesses (PVP, 1922, is a late anthology), hence C ("attribution by GPT only"; cf. Lochana's padas from
PK in chapter 28 — B). Where a pada builds on someone else's lines (no. 5 begins with two couplets of Jnanadasa's pada PK 748), this is noted.*

*The translation is faithful to the author, without worldly vocabulary beyond the original and without softening: where a townswoman speaks of
attraction, embraces, a dream, it is translated exactly, with a note on the position of the tradition. The Bengali text, variants and word-for-word
translation are in the full version of the book. At the end — the summary of the chapter and the concluding note to the whole section of nagari padas (chapters 27–34).*

## 1. Lochana Dasa — "gaurāṅga-taraṅge nayana majila…" (GPT1 pp. 177–178, no. 62)
*Nagari-bhava. The townswoman's eyes have drowned in the waves of Gauranga: she is ready to take disgrace upon herself and leave home; all her
household work betrays her — she knows nothing but Gora, in anyone she meets she sees Gauranga; lying with her husband, she imagines Gaurahari coming
and taking her to Himself. Raga pahida.*[^34-1]

**1.1.** In the waves of Gauranga my eyes have drowned — what now shall I choose?
Lifting the basket of disgrace onto my head, I will stay at home no more.

**1.2.** *(Refrain)* Friend, what am I to do now?
Giving myself away for Gaurangachand, I will make an end of the house.[^34-2]

**1.3.** All my household work — it is plain to everyone now: I know nothing but Gora;
seeing another, mistaking him in my confusion, I say: "Gauranga!"

**1.4.** When I lie with my husband, Gauranga awakens in my heart:
Gaurahari, my life, comes in haste and throws my husband down on the ground;

**1.5.** He takes me, places me on His breast, presses face to face;
in ecstasy Gauranga pours out nectar — it flows down over every limb.[^34-3]

**1.6.** Gauranga, the jewel, I will carefully enfold in my arms;
bidding farewell to all, I have let everything float away, — says this servant Lochana.[^34-4]

[^34-1]: Signature: "e dāsa locana" ("this servant Lochana"). GPT1 — pp. 177–178, no. 62 (raga pahida; scan PDF pp. 436–437); GPT2 — sect. 3.2, no. 62
(same text). The pada is not in PK, the *Padamrita-samudra*, KGC or the *Chaitanya-mangala*; no other witnesses have been found. On Lochana Dasa see
chapter 28, note 75, and the note at the beginning of this chapter: a disciple of Narahari Sarakara, a younger contemporary of the Lord's associates;
attribution by GPT only — C. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-2]: "Lifting the basket of disgrace onto my head" (kalaṅkera ḍāli māthāya dhariyā) — a saying: to take ill fame upon oneself openly. "Giving myself
away for Gaurangachand" (nichani laiyā) — the nichhani rite (chapter 27, note 10). "I will make an end of the house" (gṛhe samādhāna di) — lit. "I will
give the house its conclusion."
[^34-3]: The scene in 1.4–1.5 is the speaker's imagination: "Gauranga awakens in my heart," and she goes on to picture what He would do. It is translated
as in the original, without softening. This is precisely the notion of Gaura as the lover of the townswomen ("gaura-nagari") which the Gaudiya
tradition rejects: according to the *Chaitanya-bhagavata* (Adi-khanda), the Lord in this incarnation did not look at any woman; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta
Sarasvati counts "gaura-nagari" among the apasampradayas (introductory note). According to Majumdar, nagari padas known only from GPT are an
unreliable and late layer. "Pours out nectar" (sudhā ugāraye) is an image of sweetness common in padas on Krishna.
[^34-4]: "Bidding farewell to all" (tilāñjali diyā) — lit. "giving the farewell handful of water with sesame" (as to the dead): leaving for ever. "I have
let float away" (bhāsānu) is in the past tense, while "I will enfold" (laiva) is in the future; so in the original.

## 2. Lochana Dasa — "śuna śuna sai āra kichu kai…" (GPT1 p. 178, no. 63)
*Nagari-bhava. "Listen, friend: Gauranga is not a man!" Ever since the townswoman saw the moon of His face, her eyes have drowned in the ocean of
beauty; at the ghat and in the field she sees Gora, the colour of a golden filament; sitting among the elders, she remembers His face; giving herself
away for Him, she will leave everything. Raga kamoda.*[^34-5]

**2.1.** Listen, listen, friend, I will tell you more: Gauranga is not a man!
In all the world, to what can the son of Shachi be compared?[^34-6]

**2.2.** Since I saw the moon of Gauranga's face, I cannot turn away [from it]:
in that ocean of beauty my eyes have drowned, the noose of love has tightened.

**2.3.** Whether I go to the ghat or the field — I see Gora all the time, the golden filament;
the honour of family, dharma and custom — all this He has made me leave.[^34-7]

**2.4.** Sitting among the elders, I see Him with my eyes, His face comes to my mind;
I try to hold myself back — I cannot: He has thrown my soul into turmoil.

**2.5.** Giving myself away for Gaurangachand, I will leave everything.
On Lochana's mind night and day: "I will place Him in my heart."

[^34-5]: Signature: "on Lochana's mind" (locanera mane). GPT1 — p. 178, no. 63 (raga kamoda; scan PDF p. 437); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 63 (same text). No other
witnesses; attribution by GPT only — C. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-6]: "Gauranga is not a man" — a praise that agrees with the teaching: Gaura is Bhagavan Himself (CC Adi 1–4); the townswoman says it out of
amazement at His beauty.
[^34-7]: "Golden filament" (kanaka-keśara) — the colour of Gora's body is compared to the golden filaments (keshara) of a flower. Leaving "the honour of
family, dharma and custom" is a motif of the padas on the gopis (*Bhag.* 10.29) transferred to the townswomen of Nadia; it is this transfer that the
tradition rejects (introductory note; cf. chapter 27, note 43).

## 3. Lochana Dasa — "hiyāra mājhāre gaurāṅga rākhiyā…" (GPT1 p. 178, no. 64)
*Nagari-bhava (only in the address to a friend). Having placed Gauranga in her heart, the townswoman will sit in solitude and look at the moon of His
face; she has heard that He who was formerly in Gokula, in Nanda's house, has now appeared in Navadvipa, in Shachi's house. Raga kamoda.*[^34-8]

**3.1.** Having placed Gauranga in my heart, I will sit in solitude;
to my heart's content I will keep that moon of a face before my eyes.

**3.2.** I have heard: He who formerly [was] in Gokula, in the house of Nanda, —
He has come to Navadvipa and revealed Himself in the house of Shachi.[^34-9]

**3.3.** The word of Lochana: listen, friend, what more shall I tell you?
I saw the face — and the mind forgot itself: I cannot forget Him.

[^34-8]: Signature: "the word of Lochana" (locanera vāṇī). GPT1 — p. 178, no. 64 (raga kamoda; scan PDF p. 437); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 64 (same text). No other
witnesses; attribution by GPT only — C. The nagari motif is only in the address "friend": in substance this is a praise of Gaura and contemplation of Him in the heart. On
nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-9]: Gaura is the same Krishna, the son of Nanda, who has appeared in Shachi's house (CC Adi 1–4); in Lochana this thought runs through the whole
*Chaitanya-mangala*.

## 4. Lochana Dasa — "gaurāṅgavadane harila cetane…" (GPT1 p. 178, no. 65)
*Nagari-bhava. Gauranga's face has stolen the townswoman's reason: she wants to forget — she cannot. Refrain: "Gora has entered the heart; the
townswomen of Nadia have gone mad — I have understood it by myself." Seeing Gauranga's feet, a noble wife leaves her husband; whether it is righteous
or not — it is shameful even to say. Raga kamoda.*[^34-10]

**4.1.** Gauranga's face has stolen my reason — I see a great calamity has come;
I want to forget — I cannot forget; tell me, friend, what am I to do?

**4.2.** *(Refrain)* Gora has entered the heart.
The townswomen of Nadia have gone mad — I have understood it by myself.

**4.3.** As soon as I saw Gauranga's feet, He at once stole my mind;
a young noble faithful wife, whoever she may be, leaves her treasure — her husband.[^34-11]

**4.4.** I do not know whether by dharma or by karma — I am ashamed even to say;
Lochana Dasa is troubled in soul: now he too has understood what it is.

[^34-10]: Signature: "Lochana Dasa." GPT1 — p. 178, no. 65 (raga kamoda; refrain marked "dhru"; scan PDF p. 437); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 65 (same text). No other
witnesses; attribution by GPT only — C. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-11]: "Leaves her treasure — her husband" (tyaje nija patidhana) is the parakiya motif of the padas on the gopis transferred to the noble wives of
Nadia (see note 7); translated exactly. "Whether by dharma or by karma" (4.4) — i.e., one cannot tell whether it is righteous or sinful. In 4.4b the poet
speaks of himself in the third person: he too has "understood by himself" the power of Gaura's form (cf. the refrain).

## 5. Lochana Dasa — "(gaurera) rūpa lāgi ām̐khi jhore…" (GPT1 pp. 179–180, no. 67)
*Nagari-bhava. The townswoman's eyes weep for Gaura's form, each of her limbs for each of His; why did she go to the Suradhuni, why did she look at
Gaura — He pierced her with the arrows of His eyes; her eyes want to go and look, her mind wants to become His maidservant; her mind slipped on the
slippery ghat of the ocean of His beauty. She will cut open her breast and hide Him there together with her life. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-12]

**5.1.** For the form (of Gaura) my eyes weep, my mind is enraptured by His virtues;
for each [of His] limbs each of my limbs weeps.

**5.2.** For the touch of [His] breast my breast weeps;
my heart cannot hold the darling doll of my soul.[^34-13]

**5.3.** Why did I go to the Suradhuni (I went! I went!!),
why did I turn my eyes to the form of Gaura?

**5.4.** Why ever did I look at Gaura?
(Gaura) pierced me with the two arrows of His eyes.

**5.5.** My eyes say: "Let us go and look at that form";
my mind says: "I will become His maidservant."

**5.6.** He comes and goes by the path of the eyes;
He has cut through my ribs and made Himself a dwelling [there].[^34-14]

**5.7.** At the slippery ghat of the ocean that is Gaura's form
my mind went down, slipped and fell.

**5.8.** As if Gaura's form were not enough — it is steeped in love besides,
(and on top of that) a slight smile and a sidelong glance.

**5.9.** (Gaura has) as many forms as He has adornments;
oh! He! — He scorches me till my ribs are spent.[^34-15]

**5.10.** For the form (of Gaura) my eyes weep;
His virtues intoxicate my mind.

**5.11.** Not for a moment can I forget (Gaura's form);
in what an hour did I place (Gauranga's form) in my heart!

**5.12.** I will cut open this breast and hide [Him] there together with my very life;
when I wish, I will take Him out and look at the moon of His face.[^34-16]

**5.13.** At the sight of Gaura's form everyone's heart rejoices;
with joy in his heart says this Lochana Dasa.

[^34-12]: Signature: "e locana dāsa." GPT1 — pp. 179–180, no. 67 (raga "yatharaga"; scan PDF pp. 438–439); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 67 (same text). The first
two couplets (5.1–5.2) are the beginning of Jnanadasa's pada PK 748 "rūpa lāgi ām̐khi jhure guṇe mana bhora…" (PK vol. 2, 8th pallava, signature
"jñāna"; also in the *Padamrita-samudra*), where Radha weeps for Shyama; here "(gaurera)" — "of Gaura" — is added, and the whole pada is turned to
Gaura; from then on it is colloquial Bengali. Developing the opening lines of a well-known pada is a usual practice of kirtaniyas; the pada is a
composite, and its attribution to Lochana rests only on the signature in GPT (C). On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-13]: The words in brackets — "(gaurera)", "(gaura)", "(gelāma! gelāma!!)", "(tāte āvāra)", "(gaurarūpa)", "(gaurāṅgarūpa)" — are insertions of
the kirtana singers (akhar), as GPT prints them; they are translated in brackets. "The darling doll of my soul" (parāṇa putalī) — what is dearest;
PK 748 has here "parāṇa pirīti lāgi," while "parāṇa-putalī mora" is the reading of MS P-R-Sa in the PK apparatus: GPT follows it.
[^34-14]: "Made a dwelling" (karala khānā): khānā is "house, dwelling" (Pers. khana) or "pieces" ("cut to pieces"); both readings are possible.
[^34-15]: "Scorches" (bhājite) — lit. "frying"; the sense of the line is unclear, the translation is conjectural.
[^34-16]: The wish to keep the Lord's form in the heart for ever; "to cut open the breast" is a hyperbole of love poetry, known also from padas on Radha.

## 6. Lochana Dasa — "uṣaḥkāle sakhī mile jala bharite yāya…" (GPT1 pp. 180–181, no. 68)
*Nagari-bhava. At dawn a young wife goes with her friends for water and meets Gora with His friends on the road; having filled her pitcher, she stands
as if stunned and gazes: who is this — a god of rasa? Brows, eyes, nose, teeth, the colour of His body, arms, necklace, white cloth, ringing anklets;
the nagara of beauty has risen — and the mind of "the nagari Lochana" is swept away. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-17]

**6.1.** At dawn, together with her friends, she goes to fetch water;
on the road — a meeting: Gora-raya with His friends.

**6.2.** Dying at heart, I filled the pitcher and lifted it onto my hip;
the young wife stands as if stunned, beside herself, and gazes.[^34-18]

**6.3.** "Who is this — a god of rasa? there is no limit to His beauty;
what creator has gathered the treasure of rasa in one place?

**6.4.** The pair of brows — the teacher of Kama — shoots flower-arrows;
with what ink, with what brush were they made?

**6.5.** The depths of the eyes are spotless petals of a blue lotus;
the two lids, reddish, glisten moist.

**6.6.** A sesame flower — how could it compare? such is the beauty of the nose;
turned on a lathe, even — what a lustre of teeth!

**6.7.** Vermilion and orpiment were kneaded with fresh butter;
pure gold, the moon — laid on and burnished.

**6.8.** Dissolving lac-dye in milk, they moulded the hands;
they brought the moon, sifted it and sifted it — and skilfully set it there.[^34-19]

**6.9.** On His neck a necklace — how it shines! and what a splendour of arms! —
as if a golden elephant had come down from the sky to draw water.

**6.10.** Neatly girt, the white cloth adorns Him;
graceful, conquering the world, the anklets ring on His feet.

**6.11.** The nagara of beauty, the ocean of rasa, has come and risen [like the sun];
by this the mind of the nagari Lochana has been swept away."[^34-20]

[^34-17]: Signature: "the nagari Lochana." GPT1 — pp. 180–181, no. 68 (raga "yatharaga"; scan PDF pp. 439–440); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 68 (same text). No other
witnesses; attribution by GPT only — C. The pada begins as a narrative in the third person ("goes") and passes into the first ("I filled"); so in the original. On nagari-bhava
see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-18]: "The young wife" — GPT1 has "vam̐dhu" (usually "beloved, friend"); from the sense (stupor, bewilderment) it apparently stands here for vadhū,
"young wife": the speaker about herself. "Beside herself" (cauura hārā) — the meaning is conjectural. "Friends" (sakhā) — the Lord's associates.
[^34-19]: 6.3–6.10 describe the form from the brows to the feet, as in padas on Krishna: the brows are "the teacher of Kama" (they teach him to shoot), the
colour of the body is a mixture of vermilion, orpiment and butter burnished like pure gold; "the moon sifted and set" in the hands is apparently the
nails (cf. "the moons of the nails"). "A god of rasa" (rasera de) is conjectural (de = deva).
[^34-20]: "The nagari Lochana": the poet calls himself a townswoman — he sings in the bhava of a nagari, putting himself in the heroine's place. The
tradition does not accept such worship of Gaura (introductory note). "The nagara of beauty" is an epithet of Gaura in nagari-bhava (ibid.).

## 7. Lochana Dasa — "śacīra gorā kāmera koṛā…" (GPT1 p. 181, no. 69)
*Nagari-bhava. The townswoman saw Gora at the ghat: curly hair, a garland of malati round His forehead; it is distasteful even to compare pure gold
with Him. She cannot explain it to her friend: she saw Him on the way to bathe and cannot take her eyes away; the secret has stayed in her heart; awake
and asleep Gaura is in her heart. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-21]

**7.1.** Shachi's Gora — the whip of Kama — I saw on the bank by the ghat:
curly hair, round the forehead a garland of fresh malati.

**7.2.** Pure gold — it is distasteful even to compare it with His beauty;
(such) a thief of hearts, a charmer of minds, is not on earth.

**7.3.** What more are you saying, friend — how shall I explain (to you)?
(From the roof?) — going to bathe with my friends, I saw Gaura.

**7.4.** Seeing (that) form, I cannot turn my two eyes away;
how I long to see Him again!

**7.5.** What more are you saying, friend — you are well off;
but my heart's secret has stayed in my heart.

**7.6.** Awake or asleep, Gaura is always in my heart;
says Lochana: whoever has seen, he knows it.

[^34-21]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — p. 181, no. 69 (raga "yatharaga"; scan PDF p. 440); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 69 (same text). No other witnesses;
attribution by GPT only — C. "The whip
of Kama" (kāmera koṛā) is an unclear image: "whip," or, reading kom̐ṛā, "shoot"; in sense — the One stronger than Kama (cf. "Madana-mohana,"
introductory note). The insertion "(chāde)" in 7.3 — "on the roof" (?): the sense is unclear. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section
(chapter 27).

## 8. Lochana Dasa — "eka nāgarī vale didi nāite yakhana yāi…" (GPT1 pp. 181–182, no. 70)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman tells how, going to bathe, she put back her veil and saw Gaura; she ran home, but her eyes stayed with Him; her body
trembles; the ghat shines with His body, young women crowd; with the rope of anuraga He pulls her soul. She playfully warns her friend: look — and
you are lost; if you would keep the family honour, stay at home. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-22]

**8.1.** One nagari says: "Sister, when I went to bathe,
I put back my veil, raised my face — and saw Him.

**8.2.** Seeing the form, I started — and ran home;
but my two eyes stayed tied — gazing at Gaura.

**8.3.** My body trembles, all my limbs shake;
the pendant in the nose, flashing, leaps into my very heart.[^34-23]

**8.4.** The ghat is lit by the radiance of Gaura's body;
to see His beauty, crowds of young women throng.

**8.5.** I went to look out of curiosity — who knew it would be like this?
With the rope of anuraga He pulls my soul.

**8.6.** My soul longs to fly away, I cannot stay at home;
not seeing Gaurachand, I do not know what is happening to my soul.

**8.7.** Look — and your eyes will stay tied: His form steals the heart;
the smiling face, the reddish eyes — here it is, the well of rasa!

**8.8.** Look — mind you, you will die gone mad, your family honour will not survive;
if you would keep family and good conduct — stay in a secluded place.

**8.9.** You will lose your family, you will go crazy, the wave of rasa will strike."
Says Lochana: only one who knows rasa can understand this.[^34-24]

[^34-22]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — pp. 181–182, no. 70 (raga "yatharaga"; scan PDF pp. 440–441); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 70 (same text). No other witnesses;
attribution by GPT only — C. Lines 8.3 and 8.5b recur almost word for word in no. 13 (no. 75, 13.4b, 13.6) — lines common to these songs. On nagari-bhava see the introductory
note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-23]: "The pendant in the nose" (nāsāra nolaka) is apparently Gaura's ornament (cf. no. 13, 13.3, 13.6: "a pendant swings in the nose… at Gora's
laughter"); in padas on Krishna — the pearl (veshara) in His nose. Translated as in the original.
[^34-24]: 8.7–8.9 are a playful "warning" to the friend: so great is the power of the Lord's form. "Crazy" (vauri = vāurī). The motif of "losing the
family" — see note 7.

## 9. Lochana Dasa — "gorārūpa rasera kūpa sahajei eta…" (GPT1 p. 182, no. 71)
*Nagari-bhava. Gora's form is a well of rasa just by itself — and if He were to use His art, what then! Should He arrange His curls, a noble wife
could not keep her family honour; should He glance sidelong, should He ask — who could withstand? Rati herself, leaving Kama, worships Gora's feet.
The poet: "Now I have made Gora my all." Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-25]

**9.1.** Gora's form — a well of rasa — is so much just by itself;
and if He uses His art, the wiles of rasa, — what will it be then!

**9.2.** If He gracefully arranges His soft curling hair,
then a faithful, noble wife cannot keep her family honour.

**9.3.** Whomever He glances at sidelong — will her pride remain?
and if He should ask — would the rasavati survive?[^34-26]

**9.4.** With a garland on His neck, swinging His arms, He passes by —
Rati herself, Kama's wife, leaving her husband, worships Gora's feet.[^34-27]

**9.5.** Our Gora fills the breast: look — and the breast is full;
as if one held Him in one's arms — joy upon joy.

**9.6.** The stream of His smile, like nectar, cools the soul;
subject to rasa, He is (everything) all my wealth, the form of my longing.[^34-28]

**9.7.** Listen, friend dear to my heart, what more shall I say?
Says Lochana: now I have made Gora my all.

[^34-25]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — p. 182, no. 71 (raga "yatharaga"; scan PDF p. 441); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 71 (same text). No other witnesses;
attribution by GPT only — C. Couplets
9.1–9.4 recur almost word for word in no. 20 (no. 83, 20.4–20.6, 20.8) — lines common to these songs. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the
section (chapter 27).
[^34-26]: 9.2–9.3 are all in the conditional ("if"): the townswoman pictures what would happen if Gora wished to charm. Translated exactly. According to CB
(Adi-khanda), the Lord in Navadvipa did not look at women; the notion of Him as a nagara seeking the townswomen's love is rejected by the tradition
(note 3; introductory note). "Rasavati" (rasavatī) — "she who is full of rasa," the heroine.
[^34-27]: Rati is the wife of Kama, the god of love: even she would leave her husband for Gora — a hyperbole of a beauty surpassing Kama himself (cf.
Krishna's epithet "Madana-mohana," "the charmer of the god of love").
[^34-28]: "(sarvvasva)" is the GPT compiler's gloss on saravasa ("all one's wealth"); translated in brackets. "Subject to rasa" (rasavaśa) — in GPT1 joined
to "all my wealth"; it may also be understood of the speaker herself: "overcome by rasa."

## 10. Lochana Dasa — "gaura-ratana ka're yatana rākhava hiyāra mājhe…" (GPT1 pp. 182–183, no. 72)
*Nagari-bhava. The townswoman will carefully keep the jewel Gaura in her heart, put on ornaments of His colour, write "Gaura" on her body with
gorochana, walk proudly along the road repeating "Gaura," tear up her family by the roots and give shame to the fire; Gaurachand has set the snares of
rasa in every house. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-29]

**10.1.** The jewel Gaura I will carefully keep in my heart;
I will put on ornaments of Gaura's colour — whichever suits where.

**10.2.** With golden flowers in my jhapa I will tie my hair in a knot;
saying "Gaura," I will walk along the road with pride.[^34-30]

**10.3.** With golden gorochana I will write "Gaura" on my body;
saying "Gaura," I will lay my beauty and youth at [His] feet.

**10.4.** Tearing up my family by the roots, I will float it away on the waters of the Ganga;
giving shame to the funeral fire, I will go about saying "Gaura."

**10.5.** Gaurachand has set the snares of rasa in every house:
the faithful wife, leaving her husband, longs to give [Him] her body.[^34-31]

**10.6.** (You) say what you like — in the ocean of beauty everything has floated away.
Says Lochana with delight: sit and wait — you will see.

[^34-29]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — pp. 182–183, no. 72 (raga "yatharaga"; scan PDF pp. 441–442); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 72 (same text). No other witnesses;
attribution by GPT only — C.
On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).

braids; "knot" (loṭana) — a loosely tied bun. Gorochana is a yellow pigment used for tilaka; "to write the name on the body" — as Vaishnavas write the
names of the Lord with sandal paste.

"putting fire to the face of shame," as to the dead.

## 11. Lochana Dasa — "nayane nayana diye ki guṇa karila priye…" (GPT1 p. 183, no. 73)
*Nagari-bhava (a dream). Refrain: "What spell has the Beloved cast with a single glance!" A townswoman tells in tears: she had long wished to drink
the nectar of His lips and, pining, lay down at night; at midnight she dreamed that Gora was on her breast, embracing and kissing her; waking at
dawn, she reproaches the creator and cannot stay at home. The poet: do not weep — go into your own house, hold Gorachand in your heart. Raga
"yatharaga".*[^34-32]

**11.1.** *(Refrain)* Eye to eye — what a spell the Beloved has cast!
(King of exorcists, crest-jewel of sorcerers!)

**11.2.** With tears in her eyes one nagari says:
"What do I know of Gaura's love? — my body melts with rasa.

**11.3.** For many days I had the wish to drink the nectar of [His] lips;
with sorrow in my heart, brooding, I lay down at night.

**11.4.** When at midnight I was lost in sleep,
then I see — as if Gora were upon my breast.[^34-33]

**11.5.** A fresh youth, His body like fresh butter;
binding me with His creeper-arms, He says: 'Why should I let you go?'

**11.6.** Thus, my heart immersed, I was caught in a sweet torment:
His face bent down — the nectar of His lips fell into my mouth.

**11.7.** I tasted the nectar of His lips — and my thirsting soul grew cool;
after the play, in due time, the night came to an end.

**11.8.** 'Alas, alas, alas!' I cried and started up:
'Ah, creator, the treasure of rasa — why did you give it and take it away?'

**11.9.** My soul aches, my heart aches,
half my head is throbbing — I cannot stay at home."

**11.10.** Says Lochana: "Why are you weeping? Go into your own house:
deep in your heart hold Gorachand, immersing your mind in Him."[^34-34]

[^34-32]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — p. 183, no. 73 (raga "yatharaga"; refrain marked "dhru" in brackets; scan PDF p. 442); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 73 (same
text). No other witnesses; attribution by GPT only — C. "Spell" (guṇa) — the sorcery of an exorcist (ojhā): Gaura's glance as a charm. On nagari-bhava
see the introductory note
to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-33]: 11.4–11.7 are a dream with a direct motif of sambhoga (embrace, kiss, "play"); translated exactly, without softening. The dream is the
townswoman's imagination, not an event of the lila; the Lord in His lila did not touch women and in Navadvipa did not look at them (CB, Adi-khanda);
the tradition does not accept "gaura-nagari" (Bhaktisiddhanta; introductory note); according to Majumdar, such padas of GPT are a late layer. GPT1
gives under the line a variant to 11.4b: "I look — on my breast is Gora, Shachi's darling."
[^34-34]: "Go into your own house" (ḍhoka āpanāra ghara) — the poet answers the heroine: do not weep over the dream, but turn inward and hold Gora in
your heart. The same ending in no. 13 (13.13), a similar one in no. 20 (20.10).

## 12. Lochana Dasa — "hem̐i go hem̐i go gorā kene nā yāya pāsarā…" (GPT1 pp. 183–184, no. 74)
*Nagari-bhava. The townswoman cannot forget Gora: the secret came out within a couple of days; in sleep He is on her heart, even in her husband's
arms; going to bathe, she remembers Him and falls on the spot. The poet jokes: "Go and tell why your foot slipped!" Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-35]

**12.1.** Hey, hey! why can Gora not be forgotten?
Gora's form has swallowed my mind — I have become as if mad.

**12.2.** Gora has lodged in my eyes — what am I to do, friend?
The secret has come out — not even two or four days have passed.

**12.3.** In sleep and in dreams Gora is upon my heart;
even lying in my own husband's arms — what more will you tell me?[^34-36]

**12.4.** If, taking a cup of oil, I go to bathe —
Gora's form comes to mind, and I fall right there.

**12.5.** My body trembles, my limbs shake — I cannot say anything.[^34-37]

**12.6.** Night and day He wakes in my heart — what shall I say of it?
Says Lochana: "Go and tell why your foot has slipped!"

[^34-35]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — pp. 183–184, no. 74 (raga "yatharaga"; scan PDF pp. 442–443); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 74 (same text). No other witnesses;
attribution by GPT only — C.
"Mad" (vāula) — lit. "baul," possessed, "beside oneself." On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-36]: Gora is on her heart "even in her own husband's arms" — the parakiya motif transferred to the townswomen (notes 7, 11).
[^34-37]: In GPT1 and GPT2 this is a single line (with the mark ॥); its pair has apparently dropped out. "Your foot has slipped" (12.6) — the poet's joke:
the heroine has "stumbled," losing her head over Gora.

## 13. Lochana Dasa — "eka nāgarī hese vale śunago marama sai…" (GPT1 pp. 184–185, no. 75)
*Nagari-bhava. One townswoman, laughing, tells her intimate friend: they have never seen such a "man of rasa" — the pendant swings, at His laughter
one cannot be still; she went to look by chance — and He pulls her heart with the rope of anuraga; from under her veil she saw the dancer of rasa go
dancing through the bazaar of Nadia. Another answers: I will go to another land — shut the doors of this one, go to the "inner village"; a jewel
must be kept secret. The poet: go into your own house, hold Gorachand in your heart. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-38]

**13.1.** One nagari, laughing, says: "Listen, my intimate friend:
you know what is hidden, you know rasa — that is why I tell you.

**13.2.** Besides you, to whom should I speak of rasa?
Such a man of rasa as our [Gora] we have never seen.

**13.3.** How it burns, how it flashes, the pearl — a pendant swings in the nose;
I cannot be still for the waves of Gora's laughter.

**13.4.** By chance I went to look — who knew it would be like this?
With the rope of anuraga He has seized my heart and pulls it.

**13.5.** The form, the radiance of beauty — He goes along the road;
at the sight of the grace of Gaura's form my whole body starts.

**13.6.** My body trembles, all my limbs shake;
the pendant in the nose, the radiance of beauty leap into my very heart.

**13.7.** Sidelong, from under my veil, I looked at Him:
the dancer of rasa goes dancing through the bazaar of Nadia.

**13.8.** You are deep, deep sunk in rasa, while we are beggars of rasa;
you have gained in rasa the basket of rasa — young Gora!"[^34-39]

**13.9.** Another nagari says: "I will not stay in this land;
putting the garland of rasa on my neck, I will go to another land.

**13.10.** Shut the doors of this land — and I gain that land:
there is nothing to do in the outer village — let us go to the inner village.

**13.11.** The jewel of a snake — if you take it out, you may lose the jewel;
and if the snake loses its jewel, it does not live.

**13.12.** A jewel must be kept carefully, not brought out;
if you bring out the treasure of your soul, you will have to stand guard."[^34-40]

**13.13.** Says Lochana: "Why are you brooding? Go into your own house:
deep in your heart hold Gorachand, immersing your mind in Him."

[^34-38]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — pp. 184–185, no. 75 (raga "yatharaga"; scan PDF pp. 443–444); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 75 (same text). No other witnesses;
attribution by GPT only — C. Lines 13.4b and 13.6 occur almost word for word in no. 8 (8.5b, 8.3), the ending 13.13 in no. 11 (11.10). On nagari-bhava
see the introductory note to
the section (chapter 27).
[^34-39]: In 13.8 the townswoman apparently envies her friends who have seen Gora more closely: "you" are rich in rasa, "we" are its beggars; the sense of
the couplet is conjectural. "The dancer of rasa" (rasera neṭo) is Gaura in kirtana.
[^34-40]: 13.10–13.12 are images of hidden devotion: the "outer" and the "inner village," the snake's jewel (by popular belief a snake dies without its
jewel), a treasure kept secret: love for Gaura is held in the heart, not displayed; the ending agrees with this (13.13; cf. no. 11, 11.10). Translated
as in the original.

## 14. Lochana Dasa — "āmāra gaurāṅga nāce hemakiraṇiyā…" (GPT1 p. 185, no. 76)
*Nagari-bhava (only in the frame). Gauranga dances, shining like gold — the juice of prema drips from the golden tree; His gestures, the curve of His
waist, His smile; crowds of young women throng to see Him; the flood of prema flows, even Madana loses his head. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-41]

**14.1.** My Gauranga dances, shining with golden rays;
from the golden tree, drop by drop, the juice of prema falls.

**14.2.** Gestures, graceful poses, the curved waist, a smile steeped in sweetness;
looking at the form, I feel I am about to lose caste and family.

**14.3.** The wondrous bearing of the dance, the radiance of Gora's body;
to see His form, crowds of young women throng.

**14.4.** The mind is absorbed, the family drowned — the flood of prema flows;
says Lochana: even Madana loses his head — what more is there to say?[^34-42]

[^34-41]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — p. 185, no. 76 (raga "yatharaga"; scan PDF p. 444); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 76 (same text). No other witnesses; attribution by GPT only — C. In
substance a praise of Gaura's dance in kirtana; the nagari motif is in the frame (caste and family, the crowd of young women). Line 14.3b coincides with
8.4b. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-42]: "The flood of prema" is the Lord's kirtana that flooded Nadia (CB, Madhya-khanda); "even Madana loses his head" — cf. the epithet
"Madana-mohana" (note 27).

## 15. Lochana Dasa — "kivā se lāvaṇya rūpa vayase utthāna…" (GPT1 p. 185, no. 77)
*Nagari-bhava. The townswoman describes Gauranga's form: the hair, the brows — Kama's bow, the eyes; whether she dives into water or closes her eyes,
she still sees Him; she would spread her breast over all Nadia for Gauranga to dance and walk on; let them call her "disgraced by Gaura." At the end
the poet looks on from outside: Gaurachand walks through Nadia, and the townswomen's eyes, like bees, drink the honey of His face. Raga
"yatharaga".*[^34-43]

**15.1.** What loveliness, what beauty, youth in its very rising!
When one looks at Gauranga, the eyes slip.

**15.2.** Each limb is matchless — to what shall I compare it?
I only gather together my heart's longing.

**15.3.** Seeing the loveliness of the hair, the soul cannot hold;
the brows are Kama's bow, the high nose — the arrow.

**15.4.** Whomever those moving, long eyes look at —
who goes home without giving her family away for Him?

**15.5.** If I dive into the water, still I see Gora;
the three worlds are immersed [in Him] — Gora has become like the moon.[^34-44]

**15.6.** If in my heart's longing I close both eyes —
still deep in my heart I see Gaura's form.

**15.7.** Surpassing an elephant's trunk — how the arms sway!
On the heaving chest the malati garland swings.

**15.8.** I think: I will spread this breast of mine over all Nadia
and on it make Gauranga dance.

**15.9.** I think: let my heart cover all Nadia,
and Gauranga walk upon it, stepping out.[^34-45]

**15.10.** Let them, let all the people call me "disgraced by Gaura";
shame on those wives of noble families who keep their family honour!

**15.11.** Through the town of Nadia Gaurachand goes,
with moving eyes He looks to both sides.

**15.12.** The townswomen's eyes are like rows of bees:
they drink the honey of the lotus of Gaura's face, drunk and drunker.

**15.13.** Seeing their delight as they drink the lotus honey,
this Lochana Dasa joyfully sings of Gaura's virtues.[^34-46]

[^34-43]: Signature: "e locana dāsa." GPT1 — p. 185, no. 77 (raga "yatharaga"; payar metre, a couplet to a line; scan PDF p. 444); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 77 (same
text). No other witnesses; attribution by GPT only — C. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-44]: The moon, whose light floods all the three worlds and is reflected in any water — that is why the townswoman sees Gora even in the water; the
interpretation is conjectural.
[^34-45]: 15.8–15.9 — the wish that the Lord's feet should tread on one's heart: a mood of service known from the song of the gopis (*Bhag.* 10.31).
"Disgraced by Gaura" (gaurakalaṅkinī, 15.10) is modelled on "disgraced by Krishna" (kṛṣṇakalaṅkinī), as Radha is called; on the transfer of the parakiya
motif see note 7.
[^34-46]: 15.11 "He looks to both sides" is the poet's image; according to CB (Adi-khanda) the Lord in Navadvipa did not look at women (note 3). The last
three couplets are the poet's view from outside: he sees the townswomen's delight and sings of it, as he sings of Gaura's virtues.

## 16. Lochana Dasa — "ehena sundara gorā kothā vā āchila go…" (GPT1 p. 186, no. 78)
*Nagari-bhava (only in the frame). Where was such a beautiful Gora before, who brought Him to Nadia? In bhava He has gone limp, His eyes are moist with
prema; the creator made Him from the treasure of bliss. The dancer of Gokula, Kanu, was bent and crooked of heart — Radha's love straightened Him: He
it is who now sports in Nadia. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-47]

**16.1.** Where was such a beautiful Gora before, o,
who brought Him to the town of Nadia?
As soon as I looked at Gaura's form, He entered my heart, o;
my body trembles, filled with thrill.

**16.2.** In the rapture of bhava, friend, He has gone all limp, o,
His eyes glisten moist with prema;
I look and look — and it seems to me, o:
I would make Him the darling doll of my soul and keep Him.

**16.3.** Did the creator churn the treasure of bliss to make Him, o?
what a craftsman it was who shaped Him!
On the lathe of love he turned Him, o,
and turned (His) eyes with Kama's arrows.

**16.4.** The dancer of Gokula, Kanu, was bent, o,
dark and crooked was He at heart;
Radha's love has made Him straight, o, —
He it is who now sports in Nadia.[^34-48]

**16.5.** The secret of my heart — to whom shall I tell it, o?
as if a thief had stolen my heart;
Lochana dies of thirst, seeing that form, o:
the creator has cheated me.

[^34-47]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — p. 186, no. 78 (raga "yatharaga"; tripadi; scan PDF p. 445); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 78 (same text). The pada is also in the *Padamrita-sindhu (Prachina-vaishnava-padavali)*, vol. 1 (collection of Chandranatha Bandyopadhyaya, publ. 1922; hereafter PVP), p. 114, with the same
signature and with an extra stanza after 16.4 (see note 48); PVP is a late anthology, not an independent witness; attribution by GPT only — C. "O"
(go) at the ends of the half-lines is a refrain exclamation. On nagari-bhava see the
introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-48]: Stanza 16.4 is the heart of the pada: Gaura is the same Krishna, the "bent" (tribhanga) and "crooked" Kanu of Gokula, whom Radha's love has made
"straight": He has taken Radha's bhava (CC Adi 4). PVP: "Kanu, Nanda's son, was bent in Gokula… by Rai's love He was tamed" (damana karila), followed by
an extra stanza: "Thinking of Radha's form, Gora became a golden body; formerly this turned into a gift of prema; whose heart does not drown in His
deeds — shame on him!" "The darling doll of my soul" (16.2) — what is dearest (note 13).

## 17. Lochana Dasa — "śāradacandrikā svarṇa dhik campakera varṇa…" (GPT1 p. 186, no. 79)
*A praise of Gaura's form (in content not nagari-bhava: the nagari motif is only the address "friend"). Neither gold nor moonlight, nor champaka, nor
precious stones, nor lightning compare with Gora: all these are forms of the world of prakriti, while He is the king of rasa beyond the world; He can
be compared only with Himself. As a bird flies in the sky as far as its strength allows, so the poet sings of Him. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-49]

**17.1.** Autumn moonlight, gold — shame on the colour of the champaka, on the red shona flower, on gorochana!
Orpiment — what a trifle, a modification of clay — can it compare with Gora's form?

**17.2.** Shame on the moonstone — how should its colour be reckoned? — on the serpent's jewel and on lightning!
All these are forms of the world of prakriti; He is the king of rasa beyond prakriti: to what shall I compare Him?[^34-50]

**17.3.** All the descriptions you see are only uddipana by likeness: who can describe Gaura's form?
Do you not know: that very Gora, taking a body in earthly form, drives away steadfastness by His mere sight?

**17.4.** Listen, o dear friend: where in the world is a comparison? to what then shall I compare Him?
There is no comparison in the world; He who is comparable only to Himself — why mix nectar with poison?

**17.5.** Who can sing His virtues, who can find their end, who can describe His form?
The form cannot be described, who can tell the virtues? — thinking of this, the mind has gone mad.

**17.6.** As a bird in the sky learns nothing [of its end], flying as far as its strength allows,
so of Gauranga's beauty [the end] cannot be known: as far as he is able, this Lochana sings.[^34-51]

[^34-49]: Signature: "e locana." GPT1 — p. 186, no. 79 (raga "yatharaga"; tripadi; scan PDF p. 445); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 79 (same text). The pada is also in PVP (vol. 1, pp. c. 122–123; see note 47), with Lochana's signature: the stanzas in a different order, with variants and with an extra opening stanza
("The colour of Gaurangachand surpasses the gold of the Jambu river — so the great describe it; since my birth I have nowhere seen the gold of the
Jambu: in my heart is the vision of Gauranga"); PVP is a late anthology, not an independent witness; attribution by GPT only — C. In the GPT section of nagari padas the pada stands because of the address to a friend; on
nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-50]: "Forms of the world of prakriti" (prapañcarūpa): everything poets compare with belongs to the material world (prapancha); Gaura is "the king of
rasa beyond prakriti" (aprapañcarasabhūpa): His form is not material. The thought agrees with the teaching: the Lord's body is eternity, knowledge and
bliss (CC Adi 4 and elsewhere). Shona is a red flower; gorochana and orpiment are yellow pigments; "the serpent's jewel" is the gem in a snake's hood
(cf. note 40).
[^34-51]: "Uddipana" (uddīpana) — in the teaching on rasa, the "kindling" causes of feeling: the poets' comparisons only kindle feeling, they do not
describe Him. "Taking a body in earthly form" (dharārūpe aṅgadharā) — the interpretation is conjectural. "As far as he is able" (anusāre) — as a bird
flies in the boundless sky as far as its strength allows.

## 18. Lochana Dasa — "(hem̐i go hem̐i go) sai tore virala peye kai…" (GPT1 p. 187, no. 81)
*Nagari-bhava (a dream). Finding her friend alone, the townswoman tells her dream: Shachi's Gora, with a garland of malati and a thin sacred thread,
came up smiling, put a garland on her neck, wiped her face with His cloth, took her hand — as her heart had wished; Gora's love is like gold, it cannot
be forgotten. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-52]

**18.1.** (Hey, hey!) Friend, finding you alone, I will tell you:
lying asleep, I saw Shachi's Gora in a dream.

**18.2.** A malati garland lights up His neck, a thin sacred thread on His shoulder;
how many streams, like nectar, flow over the moon of His face!

**18.3.** Smiling, He comes near and puts a garland on my neck;
what He did, I am ashamed to tell: how many wiles He knows!

**18.4.** With His own cloth He wipes my face and gazes again;
taking my hand, He caresses me — just as my heart desired.[^34-53]

**18.5.** Gora's love is like gold: I cannot forget it.
Says Lochana: "Sit in solitude — come here, I die of grief."

[^34-52]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — p. 187, no. 81 (raga "yatharaga"; scan PDF p. 446); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 81 (same text). No other witnesses; attribution by GPT only — C. "(Hey,
hey!)" is an insertion in brackets (cf. no. 12, 12.1). The sacred thread — Gaura as a young brahmana, before the sannyasa. On nagari-bhava see the
introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-53]: 18.3–18.4 are a dream with the motif of sambhoga (a garland on the neck — the sign of being chosen, "what He did, I am ashamed to tell,"
caresses); translated exactly. The dream is the townswoman's imagination; see note 33. 18.5b — the sense is conjectural: the poet apparently shares the
heroine's longing.

## 19. Lochana Dasa — "hera āya go manera kathā virala peye kai…" (GPT1 p. 187, no. 82)
*Nagari-bhava. The townswoman calls her friend: in the late afternoon she went to see Shachi's son — a moon anointed with sandal, a sandal mark on the
forehead, a snare for the heart; out of shame she held herself back, but, seeing His long eyes, she could not come away. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-54]

**19.1.** Come here, friend — finding you alone, I will tell what is on my heart:
in the late afternoon I went to see the son of Shachi, friend.

**19.2.** A moon anointed with sandal, o friend! A moon anointed with sandal:
the sandal mark on His forehead — a snare to catch the heart.

**19.3.** Out of decorum and shame I at once held myself back;
but, seeing those long eyes, friend, — could I come away?

**19.4.** At the sight of Gaura's form the heart rejoices;
with joy in his heart says this Lochana Dasa.

"The son of Shachi" (śacīra rāya) — lit. "Shachi's Raya." The ending 19.4 nearly coincides with 5.13. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the

## 20. Lochana Dasa — "mukha jhalamala vadana-kamala dīghala ām̐khi duṭi…" (GPT1 p. 188, no. 83)
*Nagari-bhava. The townswoman describes Gaura: the radiant lotus face, the long eyes, the reddish soles; walking, swaying, He leans on His friends;
once He glanced at her from the corner of His eye — and the doe of her heart was caught in the snare of His brows. Then come couplets shared with
no. 9; others seek Him by austerity through many births, while she keeps Him in her heart. The poet: hold the nagara Gora captive in your heart. Raga
"yatharaga".*[^34-55]

**20.1.** A radiant face, a lotus face, two long eyes;
seeing them, millions of wagtails are in shame and sorrow.

**20.2.** On His soles the dawn plays, lotuses shine on them;
walking, walking, swaying, swaying, He leans on His friends.[^34-56]

**20.3.** From the corner of His eye He once glanced at me —
the doe of my heart was caught in the snare of His brows.

**20.4.** Gaura's form — a well of rasa — is so much just by itself;
if He uses His art, the wiles of rasa, — what will it be then!

**20.5.** If He gracefully arranges His soft curling hair,
then a faithful, noble wife cannot keep her family honour.

**20.6.** Whomever He calls with a sidelong glance — will her pride remain?
and if He should ask — would the rasavati survive?

**20.7.** If He smiles — what heaps of diamonds appear!
Eyes, mind, the treasure of the soul — who will take them back? come!

**20.8.** With a garland on His neck, swinging His arms, He passes by —
Rati herself, Kama's wife, leaving her husband, worships Gora's feet.

**20.9.** [Others] practise harsh austerity and japa, wandering birth after birth;
but I, keeping [Him] in my heart, giving my life, gaze at Him to my fill.

**20.10.** Says Lochana: "Why are you brooding? Stay in your own house:
deep in your heart hold the nagara Gora captive."[^34-57]

20.8 = no. 9, 9.1–9.4 (in 20.6 "whom He calls," yāre ḍāke, instead of "whom He looks at," yām̐re dekhe); on the motifs of these couplets see notes 26–27.
On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-56]: Gaura, swaying in bhava, leans on His associates — as in the descriptions of His kirtana (CB, Madhya-khanda). "He glanced at me" (20.3) is how it
seems to the heroine; according to CB (Adi-khanda) the Lord did not look at women (note 3). The wagtail (khañjana) is an image of restless eyes.
[^34-57]: 20.9 contrasts austerity and love: others seek Him by harsh feats through many births, while she has found Him by keeping Him in her heart. 20.10
is the same turn inward as in nos. 11 and 13 (11.10, 13.13); "the nagara Gora" is an epithet of nagari-bhava (introductory note). 20.7b — the sense is
conjectural.

## 21. Lochana Dasa — "navadvīpanāgarī āgari gorārase…" (GPT1 p. 189, no. 85)
*Nagari-bhava. A townswoman of Navadvipa, foremost in the rasa of Gora, floats in tears of prema as she speaks of Gauranga; in her ears, eyes and
mind — Gora; she writes His name on her body with gorochana and performs puja to Him in her mind: tears are the abhisheka, love the naivedya, words the
betel, the radiance of her body the lamp, the jingling of her bangles the bell; her anuraga grows day by day. The poet: at last the thorn of knowledge
is gone. Raga "yatharaga".*[^34-58]

**21.1.** A townswoman of Navadvipa, foremost in the rasa of Gora,
speaking of Gauranga, floats in tears of prema.

**21.2.** Overflowing with bhava, the loving one is beside herself with thrill:
in her ears, in her eyes, in her mind — Gora, Gora, Gora.

**21.3.** Gora's form and virtues she wears as ornaments in her ears;
day and night she knows nothing but Gora.

**21.4.** She thickly anoints her body with gorochana
and carefully writes Gora's name on it.

**21.5.** Making a little figure of gorochana and turmeric,
she worships it with the water of her eyes, offering the flower of her life.

**21.6.** From her loving eyes tears of prema stream —
with them she performs the abhisheka of Gora's reddish feet.

**21.7.** Love is her naivedya, her words the betel;
she serves with the bhava fitting the hour.

**21.8.** With the radiance of her body as the lamp she performs arati;
the jingling of her bangles is the bell; her joy grows ever greater.

**21.9.** The fragrance of her body — incense and fragrant smoke — rises in anuraga;
having done the puja, she begs for the rasa of seeing and touching [Him].[^34-59]

**21.10.** Day by day her anuraga grew;
says Lochana: at last the thorn of knowledge is gone.[^34-60]

[^34-58]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — p. 189, no. 85 (raga "yatharaga"; payar metre, a couplet to a line; scan PDF p. 448); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 85 (same text). No
other witnesses; attribution by GPT only — C. On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-59]: 21.5–21.9 are a mental puja (manasa-puja): all the articles of worship come from the feelings and body of the loving one: tears are the water of
the abhisheka, love the naivedya, words the betel, the radiance of the body the arati lamp, the jingling of bangles the bell, the fragrance of the body
the incense. The little figure of gorochana and turmeric (putalī) is an image of Gaura made by herself; translated as in the original. The request "to
see and to touch" (daraśa-paraśarasa) is a motif of nagari-bhava (introductory note).
[^34-60]: "The thorn of knowledge" (jñānaśela) — knowledge (jnana) that obstructs love like a splinter; as anuraga grows it goes away — the thought of
the superiority of bhakti over jnana (cf. CC Madhya 19 — pure bhakti, "not covered by knowledge and karma").

## 22. Lochana Dasa — "gorāpade sudhāhrade mana ḍuvāye thāki…" (GPT1 p. 204, no. 116)
*A praise of Gaura (the nagari motif is only in the address "mother"). The poet keeps his mind immersed in Gora's feet as in a lake of nectar; refrain:
"Such a Gora, rapt in rasa, I have never seen anywhere." In the midst of Nadia He has come in the guise of a devotee, covered with Radha's form;
steady, calm, self-controlled — meditate on Gora in your heart. Raga suhai.*[^34-61]

**22.1.** In Gora's feet, a lake of nectar, I keep my mind immersed;
opening the doors, opening my eyes, I gaze at Gorachand.

**22.2.** *(Refrain)* Ah, mother!
Such a Gora, rapt in rasa, I have never seen anywhere.

**22.3.** In the midst of Nadia, in the guise of a devotee, He has come in the dress of rasa;
Gora, covered with Radha's form — how He enchants with rasa![^34-62]

**22.4.** The radiance of His beauty is like ground lightning; His form enchants the world;
Gora's form is the king of the world: no one can forget it.

**22.5.** Steady, calm, self-controlled even in rasa — if you see Him even from the corner of your eye…
Says Lochana with joy: meditate on Gora in your heart.[^34-63]

[^34-61]: Signature: "Lochana." GPT1 — p. 204, no. 116 (raga suhai; refrain marked "dhru"; scan PDF p. 463), among the padas of Vasu Ghosha (nos. 111–115) and
before the padas of Jnanadasa (nos. 117–118); GPT2 — 3.2, no. 116 (same text). No other witnesses; attribution by GPT only — C. "Ah, mother!" (āi go māi) is an exclamation in
women's speech (chapter 29, glossary). On nagari-bhava see the introductory note to the section (chapter 27).
[^34-62]: "In the guise of a devotee" (bhakta sāje) and "covered with Radha's form" (rādhārūpe mākhā) are an exact formula of the teaching: Gaura is
Krishna, who has taken the form of a devotee and the bhava and radiance of Radha (CC Adi 1.5; Adi 4). "The dress of rasa" — His form as the one who
tastes rasa.
[^34-63]: "Steady, calm, self-controlled" (dhīra śānta dānta) — so the tradition too sees Gaura (CB, Adi-khanda, on the Lord's strictness). "Ground
lightning" (vijurī vāṭā) — the interpretation is conjectural. "Opening the doors" (22.1) — cf. the "inner village" of no. 13 (13.10).

## Summary of Chapter 34

*Chapter 34 completes the nagari padas of Lochana Dasa: of the 26 padas with his signature in section 3.2 of GPT, 22 are translated here (nos. 62–65,
67–79, 81–83, 85, 116; records pad-0735…0756); nos. 61 and 66 (= PK 2178, 2174) were translated in chapter 28; no. 80 (= PK 2088) is a passage of the
*Chaitanya-mangala* (Madhya-khanda, part 4, vv. 110–118), no. 84 (= PK 777) is a pada of Vasu Ghosha (chapter 27, no. 16; in GPT1 it
stands twice — as no. 17 with Vasu's signature and as no. 84 with Lochana's). All 22 padas are known only from GPT (nos. 16, 17 also from PVP, 1922, with
the same signature); all are C: attribution by GPT only (the signature of a recognized author, but without independent witnesses; PVP, 1922, is a late
anthology); no. 5 begins with two couplets of Jnanadasa's pada PK 748. In content: the purvaraga and anuraga of the townswomen (nos. 1–2, 4–10, 12–13, 15, 19–21); an imagined meeting and dreams with the
motif of sambhoga (no. 1 — a fancy beside her husband; nos. 11, 18 — dreams); praise of Gaura's form and dance, where the nagari motif is only in the
frame or the address (nos. 3, 14, 16) or absent in content (nos. 17, 22). Separate notes on attraction and sambhoga — 3, 26, 31, 33, 53; on the motif
of "leaving family and husband" — 7, 11, 36, 45; on the Lord's looking at women — 26, 46, 56. Many of Lochana's padas end with a turn inward — "go into
your own house, hold Gora in your heart" (nos. 11, 13, 20; cf. nos. 3, 22), and in several the teaching is voiced directly: Gaura is the same Krishna,
"straightened" by Radha's love (16.4); His form is beyond prakriti (17.2); He has come in the guise of a devotee, covered with Radha's form (22.3).
Doubtful places: the meaning of a number of colloquial words (5.6, 5.9, 6.2, 6.3, 7.1, 7.3, 13.8, 15.5, 18.5, 20.7, 22.4) — translated conjecturally,
with notes; line 12.5 has no pair (lost in GPT).*

## Concluding Note to the Section of Nagari Padas (Chapters 27–34)

*1. **How many and whose.** The section contains 183 padas in eight chapters: Vasu Ghosha — 40 (chapter 27 — 25 padas from PK; chapter 28 — 15 padas
known from GPT); Nayanananda — 5; Yadunandana — 6 (the cycle of the 12th wave of the *Bhakti-ratnakara*, chapter 29; one signed "Yadu"); Yadu — 2;
Murari — 2 (Murari Gupta by the GPT signature and Dasa Murari); Balarama Dasa — 1; Chandrashekhara — 1; Lochana Dasa — 24 (two padas from PK in
chapter 28 and 22 from GPT in chapter 34); "Narahari" — 102 (chapters 29–33; nearly all by Narahari Chakravarti; their concluding note is at the end of
chapter 33).*

*2. **Attribution** (scale — see the preface). **A — 30**: 26 padas of Vasu Ghosha (25 from PK and one confirmed by the *Kshanada-gita-chintamani*) and 4
padas of Nayanananda from PK. **B — 90**: "probably Chakravarti" — 81 (75 found in the *Gaura-charita-chintamani*, 6 only in the
*Bhakti-ratnakara*), Yadunandana — 6, Lochana Dasa — 2 (padas from PK, chapter 28), Vasu — 1 (GPT and the *Gita-chandrodaya*). **C — 62**: Lochana Dasa —
22 (chapter 34: signature only in GPT, without independent witnesses — "attribution by GPT only"), "Narahari" — 21 (padas only from GPT;
some stand in place of the lost pages of GCC), Vasu — 12 (GPT only), Nayanananda — 1, Yadu — 2, Murari — 2, Balarama — 1, Chandrashekhara — 1.
**D — 1** (a pada signed Vasu, according to Majumdar a reworking of a pada on Krishna; chapter 28, no. 13). The earliest and most reliable layer is the
padas of Vasu Ghosha and Nayanananda from the *Padakalpataru*; the rest is a poetic development of the nagari motif: Lochana Dasa (a disciple of
Narahari Sarakara), Yadunandana (a disciple of Gadadhara Dasa) and, most of all, Narahari Chakravarti (first half of the eighteenth century).*

*3. **Who speaks.** In the great majority of padas the townswomen of Nadia speak — to a friend, to themselves, to the elders; in 25 "Narahari" padas
(GPT 3.2 nos. 158–180 and 3.1 nos. 129–130 = GCC, kiranas 10–11) heavenly women speak, who only look at Nadia from the sky; in a few, the poet himself,
putting himself in a townswoman's place ("the nagari Lochana," 34/6.11) or looking on from outside (34/15.11–15.13). Not nagari-bhava in content — 6
padas: Gaura's words in sleep in the words of Krishna (31/1), the heavenly women's replies praising the Lord's strictness (32/19–20, 33/3), Lochana's
praise of Gaura's form (34/17, 22); in a number of other padas the nagari motif is only the address "friend" or the frame (28/1, 34/3, 14, 16 and
others). Three padas are laments after the Lord's sannyasa (in 28/15 the speaker is probably Vishnupriya — then it is a lament of separation, not nagari-bhava), four are the women's words at His wedding.*

*4. **What the corpus shows.** The nagari padas speak of Gaura in the language of purvaraga and anuraga from the padas on Radha and the gopis: deceiving
the elders, "leaving family and husband," dreams of a meeting. The later the layer, the more outspoken the motif: in Vasu Ghosha (PK) it is mostly
admiration and longing; in the "Narahari" padas from GCC and in Lochana's colloquial padas — dreams with embraces and direct words of attraction. Yet
even in them Gaura in the lila itself does not respond to attraction: He passes by, dances in kirtana, leans on His associates; the "meeting" happens
only in the heroine's dream and fancy; in Narahari Chakravarti the Lord turns away and hurries off, and Lochana ends many padas with a call to "go into
your own house" and keep Gora in the heart and voices the teaching directly (34/16.4, 17.2, 22.3).*

*5. **The position of the tradition** (briefly). The Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition does not accept the worship of Gaura in the mood of the nagaris.
Vrindavana Dasa (*Chaitanya-bhagavata*, Adi-khanda) testifies that the Lord in this incarnation did not look at any woman and that the wise do not
glorify Him as "Gauranga-nagara"; Krishnadasa Kaviraja (*Chaitanya-charitamrita*, Adi 1.5–6; Adi 4) reveals that Gaura is Krishna Himself in the bhava
and radiance of Radha, who came to taste Her love as a devotee, not as an enjoying hero; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati counts "gaura-nagari" among
the apasampradayas — and, publishing Lochana's *Chaitanya-mangala*, refuses to ascribe this doctrine to it. The nagari padas have been translated for
the completeness of the corpus of padas on Gaura and as a historical document — faithfully to the author, without worldly vocabulary beyond the
original and without softening, with notes on the position of the tradition; they are not a basis for worshipping Gaura as a nagara (introductory
note, chapter 27).*
